[2026-06-13T17:57:36.100Z] [INFO]       "content": "# Case Study: Issue #41 — How can the performance of the in-browser VM be improved?\n\nIssue: <https://github.com/link-foundation/rust-web-box/issues/41>\n\nPR: <https://github.com/link-foundation/rust-web-box/pull/42>\n\n## Summary\n\nThe reporter opened the deployed app\n(<https://link-foundation.github.io/rust-web-box/>), ran `cargo run`\ntwice, and captured the timings\n([`evidence/issue-screenshot.jpg`](./evidence/issue-screenshot.jpg),\ntranscribed in [`evidence/terminal-transcript.md`](./evidence/terminal-transcript.md)):\n\n```text\nroot@rust-web-box:/workspace# cargo run\n    Finished `dev` profile [unoptimized] target(s) in 23.96s    # no-op, nothing compiled\n     Running `target/debug/hello`\nHello, world!\nroot@rust-web-box:/workspace# cargo run                          # after a one-line edit\n   Compiling hello v0.1.0 (/workspace)\n    Finished `dev` profile [unoptimized] target(s) in 6m 04s\n     Running `target/debug/hello`\nHello, rust world!\n```\n\n**A one-line edit to a single-file, zero-dependency crate takes 6 min\n04 s to rebuild**, and even a *no-op* `cargo run` takes 24 s. The same\nbuild is `<0.3 s` natively.\n\nThis document was **redone from measurement, not assumption.** Every\nclaim below is backed by a number from a reproducible experiment on the\n*exact* i386 Alpine toolchain the disk ships\n([`experiments/issue-41/`](../../../experiments/issue-41/)), plus\nopt-in tracing added to the WebVM itself so the same numbers can be taken\nin the browser, on the real VM\n([How to measure it in the browser](#how-to-measure-it-in-the-browser-the-tracing-we-added)),\nplus the project's own end-to-end CI, which boots the real CheerpX VM and\ntimes a real edited `cargo run`\n([Measurement 4](#measurement-4--the-decisive-test-the-real-vm-overturns-the-native-proxy)).\n\n**The short answer to \"what can we actually do to speed up the real\nbuild, with no workaround or hack?\"**\n\n> The 6 minutes is **filesystem-syscall** time, not CPU time: under\n> CheerpX every syscall crosses the WASM/JS boundary into the IndexedDB\n> overlay, and a hello-world rebuild issues ~14,700 of them. The **lean\n> dev profile + warm pre-bakes already shipped for issues #17/#31**\n> (`debug = 0`, `codegen-units = 1`, `incremental = false`, plus a\n> baked debug *and* release `target/`) are what already cut the **real**\n> in-browser rebuild from the reported minutes to **~58 s** — proven, not\n> assumed, by the end-to-end CI below. On top of that this PR ships a\n> **`cargo check` fast-feedback path** (sub-second error checking, baked\n> and surfaced as a task) and the **in-VM tracing** the review asked for.\n\n> **The one change that looked like the headline fix — swapping the\n> linker from GNU `ld` to `lld` — was investigated, measured, and then\n> *rejected*.** On native i386 it cuts the rebuild's filesystem syscalls\n> by **85 %** (14,736 → 2,157), which is exactly the cost CheerpX\n> multiplies, so it looked decisive. But when measured **in the real\n> VM** (the issue's own \"is it fake?\" requirement, enforced by the e2e),\n> `lld` *regressed* the edited `cargo run` from **~58 s to a >180 s\n> timeout**: CheerpX must x86→WASM-JIT the much larger LLVM linker on\n> first use, and that cold-JIT cost dwarfs the syscall saving. **Native\n> syscall count was the wrong proxy for in-VM wall-clock.** This is the\n> central lesson of the case study, and the in-VM test is what caught it.\n\nThe larger architectural win — moving `target/` off the IndexedDB overlay\n(S2), which also unblocks re-enabling incremental compilation (S3) — is\nspecified and measured here as the recommended follow-up.\n\n## What we can actually do to speed up the *real* build (direct answer)\n\nRanked by **measured in-VM effect** (the metric that matters is real\nin-browser wall-clock on the live disk — see why native syscall count\nalone is *not* sufficient in\n[Measurement 4](#measurement-4--the-decisive-test-the-real-vm-overturns-the-native-proxy)):\n\n| # | Change | What it does to the **real** `cargo run` | Measured effect | Status |\n|---|--------|------------------------------------------|-----------------|--------|\n| **S1** | **Lean dev profile + warm pre-bakes** (`debug = 0`, `codegen-units = 1`, `incremental = false`; baked debug *and* release `target/`) | Removes debug-info IO and extra codegen units, and lets cargo's freshness check finish without re-allocating overlay inodes | Real in-VM edited `cargo run` at **~58 s** (CI-measured), versus the reported minutes | ✅ Shipped in #17/#31; **verified in-VM here** |\n| **C1** | **`cargo check` fast-feedback path** (baked fingerprint + `cargo check (fast)` task) | Skips codegen *and* linking, so errors surface in seconds; complements — does not replace — `cargo run` | **1,029** vs 14,736 filesystem syscalls | ✅ **NEW in this PR** |\n| **S2** | **Move `target/` off the IndexedDB overlay** (in-memory/tmpfs build dir) | Makes every *remaining* artifact syscall RAM-fast instead of IndexedDB-slow, and stops allocating fragile overlay inodes | Removes Factor-1 IO and **unblocks S3** | Proposed (specified + measured rationale) |\n| **S3** | **Re-enable incremental compilation** (`CARGO_INCREMENTAL=1`) | Restores the normal \"I changed one line\" accelerator that #17 had to disable for the wedge | Only safe **after S2** removes the fresh-inode wedge | Proposed (depends on S2) |\n| **S4** | **Track CheerpX upstream** (JIT/FP-vector, persistent translation cache) | Lowers the per-syscall and cold-`rustc` interpretation cost at the engine layer | Free speed as the engine improves | Ongoing |\n| **✗** | ~~**Link with `lld`** instead of GNU `ld`~~ | Fewer linker syscalls, but CheerpX must cold-JIT the much larger LLVM linker | **−85 % native syscalls but +163 s in-VM** (58 s → >180 s timeout) | ❌ **Investigated, measured, REJECTED** (see [below](#rejected-after-measurement--link-with-lld)) |\n\nEverything else (cranelift backend, `wasm32-wasi` host `rustc`, boot\ntrims) is real but either blocked on our toolchain or orthogonal to the\n6-minute rebuild — catalogued honestly in\n[Solution catalogue](#solution-catalogue).\n\n## Evidence collected\n\n| File | Purpose |\n|------|---------|\n| [`evidence/issue.json`](./evidence/issue.json) | Full GitHub issue payload (`gh issue view`). Labels: `documentation`, `enhancement`, `question`. |\n| [`evidence/issue-comments.json`](./evidence/issue-comments.json) | Issue comments via the API — empty at capture; the body + screenshot are the whole report. |\n| [`evidence/issue-screenshot.jpg`](./evidence/issue-screenshot.jpg) | The reporter's screenshot: VS Code Web, `main.rs` edited to `\"Hello, rust world!\"`, terminal showing the 23.96 s no-op and 6 m 04 s rebuild. |\n| [`evidence/terminal-transcript.md`](./evidence/terminal-transcript.md) | Verbatim transcription + the two-run analysis that anchors the root cause. |\n| [`../../../experiments/issue-41/`](../../../experiments/issue-41/) | **The measurement rig.** `Dockerfile.measure` mirrors the shipped i386 disk; `measure.sh`/`measure-syscalls.sh`/`measure-linker.sh` produce the numbers in `results/` (wall-clock by profile, syscall census, the GNU `ld` vs `lld` comparison). `results/in-vm-ab.md` records the decisive in-VM e2e A/B. |\n| [`online-research.md`](./online-research.md) | Cited online research on CheerpX overhead, single-core execution, and Rust compile-time levers. |\n\n## Is the VM real? (anti-fake verification)\n\nThe issue explicitly asks us to \"double check that our solution is not\nfake, and we actually use [a] virtual machine to execute commands.\" The\nevidence is conclusive on **both** directions — and this requirement did\nreal work: it is exactly the in-VM check that caught the `lld`\nfake-good optimization\n([Measurement 4](#measurement-4--the-decisive-test-the-real-vm-overturns-the-native-proxy)).\n\n1. **The output tracks the edited source.** The editor shows line 2 as\n   `println!(\"Hello, rust world!\");` and the second run prints exactly\n   `Hello, rust world!` — a *different* string from the first run's\n   `Hello, world!`. A faked/mocked terminal would not recompile a\n   changed string and emit the new value. A real `rustc` did.\n2. **Cargo's own phase lines are present and internally consistent.**\n   The first run shows **only** `Finished … in 23.96s` (no `Compiling`)\n   — that is cargo's freshness fast-path on an unchanged crate. The\n   second shows `Compiling hello v0.1.0 (/workspace)` → `Finished` →\n   `Running target/debug/hello`. This is the real cargo state machine,\n   not canned text.\n3. **The slowness itself is the proof.** A fake would be *fast*. 6 m\n   04 s is the unmistakable signature of a real `rustc` + LLVM + linker\n   pipeline running under x86→WASM emulation. You cannot fake being this\n   slow in a way that *also* produces correct, edited output.\n4. **The architecture has no shortcut path.** `web/glue/webvm-server.js`\n   runs the user's command through `cx.run('/bin/bash', …)` inside\n   CheerpX (`docs/architecture.md`). There is no interception layer that\n   could substitute output; the bytes come straight from the guest PTY.\n   The new `vm.benchCargo` instrumentation reuses that **same** path — it\n   measures real `cargo run`, it does not replace it.\n5. **CI boots the real VM and runs a real edited `cargo run`.**\n   `web/tests/e2e/local-pages-e2e.test.mjs` (run by `disk-image.yml`)\n   loads the freshly built ext2 into a headless browser, boots CheerpX,\n   edits `src/main.rs`, and times an actual `cargo run`. That is the test\n   whose number flipped 58 s → timeout when `lld` was added — a faked\n   pipeline could not have regressed.\n\n**Recommended live re-verification** (anyone can run these in the app's\nterminal to confirm it is a genuine Linux VM, not a shim):\n\n```sh\nuname -a            # Linux … i686  → 32-bit x86 guest under CheerpX\nnproc               # expected: 1   → single-core (see root cause)\ncat /etc/os-release # Alpine Linux  → our pre-baked rust-alpine.ext2\nrustc --version     # the real toolchain doing the work\ntime cargo build -v # see the actual rustc + linker invocations + timing\n```\n\nConclusion: **the VM is real.** The problem is genuine compiler work\nrunning in a genuinely slow execution environment — which is precisely\nwhy it is worth optimizing, and why an optimization has to be validated\n*in that environment*, not just on native metrics.\n\n## Root-cause analysis — measured, not assumed\n\nThe prior analysis *guessed* that CPU-bound emulation of `rustc`/LLVM was\nthe dominant cost. **Measurement says otherwise.** Four experiments — the\nfirst three native+reproducible via\n[`experiments/issue-41/`](../../../experiments/issue-41/), the fourth\ntaken in the real VM by CI — together tell a story whose punchline\noverturns its own setup.\n\n### Measurement 1 — native wall-clock is emulation-invariant noise\n\n`measure.sh` runs the SAME one-line-edit rebuild on the SAME crate under\nevery profile configuration, natively on i386\n([`results/summary.md`](../../../experiments/issue-41/results/summary.md)):\n\n| scenario | cold | no-op | **rebuild** | check |\n|----------|------|-------|-------------|-------|\n| stock-default | 0.27s | 0.02s | **0.14s** | 0.08s |\n| shipped slow-knobs (`codegen-units=1`, `debug=0`, `incremental=0`) | 0.25s | 0.03s | **0.14s** | 0.08s |\n| incremental on | 0.26s | 0.03s | **0.15s** | 0.08s |\n| incremental + lld | 0.25s | 0.03s | **0.15s** | 0.08s |\n\n**Every config rebuilds in 0.14–0.27 s natively.** The knobs the prior\nwork tuned move the native number by *milliseconds*. So native CPU work\n**cannot** explain the 6-minute browser cost — something the emulation\nlayer multiplies does. That rules out the entire \"do less CPU codegen\"\nfamily as the lever and points at **per-syscall / per-process emulation\noverhead**.\n\n### Measurement 2 — the cost is filesystem syscalls over the overlay\n\n`measure-syscalls.sh` straces the same rebuild\n([`results/syscalls.md`](../../../experiments/issue-41/results/syscalls.md)):\n\n| command | process spawns (`execve`) | total syscalls | **filesystem syscalls** |\n|---------|---------------------------|----------------|-------------------------|\n| `cargo build` (one-line-edit rebuild) | 12 | 16,812 | **14,736** |\n| `cargo check` (same edit) | 5 | 1,645 | 1,029 |\n\nA *zero-dependency hello-world rebuild* issues **~14,700 filesystem\nsyscalls**. Natively those are free page-cache hits. Under CheerpX each\none crosses the WASM/JS boundary and hits the\n`OverlayDevice(cloud, IDBDevice)` IndexedDB layer — that boundary crossing,\nmultiplied ~14,700×, is the bulk of the 6 minutes. **The bottleneck is\nI/O, not CPU.** (The 24 s no-op is the same cost in miniature: cargo\n`stat()`-walks `target/` over the overlay to prove nothing changed.) This\nis also why `cargo check`, at **1,029** filesystem syscalls, is a genuine\nfast-feedback win (C1) — though it builds no binary, so it does not\nreplace `cargo run`.\n\n### Measurement 3 — the linker is the dominant syscall source (the `lld` hypothesis)\n\n`rustc -Z time-passes` shows `link_binary` is **0.049 s of 0.072 s total\n(68 %)** — the single largest compile phase, and it is filesystem-bound.\n`measure-linker.sh` then counts the rebuild's syscalls with GNU `ld` vs\n`lld` ([`results/linker.md`](../../../experiments/issue-41/results/linker.md)):\n\n| linker | process spawns | total syscalls | **filesystem syscalls** |\n|--------|----------------|----------------|-------------------------|\n| GNU `ld` (shipped default) | 12 | ~16,880 | **14,736** |\n| `lld` (`-C link-arg=-fuse-ld=lld`) | 12 | ~6,860 | **2,157** |\n\n**On native i386, switching the linker cuts filesystem syscalls by 85 %**\nwith the process count unchanged. GNU `ld` walks the libc archive with\nthousands of `_llseek`/`readv` calls; `lld` mmaps it. Because file\nsyscalls are exactly the cost CheerpX multiplies, **this looked like the\nsingle highest-leverage, no-hack fix** — and an earlier revision of this\nPR shipped it. The native numbers are real and reproduce deterministically.\n**They were also the wrong proxy.** Measurement 4 is why.\n\n### Measurement 4 — the decisive test: the real VM overturns the native proxy\n\nNative strace counts syscalls; it does **not** count what CheerpX pays to\n*execute the linker itself*. CheerpX x86→WASM-JITs guest code on first\nuse, and `lld` is a far larger binary than GNU `ld`. The only way to know\nthe net effect is to measure **in the real VM** — which is exactly what\nthe project's end-to-end CI does. `disk-image.yml` builds the ext2, boots\nit in a headless browser via CheerpX, and `local-pages-e2e.test.mjs`\nsubtest 2 edits `src/main.rs` and runs a **real** `cargo run` (Stage G,\ngated on the lean dev profile being present, with a 180 s ceiling).\n\nHolding everything else constant and changing **only** the linker:\n\n| disk build | linker | CI run | subtest 2 (real edited `cargo run`) | result |\n|------------|--------|--------|-------------------------------------|--------|\n| `b861a2f` (pre-swap) | GNU `ld` | [27462524216](https://github.com/link-foundation/rust-web-box/actions/runs/27462524216) | **58.5 s** (`duration_ms: 58458.9`) | ✅ `ok 2` |\n| `7c66bc7` | `lld` | [27467098552](https://github.com/link-foundation/rust-web-box/actions/runs/27467098552) | **221.3 s** (`duration_ms: 221306.5`) | ❌ `not ok 2` — timed out |\n| `766eece` (lld + guard fix) | `lld` | [27468491003](https://github.com/link-foundation/rust-web-box/actions/runs/27468491003) | **220.8 s** (`duration_ms: 220807.7`) | ❌ `not ok 2` — timed out |\n\n**The single variable across these three disk builds is the linker.**\nGNU `ld` passes at ~58 s; `lld` blows through the 180 s ceiling, twice,\non two independent commits. (221 s ≈ ~41 s of boot/earlier stages + the\n180 s Stage-G timeout.) So the native −85 % syscall win is **more than\nerased** in the VM by the cold-JIT cost of the bigger linker. The\nfilesystem-syscall count was a good *diagnosis* of where native time goes\nbut a **bad predictor of in-VM wall-clock**, because it omits CheerpX's\nper-binary translation cost entirely.\n\n**`lld` was therefore reverted** (commit `5fa7df3`); the disk keeps GNU\n`ld`. This is the case study's headline finding, and it is only knowable\nbecause the issue insisted the solution be validated on the *real* VM.\n\n### The meta-root-cause (unchanged, now quantified)\n\nSeveral speed knobs were turned the *slow* way on purpose to dodge the\nCheerpX `OverlayDevice` \"`a1`\" fresh-inode wedge (`CARGO_INCREMENTAL=0`\n#17; `codegen-units=1`, `debug=0` #31). Measurement 1 shows those cost\nalmost nothing natively — but they exist *because* of the overlay, and\n(per Measurement 4) they are already enough to get the real rebuild to\n~58 s. So the highest-leverage architectural move that *remains* is\n**getting build artifacts off the IndexedDB overlay** (S2): it makes the\nremaining syscalls fast *and* removes the wedge that forced the slow\nknobs, unblocking incremental (S3). Unlike `lld`, S2 reduces work CheerpX\nmust emulate rather than adding a large new binary for it to JIT.\n\n## How to measure it in the browser (the tracing we added)\n\nNative docker proves *where* the cost is in an emulation-invariant way,\nand CI's e2e proves the *net* in-VM effect. To let a maintainer take the\nsame numbers ad-hoc **in the browser on the real VM** — and to keep us\nhonest about future changes — this PR adds opt-in tracing to the WebVM\ncommand path (`web/glue/`), zero-overhead when off:\n\n- **`globalThis.__RWB_DEBUG_VM_TIMING = true`** — records wall-clock for\n  every `cx.run` the server issues (mirrors the existing\n  `__RWB_DEBUG_TERMINAL_STREAM` pattern). Read it back with the server\n  handle's `vmTimings.snapshot()`.\n- **`vm.benchCargo` bus method** (`web/glue/cargo-bench.js`) — runs the\n  user's **real** `cargo run` / `cargo build` / `cargo check` inside the\n  guest across four phases (no-op run, one-line-edit run, edit build, edit\n  check) plus an optional `rustc -Z time-passes` split, and ships per-phase\n  wall-clock back over the same OSC-frame stdout channel `workspace-sync`\n  uses. It only ever rewrites the existing `src/main.rs` inode and restores\n  the baseline, so it never allocates fresh inodes (no `a1` wedge) and never\n  touches the `target/`/fingerprint tree. `summarizeCargoBench` renders it\n  the way the issue reports it (e.g. `cargo run (one-line edit) 6m04.1s`).\n\nThis is the in-browser counterpart to the docker rig: same real commands,\nsame real VM, structured timing out. It is how a maintainer reproduces\nthe Measurement-4 result by hand and validates any future S2/S3 change on\nthe live disk, by numbers rather than vibes. (Had this tracing existed\nfirst, the `lld` regression would have shown up before CI did.)\n\n## Requirements (every one, enumerated)\n\nParsed verbatim from the issue body and the PR-review follow-up (\"explain\nin detail what we can actually do to speed up the *actual* build, without\nworkarounds or hacks; add tracing if we lack it; use only real `cargo\nrun`\"):\n\n| # | Requirement | Where addressed |\n|---|-------------|-----------------|\n| R1 | \"Explore **all possible ways** to improve performance of [the] virtual machine in the browser.\" | [Solution catalogue](#solution-catalogue) — ranked, measured, including one option measured then rejected. |\n| R2 | \"Simple `cargo run` executes too long (5–6 minutes on second rebuild).\" — quantify & fix the **real** rebuild. | [Root-cause analysis](#root-cause-analysis--measured-not-assumed); the real rebuild is at ~58 s via the lean profile + pre-bakes (S1, verified in-VM), with S2/S3 the next lever and `lld` rejected. |\n| R3 | \"It is ok to also **optimize the WebVM itself** if you know how.\" | S2 (target off overlay), S4 (CheerpX upstream); plus the in-VM tracing we added. |\n| R4 | \"**Double check that our solution is not fake**, and we actually use [a] virtual machine to execute commands.\" | [Is the VM real?](#is-the-vm-real-anti-fake-verification) + live recipe; the bench reuses the real `cx.run` path; the e2e (Measurement 4) boots the real VM and caught the `lld` regression. |\n| R5 | \"Collect data related to the issue … compile that data to `./docs/case-studies/issue-41`.\" | This folder + [`experiments/issue-41/`](../../../experiments/issue-41/). |\n| R6 | \"Deep case study analysis.\" | This `README.md`, measurement-driven, including a measured rejection. |\n| R7 | \"Search online for additional facts and data.\" | [`online-research.md`](./online-research.md), fully cited. |\n| R8 | \"List of each and all requirements from the issue.\" | This table. |\n| R9 | \"Propose possible solutions and solution plans for each requirement.\" | [Solution catalogue](#solution-catalogue), per-requirement plans. |\n| R10 | \"Check known existing components/libraries that solve a similar problem or can help.\" | Each entry names concrete tools (lld/mold/wild, CheerpX devices, cranelift, `cargo check`). |\n| R11 | \"Plan and execute everything in this single pull request.\" | PR #42; branch `issue-41-…`. |\n| R12 | **(PR review)** Redo the analysis from **measurement**; add **tracing** if missing; speed up the **actual** build, no workarounds/hacks; use only **real `cargo run`**. | The whole rewrite: docker syscall/linker measurement, the in-VM `vm.benchCargo`/`__RWB_DEBUG_VM_TIMING` tracing, the in-VM e2e A/B (Measurement 4), and the **honest rejection of `lld`** when the real `cargo run` regressed. |\n\n## Solution catalogue\n\nEach entry: **impact** (in-browser cost removed), **effort**, **risk**\n(especially vs. the CheerpX wedge), the **existing component/library** it\nuses, and a **plan**. Ranked by *measured value today*.\n\nLegend — Impact/Effort/Risk: ⬤⬤⬤ high · ⬤⬤ medium · ⬤ low.\n\n### S1 — Lean dev profile + warm pre-bakes ✅ (shipped #17/#31, verified in-VM here)\n\n- **Maps to:** R1, R2, R3, R9, R10.\n- **Impact ⬤⬤⬤ · Effort ⬤ · Risk ⬤⬤ (must match the pre-bake fingerprint — handled).**\n- **Existing component:** Cargo profiles (`[profile.dev]`), Cargo's\n  freshness/mtime check, and a baked `target/` (debug *and* release).\n- **Why it is the real fix in place today:** Measurement 4 shows the\n  current disk — lean dev profile (`debug = 0`, `codegen-units = 1`,\n  `incremental = false`) plus a baked debug and release `target/` —\n  rebuilds an edited `cargo run` **in ~58 s in the real VM**, versus the\n  minutes the issue reported. It works by (a) not writing debug info and\n  not splitting into extra codegen units (less artifact IO over the\n  overlay) and (b) letting cargo's freshness check succeed against the\n  pre-baked artifacts without allocating fresh inodes (dodging the `a1`\n  wedge). It changes nothing the user runs.\n- **Why it is safe vs. the wedge:** the profile is baked **before** the\n  pre-bake `cargo build`, so the baked fingerprints already record it and\n  the first in-browser build stays a verified no-op. The e2e's\n  `hasLeanCargoDevProfile` gate asserts the baked\n  `/root/.cargo/config.toml` still carries `debug = 0` + `codegen-units = 1`\n  before it even runs the timed rebuild.\n- **Status:** shipped in #17/#31; this PR's contribution is to **prove it\n  in the real VM** (Measurement 4) and keep it as the load-bearing fix\n  after `lld` was rejected.\n\n### C1 — `cargo check` fast-feedback path ✅ NEW in this PR (complementary, **not** a `cargo run` speedup)\n\n- **Maps to:** R1, R2, R10; iteration-loop UX.\n- **Impact ⬤⬤ (error feedback) · Effort ⬤ · Risk ⬤.**\n- **Existing component:** Cargo's built-in `cargo check`.\n- **What it is:** `cargo check` skips codegen **and** linking, so it\n  surfaces compile errors in seconds (Measurement 2: **1,029** vs 14,736\n  filesystem syscalls). This PR **pre-bakes the check fingerprint** in the\n  disk image (so the first in-browser `cargo check` reuses inodes rather\n  than tripping the wedge) and surfaces it as a `cargo check (fast)` task\n  in the seeded `tasks.json` (with `rust-analyzer.checkOnSave` left off so\n  it does not fire the slow path on every keystroke).\n- **Why it is explicitly *not* the answer to \"make `cargo run` faster\":**\n  `cargo check` produces no binary, so you still pay the full build\n  whenever you actually want to *run* the program. It is a parallel\n  fast-feedback lever (rust-analyzer's check-on-save uses the same\n  command), which is why we ship it — but the fix to the *real build*\n  remains S1 (and the future S2/S3). Presenting `cargo check` as \"the\n  performance fix\" was the framing the PR review correctly rejected; it is\n  shipped here as a complement, not the headline.\n\n### S2 — Move `target/` off the IndexedDB overlay (in-memory build dir) — the big architectural win\n\n- **Maps to:** R1, R2, R3, R9.\n- **Impact ⬤⬤⬤ · Effort ⬤⬤⬤ · Risk ⬤⬤⬤.**\n- **Existing component:** CheerpX writable devices (`DataDevice`, the mount\n  topology in `web/glue/cheerpx-bridge.js`); Cargo's `CARGO_TARGET_DIR`.\n- **Why it is the highest-leverage *remaining* fix:** writing build\n  artifacts to `OverlayDevice(cloud, IDBDevice)` is *both* the slow-IO\n  source (every remaining artifact syscall still pays IndexedDB latency)\n  *and* the trigger for the `a1` fresh-inode wedge that forced\n  `CARGO_INCREMENTAL=0` + `codegen-units=1`. Put `target/` on an in-memory\n  writable mount and you (a) make artifact IO RAM-fast and (b) stop\n  allocating fragile overlay inodes — which unblocks **S3** (incremental).\n  Artifacts are regenerable, so losing them on reload is acceptable. Unlike\n  `lld`, this *removes* work from the emulation layer rather than adding a\n  large new binary for it to JIT.\n- **Open question / why prototyped not shipped:** CheerpX's documented\n  mount types are `ext2`, `dir` (Web/DataDevice), `devs`, `devpts`,\n  `proc`, `sys` (see `bootLinux` in `cheerpx-bridge.js`); whether a\n  *writable, full-tree, in-memory* mount usable for `target/` is exposed\n  needs an upstream check/experiment. If unavailable, file an upstream\n  request to `leaningtech/webvm`/CheerpX for a tmpfs/ramfs device.\n- **Plan:** experiment under `experiments/` to mount a writable in-memory\n  device at `/workspace/target` (or point `CARGO_TARGET_DIR` at one);\n  confirm the wedge no longer fires with `CARGO_INCREMENTAL=1`; measure the\n  rebuild with `vm.benchCargo` before/after; then ship S3.\n\n### S3 — Re-enable incremental compilation (depends on S2)\n\n- **Maps to:** R1, R2.\n- **Impact ⬤⬤⬤ (for one-line edits) · Effort ⬤ · Risk ⬤⬤⬤ until S2 lands.**\n- **Existing component:** Cargo's built-in incremental compilation.\n- **Why blocked today:** `CARGO_INCREMENTAL=0` exists because incremental\n  generates a flood of fresh inodes under `target/<profile>/incremental/`,\n  which trips the `a1` overlay wedge (#17). Incremental is *the* normal\n  accelerator for \"I changed one line\"; re-enabling it once S2 removes the\n  overlay is the natural pairing. Measurement 1 confirms incremental adds\n  no native penalty, so the only thing standing between us and it is the\n  overlay wedge.\n- **Plan:** after S2, flip `CARGO_INCREMENTAL=1` (env + `config.toml` +\n  the bench's `SHIPPED_BENCH_ENV`), re-bake, and validate with\n  `vm.benchCargo` that an edited `cargo run` drops to seconds.\n\n### S4 — Track CheerpX's own performance levers / upstream\n\n- **Maps to:** R3, R1.\n- **Impact ⬤⬤ (long-horizon) · Effort ⬤⬤⬤ · Risk ⬤⬤.**\n- **Existing component:** CheerpX itself (pinned 1.3.3 in\n  `cheerpx-bridge.js`). Its roadmap targets \"average application at most\n  5× slower than native\" by extending integer-pipeline optimizations to\n  FP/vector (online-research §1), and a persistent JIT/translation cache\n  would stop cold `rustc` re-paying interpretation cost every run — and\n  would also be what makes a bigger linker like `lld` viable (Measurement 4).\n- **Plan:** keep `CHEERPX_VERSION` current (#37 tracks this); adopt and\n  measure FP/vector JIT or a persistent translation cache when shipped;\n  file/track an upstream request for the in-memory writable device S2\n  needs and for a persistent JIT cache.\n\n### S5 — Cranelift debug codegen backend\n\n- **Maps to:** R1, R2, R10.\n- **Impact ⬤⬤ (20–30 % debug **codegen**) · Effort ⬤⬤⬤ · Risk ⬤⬤⬤.**\n- **Existing component:** `rustc_codegen_cranelift`. **Blocked here**\n  (online-research §4): nightly-only `rustup` component on **x86_64**\n  Linux; our guest is **i386** Alpine **stable** rust. And Measurement 1\n  shows codegen is the *minority* of the cost (IO dominates), so even if\n  unblocked the payoff is smaller than S1/S2. Park as research.\n\n### S6 — Run `rustc` as native WASM/WASI instead of x86-under-CheerpX\n\n- **Maps to:** R1, R3 (radical).\n- **Impact ⬤⬤⬤ (removes the emulation layer) · Effort ⬤⬤⬤ · Risk ⬤⬤⬤.**\n- **Existing component:** `wasm32-wasi` toolchain efforts. **Reality check\n  (online-research §6):** there is no supported, drop-in `wasm32-wasi` host\n  build of `rustc`+`cargo`+LLVM that runs a full edit-compile-run loop in\n  the browser today. Long-horizon research only; recorded for completeness.\n\n### S7 — Faster boot / cold-start (orthogonal to compile time)\n\n- **Maps to:** R1, R3.\n- **Impact ⬤⬤ (first-load UX) · Effort ⬤⬤ · Risk ⬤.**\n- **Existing component:** already substantial — `web/sw.js` caches\n  shell/glue, IDB overlay persists, disk ships as same-origin GitHubDevice\n  chunks, workspace renders before VM boot. Further wins: smaller ext2,\n  prefetch of disk chunks, HTTP caching headers. Does not touch the\n  6-minute rebuild; tracked for completeness.\n\n### Rejected after measurement — link with `lld`\n\n- **Maps to:** R1, R2, R10, R12 (the measured-rejection requirement).\n- **Verdict:** ❌ **investigated, measured on native i386 *and* in the real\n  VM, and reverted.**\n- **Existing component:** `lld`, the LLVM linker (Alpine `lld` package),\n  driven through gcc with `-C link-arg=-fuse-ld=lld`.\n- **Why it looked like the fix:** the link step is 68 % of compile and is\n  the dominant filesystem-syscall source (Measurement 3); `lld` mmaps the\n  libc archive instead of seeking through it, cutting the rebuild's native\n  filesystem syscalls **14,736 → 2,157 (−85 %)** — precisely the cost\n  CheerpX multiplies. An earlier revision of this PR shipped it on that\n  basis.\n- **Why it was rejected:** Measurement 4. In the real CheerpX VM the\n  edited `cargo run` **regressed from ~58 s to a >180 s timeout** across\n  two independent commits, because CheerpX must x86→WASM-JIT the much\n  larger LLVM linker on first use and that cold-JIT cost dwarfs the syscall\n  saving. The native syscall count was the wrong proxy for in-VM\n  wall-clock. Reverted in `5fa7df3`; the disk keeps GNU `ld`.\n- **When to revisit:** if S4 lands a persistent CheerpX JIT/translation\n  cache (so the linker is JIT-compiled once and reused), or if a *smaller*\n  fast linker that emulates cheaply (e.g. `mold`/`wild`, subject to musl\n  i386 support) becomes available, re-run Measurement 4 before adopting.\n- **Lesson:** validate every optimization on the **real VM**, not on a\n  native proxy. This is the concrete payoff of the issue's \"is it fake?\"\n  requirement.\n\n## What this PR ships vs. proposes (honesty statement)\n\n**Shipped & verified here:**\n\n- **The in-VM tracing** the review asked for: `vm.benchCargo` (real\n  `cargo run`/`build`/`check` timing over the real `cx.run` path) and\n  `__RWB_DEBUG_VM_TIMING` (per-`cx.run` wall-clock), with unit +\n  integration tests.\n- **The `cargo check` fast-feedback path** (C1): pre-baked check\n  fingerprint in the disk image + a `cargo check (fast)` task. New here;\n  complements `cargo run`, does not replace it.\n- **In-VM verification of the existing lean dev profile + pre-bakes** (S1,\n  from #17/#31) as the load-bearing reason the real rebuild is ~58 s — via\n  the e2e (Measurement 4), which now also guards against regressions.\n- **The measurement rig** (`experiments/issue-41/`) behind every number,\n  including `results/in-vm-ab.md` for the decisive A/B.\n- The case study (R4–R8), cited research (R7), and the full ranked plan\n  (R1, R9, R10, R12) — including the **honest, measured rejection of\n  `lld`**.\n\n**Investigated and rejected (not shipped):** the `lld` linker swap — a\n−85 % *native* syscall win that *regressed* the real in-VM rebuild\n(58 s → >180 s timeout). Reverted; documented above as the headline\nfinding.\n\n**Proposed, not shipped:** S2 (in-memory `target/`), S3 (re-enable\nincremental — depends on S2), S4–S7. S2/S3 need a CheerpX device check and\nan in-browser before/after (now possible with `vm.benchCargo`); the rest\nare blocked on our toolchain or orthogonal. Each is specified precisely\nenough to land in a focused follow-up validated by the bench harness and\n`disk-image.yml` CI.\n\n## Verification\n\n```sh\n# JS glue + this PR's regression tests (no browser/docker needed):\nnode --test web/tests/\n\n# Rust template still builds/lints/tests:\ncargo fmt --check && cargo clippy --all-targets --all-features && cargo test\n\n# Reproduce the native measurements (docker, i386):\ncd experiments/issue-41 && docker build -f Dockerfile.measure -t rwb-issue41-measure . \\\n  && docker run --rm -v \"$PWD/results:/out\" rwb-issue41-measure /measure-linker.sh\n```\n\nThe **net** in-browser behaviour of the shipped disk — the lean profile,\nthe warm pre-bakes, and the `cargo check` path — is exercised by\n`disk-image.yml`, which builds the ext2, boots it in a headless browser,\nand runs a real edited `cargo run` (`local-pages-e2e.test.mjs` subtest 2).\nThat same gate is what produced Measurement 4: GNU `ld` passes at ~58 s,\n`lld` timed out — the evidence that reverting `lld` was correct. Same-origin relative URLs intentionally fall through: they\n  // are exactly what the Pages-hosted disk manifest uses, and treating\n  // them as \"non-http\" would miss a missing chunk manifest.\n  const scheme = EXPLICIT_SCHEME_RE.exec(url)?.[0]?.toLowerCase();\n  if (scheme && scheme !== 'http:' && scheme !== 'https:') {\n    return { ok: true, reason: 'non-http' };\n  }\n  let ctrl = null;\n  let timer = null;\n  try {\n    ctrl = typeof AbortController !== 'undefined' ? new AbortController() : null;\n    timer = ctrl && setTimeout(() => ctrl.abort(), 6000);\n    // GET with Range: bytes=0-0 — one-byte payload, supported by the\n    // GitHub Releases redirect target. `mode: 'cors'` (the default) is\n    // deliberate: if the browser refuses to expose the response, fetch\n    // throws and we know XHR will fail too. That's the whole point.\n    const res = await fetchImpl(url, {\n      method: 'GET',\n      headers: { Range: 'bytes=0-0' },\n      mode: 'cors',\n      redirect: 'follow',\n      signal: ctrl?.signal,\n    });\n    if (timer) clearTimeout(timer);\n    if (res.type === 'opaque' || res.type === 'opaqueredirect') {\n      // Shouldn't happen under mode:'cors', but guard anyway — opaque\n      // means JS can't read the bytes, which is exactly what XHR needs.\n      return { ok: false, reason: 'opaque' };\n    }\n    if (res.status === 404) return { ok: false, reason: 'not-found' };\n    if (res.ok || res.status === 206 || res.status === 405) {\n      return { ok: true, reason: 'reachable' };\n    }\n    return { ok: false, reason: `http-${res.status}` };\n  } catch (err) {\n    if (timer) clearTimeout(timer);\n    // A `TypeError` from fetch under `mode: 'cors'` typically means the\n    // response was blocked by CORS — same outcome we'd get from XHR.\n    const reason =\n      err?.name === 'AbortError' ? 'timeout' :\n      err?.name === 'TypeError' ? 'cors-or-network' :\n      'fetch-error';\n    return { ok: false, reason };\n  }\n}\n\nexport function inferDiskKind(url, explicitKind) {\n  if (explicitKind === 'github' || explicitKind === 'bytes' || explicitKind === 'cloud') {\n    return explicitKind;\n  }\n  // Historical manifest spelling. It describes where CI sourced the\n  // bytes, not the browser-side CheerpX device.\n  if (explicitKind === 'release-asset') return 'bytes';\n  if (/^wss?:/i.test(url || '')) return 'cloud';\n  if (/^https?:/i.test(url || '') || /^\\.{0,2}\\//.test(url || '') || /^\\//.test(url || '')) {\n    return 'bytes';\n  }\n  return 'cloud';\n}\n\nfunction normalizeDiskEntry(entry, source) {\n  if (!entry?.url) return null;\n  return {\n    ...entry,\n    kind: inferDiskKind(entry.url, entry.kind),\n    source,\n  };\n}\n\nfunction probeTargetForDisk(entry) {\n  if (entry?.kind === 'github') return `${entry.url}.meta`;\n  return entry?.url;\n}\n\nasync function probeDiskEntry(entry, fetchImpl, probe) {\n  const target = probeTargetForDisk(entry);\n  const result = await probe(target, fetchImpl);\n  return {\n    target,\n    ok: typeof result === 'object' ? result.ok : !!result,\n    reason: typeof result === 'object' ? result.reason : 'unknown',\n  };\n}\n\n/**\n * Resolve the disk URL from web/disk/manifest.json.\n *\n * Preference order:\n *   1. `warm` entry (our pre-baked Alpine + Rust ext2 image staged on\n *      Pages), when its probe target succeeds.\n *   2. `default` entry (the public WebVM image).\n *   3. The hard-coded fallback above.\n */\nexport async function resolveDiskConfig({\n  manifestUrl = './disk/manifest.json',\n  fetchImpl = globalThis.fetch?.bind(globalThis),\n  probe = probeUrl,\n  logger = console,\n} = {}) {\n  if (typeof fetchImpl !== 'function') {\n    return { kind: 'cloud', url: FALLBACK_DISK_URL, source: 'fallback' };\n  }\n  try {\n    const res = await fetchImpl(manifestUrl, { cache: 'no-cache' });\n    if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`manifest HTTP ${res.status}`);\n    const m = await res.json();\n    const warm = normalizeDiskEntry(m?.warm, 'warm');\n    if (warm) {\n      const result = await probeDiskEntry(warm, fetchImpl, probe);\n      if (result.ok) return warm;\n      // Structured diagnostic: distinguish \"asset not built yet\" from\n      // \"asset is built but CORS-blocked\" (issue #3, root cause #2).\n      // Hosting outside disks.webvm.io requires CORS; surfacing this\n      // explicitly saves future maintainers a 30-minute debugging trip.\n      if (result.reason === 'cors-or-network' || result.reason === 'opaque') {\n        logger?.warn?.(\n          `[rust-web-box] warm disk ${warm.url} is reachable but CORS-blocked ` +\n          `(probe: ${result.target}, reason: ${result.reason}); falling back to default disk. ` +\n          `Custom disks must be served with Access-Control-Allow-Origin — see ` +\n          `docs/case-studies/issue-9/README.md`,\n        );\n      } else {\n        logger?.info?.(\n          `[rust-web-box] warm disk ${warm.url} unavailable ` +\n          `(probe: ${result.target}, reason: ${result.reason}); falling back to default disk`,\n        );\n      }\n    }\n    const fallback = normalizeDiskEntry(m?.default, 'default');\n    if (fallback) return fallback;\n  } catch (err) {\n    logger?.warn?.('[rust-web-box] disk manifest unavailable, using fallback:', err);\n  }\n  return { kind: 'cloud', url: FALLBACK_DISK_URL, source: 'fallback' };\n}\n\nexport async function resolveDiskUrl(options = {}) {\n  return (await resolveDiskConfig(options)).url;\n}\n\nexport async function createBlockDevice(CheerpX, disk) {\n  const url = typeof disk === 'string' ? disk : disk?.url;\n  const kind = typeof disk === 'string' ? inferDiskKind(url) : inferDiskKind(url, disk?.kind);\n  if (!url) throw new TypeError('createBlockDevice requires a disk URL');\n\n  if (kind === 'github') {\n    if (!CheerpX?.GitHubDevice?.create) {\n      throw new Error('CheerpX build is missing GitHubDevice.create()');\n    }\n    return CheerpX.GitHubDevice.create(url);\n  }\n\n  if (kind === 'bytes') {\n    if (!CheerpX?.HttpBytesDevice?.create) {\n      throw new Error('CheerpX build is missing HttpBytesDevice.create()');\n    }\n    return CheerpX.HttpBytesDevice.create(url);\n  }\n\n  if (!CheerpX?.CloudDevice?.create) {\n    throw new Error('CheerpX build is missing CloudDevice.create()');\n  }\n  return CheerpX.CloudDevice.create(url);\n}\n\n/**\n * Boot a CheerpX Linux VM. Returns the handle plus the device stack.\n *\n * The VM uses a CloudDevice-backed root + an IDBDevice overlay so user\n * edits survive reloads (issue #1 acceptance criterion 9). The mount\n * topology mirrors leaningtech/webvm's reference WebVM.svelte exactly so\n * the supported callbacks (cpuActivity, processCreated, ...) keep working.\n *\n * If the configured disk (typically the warm Alpine+Rust image staged\n * from `web/disk/manifest.json`) fails to mount — usually because the\n * Pages artifact does not have the generated chunks yet — we fall back\n * to the public WebVM Debian image so the workbench still comes up.\n */\nexport async function bootLinux({\n  CheerpX,\n  diskConfig,\n  diskUrl,\n  diskKind,\n  persistKey = PERSIST_KEY,\n  onProgress,\n  fallbackDiskUrl = FALLBACK_DISK_URL,\n  fallbackDiskKind = 'cloud',\n} = {}) {\n  if (!CheerpX) throw new TypeError('bootLinux requires the CheerpX module');\n  const selectedDisk = diskConfig ||\n    (diskUrl ? It returns a\n * `cxReadFunc(charCode)` that you call once per byte of stdin. We expose:\n *\n *   * `write(buf)`: enqueue bytes → CheerpX stdin (a Uint8Array or string).\n *   * `resize(cols, rows)`: TIOCSWINSZ-equivalent.\n *   * `onData(cb)`: subscribe to bytes coming out of the VM.\n *   * `dispose()`: detach.\n *\n * All output is delivered as raw `Uint8Array` chunks so xterm.js (or our\n * VS Code Pseudoterminal) can render them verbatim.\n */\nexport function attachConsole(cx, { cols = 80, rows = 24 } = {}) {\n  if (!cx) throw new TypeError('attachConsole requires a CheerpX Linux handle');\n  const listeners = new Set();\n  let currentCols = cols;\n  let currentRows = rows;\n  const writer = (buf, vt) => {\n    if (vt !== undefined && vt !== 1) return;\n    let view;\n    if (buf instanceof Uint8Array) view = buf;\n    else if (buf instanceof ArrayBuffer) view = new Uint8Array(buf);\n    else if (Array.isArray(buf)) view = new Uint8Array(buf);\n    else return;\n    for (const cb of listeners) cb(view);\n  };\n  let cxReadFunc;\n  function bindConsole() {\n    cxReadFunc = cx.setCustomConsole(writer, currentCols, currentRows);\n  }\n  if (typeof cx.setCustomConsole !== 'function') {\n    throw new Error('CheerpX build is missing setCustomConsole (need >= 1.2)');\n  }\n  bindConsole();\n  return {\n    write(input) {\n      if (typeof input === 'string') {\n        for (let i = 0; i < input.length; i++) cxReadFunc(input.charCodeAt(i));\n      } else if (input instanceof Uint8Array) {\n        for (let i = 0; i < input.length; i++) cxReadFunc(input[i]);\n      } else if (Array.isArray(input)) {\n        for (const ch of input) cxReadFunc(typeof ch === 'string' ? [2026-06-13T17:57:52.262Z] [INFO]       "content": "# Architecture: rust-web-box\n\nThis document maps each component of the in-browser Rust sandbox\ndescribed in [issue #1](https://github.com/link-foundation/rust-web-box/issues/1)\nonto its current implementation, plus the constraints carried forward\nfrom that issue.\n\n## Top-level architecture\n\n```\nGitHub Pages (static)\n├── web/index.html                       # workbench entry (no custom UI)\n├── web/glue/\n│   ├── boot.js                          # 2-stage orchestrator (workspace → VM)\n│   ├── network-shim.js                  # cargo network mediator\n│   ├── cheerpx-bridge.js                # CheerpX loader + Linux boot\n│   ├── webvm-bus.js                     # transport-agnostic RPC\n│   ├── workspace-fs.js                  # IDB-backed JS workspace store\n│   ├── workspace-server.js              # stage-1 fs.* methods (pre-VM)\n│   └── webvm-server.js                  # stage-2 server (workspace + VM)\n├── web/sw.js                            # COOP/COEP + cache\n├── web/vscode-web/                      # VS Code Web build (vendored)\n├── web/cheerpx/                         # CheerpX 1.3.3 (vendored)\n├── web/extensions/\n│   ├── webvm-host/                      # FS provider, terminal, tasks\n│   └── rust-analyzer-web/               # rust-analyzer WASM client\n├── web/disk/                            # Alpine + Rust image build\n└── web/build/                           # vendor, render, and disk-staging scripts\n```\n\n## Workspace model — JS-side store + guest mirror\n\nThe workspace lives **in the browser**, not in CheerpX. `workspace-fs.js`\nopens an IndexedDB-backed file store on page load and seeds it with a\nminimal hello-world Cargo project rooted directly at `/workspace`\n(`/workspace/Cargo.toml`, `/workspace/src/main.rs`,\n`/workspace/README.md`). The `webvm:` `FileSystemProvider` reads/writes\nthis store directly via the bus, so VS Code's Explorer populates **the\nmoment the workbench mounts** — no waiting for the 30+ second CheerpX\nboot.\n\nWhen the VM finishes booting, `webvm-server.js` mirrors the JS-side\nworkspace into the guest's `/workspace/` directory by writing a temporary\nshell script to CheerpX's `DataDevice` mount and executing it\nnon-interactively from `/data`. The visible login shell starts after that\nprime step with `/workspace` as its working directory. Subsequent saves\nfrom the editor write to both stores: JS-side immediately, guest-side via\nthe same quiet `/data` script runner.\n\nThis is why the page can show a working Explorer + editor + open file\nthe moment VS Code mounts — the alternative (gating the workspace on\nCheerpX mounting an ext2 over the network) gives the user an empty\nfolder for half a minute.\n\nThe page **looks identical to vscode.dev**. There is no custom UI: the\nworkbench fills the viewport, the only chrome we add is a hidden\nbottom-right toast that surfaces boot errors. The Rust toolchain comes\nfrom a Linux VM running inside the page (CheerpX), surfaced as a VS\nCode terminal labelled `WebVM bash`.\n\nVS Code Web runs each extension inside a dedicated Web Worker (the\nextension host). That worker has no DOM and no `SharedArrayBuffer`\naccess to CheerpX, so the page (workbench document) holds CheerpX and\neverything that needs raw browser APIs. The two halves talk over a\nsame-origin `BroadcastChannel`:\n\n```\nextension worker  ──────────────────────  page\n  webvm-host                                glue/webvm-server.js\n   FileSystemProvider                        bus methods (fs.*, proc.*, vm.*)\n   Pseudoterminal                            CheerpX (Linux + IDB overlay)\n   Cargo tasks                               network-shim (cargo proxy)\n```\n\nWhen the workbench mounts and the `webvm-host` extension activates, it\nauto-opens a terminal pane that displays:\n\n```\nrust-web-box — in-browser Rust sandbox\nPowered by CheerpX (leaningtech/webvm) and VS Code Web.\n\n[rust-web-box] Booting Linux VM… …………\n[rust-web-box] Linux VM ready ✓\n[rust-web-box] disk: ./disk/rust-alpine.ext2\n[rust-web-box] Workspace mirrored to /workspace — try `cargo run`.\n\nroot@rust-web-box:/workspace#\n```\n\nThe status updates inline (no separate boot screen) — the user is\nexactly where they would be with `vscode.dev` plus a working terminal.\n\n## Component status\n\n| # | Component                       | Status | Notes                                        |\n|---|---------------------------------|--------|----------------------------------------------|\n| 1 | Page-level network shim         | ✅     | 18 unit tests; routes static/api direct, index via proxy chain |\n| 2 | Service worker COOP/COEP cache  | ✅     | Caches shell + glue, synthesises COOP/COEP/CORP |\n| 3 | CheerpX 1.3.3 loader + boot     | ✅     | Vendored at build time (engine + tun helpers); CDN fallback at runtime. The root cause lived in the webvm-host extension: each\n418\t  // call to `makePseudoterminal().open()` did\n419\t  //   `stdoutDispose = bus.on('proc.stdout', …)`\n420\t  // without disposing the previous subscriber. The extension's fix\n439\t  //      (detachBusListeners() before re-binding) only works if calling\n440\t  //      that disposer stops further deliveries — so this is the runtime\n441\t  //      precondition for the fix.\n442\t  //\n443\t  // The narrow source-shape regression (every `bus.on('proc.stdout', …)`\n444\t  // site in extension.js is preceded by a paired `detachBusListeners()`\n445\t  // call) is asserted separately in\n446\t  // `web/tests/extension-pty-listeners.test.mjs`.\n447\t  const commander = await tryLoadBrowserCommander();\n448\t  if (bailIfMissingPrereqs(t, { commander })) return;\n449\t\n450\t  const server = await startDevServer({ basePrefix: BASE_PREFIX });\n451\t  t.after(() => server.stop());\n452\t\n453\t  await withWorkbench(server.url, async ({ page, errors, diagnostics }) => {\n454\t    const vmPhase = await waitForLinux(page, { diagnostics: { ...diagnostics, errors } });\n455\t    assert.equal(vmPhase, 'ready');\n456\t\n457\t    const result = await page.evaluate(async () => {\n458\t      const busServer = globalThis.__rustWebBox?.busServer;\n459\t      if (!busServer || typeof busServer.emit !== 'function') {\n460\t        throw new Error('page-side busServer not exposed on __rustWebBox');\n461\t      }\n462\t\n463\t      // Sentinel markers that cannot legitimately appear in the stream\n464\t      // unless we put them there.\n465\t      const MARKER_A = 'rwb_dup_check_a_' + Math.random().toString(36).slice(2, 10);\n466\t      const MARKER_B = 'rwb_dup_check_b_' + Math.random().toString(36).slice(2, 10);\n467\t\n468\t      // Spin up an *independent* BroadcastChannel subscriber — the same\n469\t      // way the webvm-host extension would in its host worker. BroadcastChannel postMessage is synchronous-ish\n485\t      // but message dispatch is on the next task; emitting too early\n486\t      // would mask the regression by losing chunks unrelated to the bug.\n487\t      await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 0));\n488\t\n489\t      // Invariant 1: page-side emit is single-delivery. Emit once and\n490\t      // give the message-event a tick to land. The pre-#27 doubled\n491\t      // pipeline would put MARKER_A in the inbox twice; the fixed\n492\t      // pipeline puts it in once.\n493\t      busServer.emit('proc.stdout', { pid: 1, chunk: MARKER_A });\n494\t      await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 100));\n495\t\n496\t      const countA = inbox.filter((c) => c === MARKER_A).length;\n497\t\n498\t      // Invariant 2: subscribers detach cleanly. The user-visible symptom was: every typed\n  // character appeared twice in the terminal, and every line of command\n  // output (e.g. `cargo run`'s \"Hello from rust-web-box!\") rendered\n  // duplicated. The root cause lived in the webvm-host extension: each\n  // call to `makePseudoterminal().open()` did\n  //   `stdoutDispose = bus.on('proc.stdout', …)`\n  // without disposing the previous subscriber. VS Code Web calls open()\n  // more than once per pty (panel reattach, terminal restore), so each\n  // reattach added a fresh listener, and the writeEmitter that fanned\n  // those subscribers into xterm received N copies of every byte.\n  //\n  // We can't reach VS Code's xterm DOM from this harness (the workbench\n  // panel only mounts after a user gesture, and the e2e harness sets\n  // `__RUST_WEB_BOX_SKIP_BASH = true` to avoid the CheerpX 1.3.x 'a1'\n  // OverlayDevice wedge), so we validate the runtime invariants the\n  // extension's fix relies on, exercised against the real page-side bus:\n  //\n  //   1. The page's busServer emits each `proc.stdout` chunk exactly once\n  //      per BroadcastChannel subscriber. (If this regressed, every\n  //      consumer — extension, debugger, future tooling — would see\n  //      doubles regardless of how disciplined they were about\n  //      subscriber lifecycle.)\n  //\n  //   2. The unsubscribe function returned by the page's bus dispatcher\n  //      actually detaches the listener. The extension's fix\n  //      (detachBusListeners() before re-binding) only works if calling\n  //      that disposer stops further deliveries — so this is the runtime\n  //      precondition for the fix.\n  //\n  // The narrow source-shape regression (every `bus.on('proc.stdout', …)`\n  // site in extension.js is preceded by a paired `detachBusListeners()`\n  // call) is asserted separately in\n  // `web/tests/extension-pty-listeners.test.mjs`.\n  const commander = await tryLoadBrowserCommander();\n  if (bailIfMissingPrereqs(t, { commander })) return;\n\n  const server = await startDevServer({ basePrefix: BASE_PREFIX });\n  t.after(() => server.stop());\n\n  await withWorkbench(server.url, async ({ page, errors, diagnostics }) => {\n    const vmPhase = await waitForLinux(page, { diagnostics: { ...diagnostics, errors } });\n    assert.equal(vmPhase, 'ready');\n\n    const result = await page.evaluate(async () => {\n      const busServer = globalThis.__rustWebBox?.busServer;\n      if (!busServer || typeof busServer.emit !== 'function') {\n        throw new Error('page-side busServer not exposed on __rustWebBox');\n      }\n\n      // Sentinel markers that cannot legitimately appear in the stream\n      // unless we put them there.\n      const MARKER_A = 'rwb_dup_check_a_' + Math.random().toString(36).slice(2, 10);\n      const MARKER_B = 'rwb_dup_check_b_' + Math.random().toString(36).slice(2, 10);\n\n      // Spin up an *independent* BroadcastChannel subscriber — the same\n      // way the webvm-host extension would in its host worker. The bus\n      // server lives in the page; this listener attaches from the same\n      // page context, which still exercises the BroadcastChannel\n      // postMessage → message-event delivery path.\n      const channel = new BroadcastChannel('rust-web-box/webvm-bus');\n      const inbox = [];\n      const onMessage = (ev) => {\n        const msg = ev.data;\n        if (msg?.kind === 'event' && msg.topic === 'proc.stdout' && msg.payload?.chunk) {\n          inbox.push(msg.payload.chunk);\n        }\n      };\n      channel.addEventListener('message', onMessage);\n\n      // Wait one microtask + one macrotask flush so the listener is wired\n      // before we emit. BroadcastChannel postMessage is synchronous-ish\n      // but message dispatch is on the next task; emitting too early\n      // would mask the regression by losing chunks unrelated to the bug.\n      await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 0));\n\n      // Invariant 1: page-side emit is single-delivery. Emit once and\n      // give the message-event a tick to land. The pre-#27 doubled\n      // pipeline would put MARKER_A in the inbox twice; the fixed\n      // pipeline puts it in once.\n      busServer.emit('proc.stdout', { pid: 1, chunk: MARKER_A });\n      await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 100));\n\n      const countA = inbox.filter((c) => c === MARKER_A).length;\n\n      // Invariant 2: subscribers detach cleanly. Remove our listener and\n      // emit a *different* marker — it must not arrive. The extension's\n      // fix (detachBusListeners() before re-binding) is built on this\n      // exact precondition. If `removeEventListener` no-ops here, the\n      // detach pattern in extension.js silently leaks listeners again.\n      channel.removeEventListener('message', onMessage);\n      busServer.emit('proc.stdout', { pid: 1, chunk: MARKER_B });\n      await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 100));\n\n      const countB = inbox.filter((c) => c === MARKER_B).length;\n\n      channel.close();\n      return {\n        markerA: MARKER_A,\n        markerB: MARKER_B,\n        countA,\n        countB,\n        inboxSize: inbox.length,\n      };\n    });\n\n    assert.equal(\n      result.countA, 1,\n      `marker ${result.markerA} should appear exactly 1x in proc.stdout ` +\n      `(single-delivery invariant), saw ${result.countA}. ` +\n      `> 1 is the regression returning.`,\n    );\n    assert.equal(\n      result.countB, 0,\n      `marker ${result.markerB} should appear 0x after the listener detached ` +\n      `(disposer invariant), saw ${result.countB}. > 0 means the unsubscribe ` +\n      `function returned by the bus did not actually remove the listener — ` +\n      `the extension's detachBusListeners() fix would silently leak.`,\n    );\n  }, { commander });\n});\n",

Since the files on such filesystems typically reside in RAM, file access is extremely fast.\n\n## Key Characteristics\n\ntmpfs is a filesystem that lives entirely in RAM (and optionally swap). It's backed by the page cache — each file's data is anonymous memory, evictable to swap under memory pressure.\n\ntmpfs puts everything into the kernel internal caches and grows and shrinks to accommodate the files it contains and is able to swap unneeded pages out to swap space.\n\n## Writable Filesystem\n\nA tmpfs filesystem is automatically created when mounting a filesystem with the type tmpfs via a command such as: $ sudo mount -t tmpfs -o size=10M tmpfs /mnt/mytmpfs. This creates a writable, in-memory filesystem that can store files and directories.\n\n## Mounting Options\n\nmount -t tmpfs -o size=10G,nr_inodes=10k,mode=700 tmpfs /mytmpfs will give you tmpfs instance on /mytmpfs which can allocate 10GB RAM/SWAP in 10240 inodes and it is only accessible by root.\n\n**Note:** The search results focus on standard Linux tmpfs rather than CheerpX specifically. Open `https://link-foundation.github.io/rust-web-box/`.\n2. Wait for the WebVM bash terminal to reach the `/workspace` prompt.\n3. Run `cargo build` or `cargo run` in the terminal.\n4. Open the browser developer console.\n\n## Observed\n\nThe console repeatedly prints messages like:\n\n```text\n[26:26] TODO: Advisory locking is only stubbed\n[28:28] TODO: Advisory locking is only stubbed\n```\n\nThe messages are emitted by the CheerpX runtime while the guest is otherwise able to run Cargo successfully.\n\n## Expected\n\nRelease builds of the runtime should not print internal `TODO` diagnostics to the browser console by default. Ideally advisory locking is implemented or documented as unsupported; if the diagnostic remains useful, it should be behind an opt-in debug flag.\n\n## Impact\n\nDownstream applications use the browser console to detect real startup failures. The purpose of the console is to interact with the running application via standard input and output.\\n\\nBuilt-in console\\n\\nCheerpX comes with a built-in console that mimics traditional console behavior. The built-in console supports standard input and output over a HTML <pre> (pre-formatted) element. Keyboard input works provided the element is in focus.\\n\\nFor more information, visit the CheerpX console reference.\\n\\nCustom console\\n\\nCheerpX also supports a custom console that allows developers to programmatically capture output and provide input. This feature is useful to integrate with a more complete terminal implementation such as xterm.js. We use xterm.js ourselves for our public WebVM environment.\\n\\nAnother possible use for the custom console is accumulating program output into a JavaScript string. You can achieve this with the following snippet:\\n\\nconst encoder = new TextEncoder(\\\"utf-8\\\");\\n\\n\\nlet accumulatedOutput = \\\"\\\"; // Initialize an empty string to accumulate output\\n\\n\\nconst send = cx.setCustomConsole((buf) => {\\n  const string = new TextDecoder(\\\"utf-8\\\").decode(buf);\\n  accumulatedOutput += string; // Accumulate the output\\n  console.log(accumulatedOutput); // log the accumulated output\\n});\\n\\n\\n// Send a string\\nconst str = \\\"Hello, custom console!\\\\n\\\";\\nconst encodedStr = encoder.encode(str);\\n\\n\\nfor (let i = 0; i < encodedStr.length; i++) {\\n  send(encodedStr[i]);\\n}\\n\\nFor more details on customizing the console, see CheerpX Custom console.\\n\\nReading Files Using IDBDevice and Redirecting Output\\n\\nIDBDevice provides a persistent, read-write filesystem using the browser’s IndexedDB. It’s ideal for storing data that should persist between sessions. You can use the readFileAsBlob method to read files from an IDBDevice as Blob objects.\\n\\nTo make a file accessible, you can copy files using commands within the virtual machine. Here’s how to do that:\\n\\nRun your program using bash -c, redirecting stdout to a file:\\nawait cx.run(\\\"/bin/bash\\\", [\\\"-c\\\", \\\"echo 'Output to capture' > /output.txt\\\"]);\\nRead the Output File:\\n\\nAfter the program finishes, you can read the contents of the output file:\\n\\nconst outputBlob = await filesDevice.readFileAsBlob(\\\"/output.txt\\\");\\nconsole.log(await outputBlob.text());\\nNote\\nThis method has a significant limitation: it doesn’t provide streaming output. This means you won’t see real-time output, and for long-running programs, you’ll have to wait until completion to see any results. Since HTTP does not have native support for file listing, index.list is essential for managing and accessing files effectively.\\n\\nCreating an index.list file\\n\\nTo generate an index.list in every directory without including it in the directory listing, use the following command:\\n\\nTerminal window\\nfind . -type d -exec sh -c 'ls \\\"{}\\\" > \\\"{}\\\"/.index.list && mv \\\"{}\\\"/.index.list \\\"{}\\\"/index.list' \\\\;\\n\\nExplanation:\\n\\nfind . -type d: finds all directories starting from the current directory (.).\\n\\n-exec sh -c: executes the following shell commands for each directory found.\\n\\nls \\\"{}\\\" > \\\"{}\\\"/.index.list: lists the directory contents and saves it to .index.list.\\n\\n&& mv \\\"{}\\\"/.index.list \\\"{}\\\"/index.list: renames .index.list to index.list in the same directory.\\n\\nWarning\\nBe careful when using this command. It will overwrite any existing index.list files in every directory it processes. Ensure you run it only in the intended directory and back up any important data before execution. Misuse in the wrong directory could cause unintentional data loss.\\nAccessing files\\n\\nFiles in the WebDevice are accessed relative to the current page’s URL. For example, if your current page is https://host/dir1/dir2/page.html, then:\\n\\n/web/example.txt would correspond to https://host/dir1/dir2/path/to/local/directory/example.txt\\n/web/images/logo.png would correspond to https://host/dir1/dir2/path/to/local/directory/images/logo.png\\nNote\\nIt’s important to note that this behavior depends on the current page’s URL, as it uses a relative path. For more predictable results, it’s recommended to use absolute paths when possible.\\nUsing application/octet-stream for WebDevice directories\\n\\napplication/octet-stream is a MIME type used to indicate that a file is binary data, instructing the server and client to treat the file as raw bytes instead of interpreting it as text or any other format.\\n\\nIn CheerpX, make sure to apply the application/octet-stream MIME type to WebDevice directories to handle files correctly as binary data, preventing issues with images, scripts, and other non-text files.\\n\\nCreating the Webdevice:\\n\\n// The path must match the nginx location block (e.g., /webdevice in the nginx configuration)\\nconst webDevice = await CheerpX.WebDevice.create(\\\"/webdevice\\\");\\n\\nNginx configuration example:\\n\\nworker_processes  1;\\nerror_log   nginx_main_error.log info;\\npid nginx_user.pid;\\ndaemon off;\\n\\n\\nevents {\\n    worker_connections  1024;\\n}\\n\\n\\nhttp {\\n    default_type  application/octet-stream;\\n    access_log  nginx_access.log;\\n    error_log   nginx_error.log info;\\n\\n\\n    sendfile        on;\\n\\n\\n    add_header 'Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy' 'same-origin' always;\\n    add_header 'Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy' 'require-corp' always;\\n\\n\\n    server {\\n        listen       8080;\\n        server_name  localhost;\\n\\n\\n        gzip on;\\n        gzip_types application/javascript application/wasm text/plain;\\n\\n\\n        charset utf-8;\\n\\n\\n        location / {\\n            root .;\\n            index  index.html index.htm;\\n        }\\n\\n\\n        # Create the WebDevice for handling files in the /webdevice directory\\n        location /webdevice/ {\\n            root .;\\n            autoindex on;\\n            types { }\\n            default_type application/octet-stream;\\n        }\\n    }\\n}\\n\\nFor a full server setup and additional details, check our basic server guide.\\n\\nIDBDevice\\n\\nIDBDevice provides a persistent, read-write filesystem using the browser’s IndexedDB. It’s ideal for storing data that should persist between sessions.\\n\\nUsage\\n\\nCreate an IDBDevice using the CheerpX.IDBDevice.create() method:\\n\\nconst idbDevice = await CheerpX.IDBDevice.create(\\\"dbName\\\");\\n\\n\\nconst cx = await CheerpX.Linux.create({\\n  mounts: [ ... , { type: \\\"dir\\\", path: \\\"/files\\\", dev: idbDevice }],\\n});\\n\\nThis setup creates a virtual filesystem at /files that is backed by IndexedDB.\\n\\nReading files from JavaScript\\n\\nYou can read files from an IDBDevice in JavaScript using the readFileAsBlob method:\\n\\nawait idbDevice.readFileAsBlob(\\\"/filename\\\");\\n\\nFor more details on reading files using IDBDevice and redirecting output, see the Input/Output guide.\\n\\nDataDevice\\n\\nDataDevice is an in-memory filesystem useful for temporary data storage or passing data from JavaScript to the CheerpX environment.\\n\\nUsage\\n\\nCreate a DataDevice using the CheerpX.DataDevice.create() method:\\n\\nconst dataDevice = await CheerpX.DataDevice.create();\\n\\n\\nconst cx = await CheerpX.Linux.create({\\n  mounts: [ ... , { type: \\\"dir\\\", path: \\\"/data\\\", dev: dataDevice }],\\n});\\nAdding files\\n\\nYou can add files to a DataDevice from JavaScript using the writeFile method:\\n\\nawait dataDevice.writeFile(\\\"/filename\\\", \\\"File content here\\\");\\nBlock devices with ext2\\n\\nCheerpX supports ext2 filesystems, which can be configured as an OverlayDevice. This allows for a flexible setup that can combine different storage types.\\n\\nUsage\\n\\nCreate an ext2 filesystem by combining a HttpBytesDevice to acess disk blocks, an IDBDevice to cache and persist data and a OverlayDevice to combine the two.\\n\\n// Create an HttpBytesDevice for streaming disk blocks via HTTP\\nconst httpDevice = await CheerpX.HttpBytesDevice.create(\\n  \\\"https://yourserver.com/image.ext2\\\"\\n);\\n\\n\\n// Create an IDBDevice for persistent local storage\\nconst idbDevice = await CheerpX.IDBDevice.create(\\\"block1\\\");\\n\\n\\nconst overlayDevice = await CheerpX.OverlayDevice.create(httpDevice, idbDevice);\\n\\n\\nconst cx = await CheerpX.Linux.create({\\n  mounts: [{ type: \\\"ext2\\\", path: \\\"/\\\", dev: overlayDevice }],\\n});\\n\\nThis setup creates an ext2 filesystem that loads its initial data from an HTTP source and uses IndexedDB for persistent storage of changes.\\n\\nDevice configuration options\\n\\nCheerpX supports various types of devices that can be used in the OverlayDevice configuration:\\n\\nHttpBytesDevice: The default choice for loading filesystem images via HTTP. Suitable for most web-hosted files.\\nGitHubDevice: Ideal for projects forked from the WebVM repository. The Integrated GitHub Action will take care of preparing disk chunks for efficient access.\\nOverlayDevice: OverlayDevice supports chaining, making it possible to efficiently fork disk images while only storing the changes from previous versions.\\nBest practices\\nUse WebDevice for read-only access to server-side files.\\nUtilize IDBDevice for persistent storage of user data or application state.\\nEmploy DataDevice for temporary storage or passing data between JavaScript and CheerpX.\\nConsider ext2 filesystems for more complex file operations or when you need a traditional Linux filesystem structure.\\n\\nBy leveraging these different filesystem types, you can create a flexible and efficient file management system within your CheerpX-powered web application.\"\n### Ran Playwright code\n```js\nawait page.evaluate('() => {\\n  const main = document.querySelector(\\'main\\') || document.body;\\n  return main.innerText.slice(0, 9000);\\n}');\n```"

WebWorkers are a message based concurrency API for the Web platform, where a WebWorker is a \"thread\" which executes a JavaScript file that is completely independent and isolated from the main page code and other WebWorkers.\n\nPThreads is the main threading API on POSIX platforms like Linux, making it possible to run concurrent threads of execution that have the same view of memory in the same address space. However, since the script inside a WebWorker has an isolated view of memory, a WebWorker is more similar to a native process than to a native thread.\n\n## Related Threading Implementations\n\nFor context, other WebAssembly compilers have more mature threading support: Emscripten provides an API-compatible implementation of the pthread library built atop Web Workers, shared memory and atomics, so that the same code can work on the web without changes. Additionally, the Wasm Workers API enables C/C++ code to leverage Web Workers and shared WebAssembly.Memory (SharedArrayBuffer) to build multithreaded programs, where each Wasm Worker shares and computes in the same WebAssembly Memory address space of the main thread.\n\nThe search results show that Cheerp's threading support is still under development compared to more established solutions.\n\n\nREMINDER: You MUST include the sources above in your response to the user using markdown hyperlinks."

To ensure smooth functioning, the server hosting these third-party resources must have the appropriate CORS headers configured. If the CORS settings are not properly arranged, browsers will block these requests, which will lead to files being inaccessible in CheerpX.\\n\\nWhy can’t I execute files directly from a DataDevice?\\n\\nDataDevice in CheerpX does not have full support for Linux mode bits, and in particular it lacks the executable bit. This means you can read data from it, but you cannot execute files directly from it. To execute files that are in a DataDevice, you need to first copy the files to a filesystem with complete support for mode bits, such as IDBDevice (IndexedDB) or Ext2.\\n\\nWhy can’t CheerpX do what v86 does in terms of disk access and networking?\\n\\nCheerpX’s architecture and use case differ significantly from v86, which affects how it handles disk access and networking:\\n\\nDisk access\\n\\nCheerpX is designed to support large scale applications and complete Operating Systems, to achieve those objectives it needs to handle large disk images (up to 2GB at the time). This means we cannot simply download the entire disk image before starting execution, as v86 might do for its smaller images. Instead, CheerpX uses a chunk-based, on-demand downloading system.\\n\\nOur cloud disk backend is based on WebSocket and distributed across a global CDN, which should provides low latency disk access to users everywhere in the world. Here’s an explanation of the issue and the recommended solution.\\n\\nSecurity restrictions and Cross-Origin Headers\\n\\nModern browsers enforce strict security policies to protect users from potentially harmful actions. Accessing files through the file:// protocol poses a security risk, as it may allow untrusted HTML files to interact with local resources and cause data breaches.\\n\\nAdditionally, SharedArrayBuffer requires cross-origin isolation to function properly, which cannot be established when serving files with the file:// protocol. This protocol does not support setting the required HTTP headers: Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy and Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy.\\n\\nRecommended solution: local web server requirement\\n\\nTo properly utilize CheerpX, you must run a local web server. This allows you to access your HTML files with a URL that starts with http:// or https://, for example http://localhost:8080/. The documented mount types are exactly `\"ext2\" | \"dir\" | \"devs\" | \"proc\"` — there is **no `tmpfs`/ramfs type**, and the only two filesystems with full Linux mode bits (i.e. that can hold and *execute* build artifacts) are IDBDevice and Ext2, both IndexedDB-backed. That is the one thing to **measure empirically** (instrument write latency inside the VM, or profile IndexedDB transaction frequency in DevTools) rather than infer.\n\n## Official guidance on build dirs / caches / `/tmp` / I/O performance\n\n**None exists.** No CheerpX or WebVM page recommends placing `target/`, `node_modules`, or `/tmp` on a particular device, and there is no I/O-tuning guide. The only adjacent official statements are:\n- The \"Best practices\" list (File-System-support): use WebDevice for read-only server files, IDBDevice for persistent user data, DataDevice for temporary JS→VM data, and \"Consider ext2 filesystems for more complex file operations or when you need a traditional Linux filesystem structure.\" (This is why your `target/` correctly lives on the ext2 root.)\n- Disk reads are chunked/on-demand over a WebSocket CDN at ~20–40 ms latency, 128 KB blocks (WebVM 2.0 blog; FAQ \"Disk access\") — relevant to cold reads, not to your `target/` write bottleneck.\n- WebVM GitHub issues contain **nothing** on tmpfs/in-memory/IndexedDB write performance (the tracker is effectively minimal — only an unrelated Pages-build issue surfaced).\n\n## Confidence + what remains uncertain\n\n- **High confidence:** No documented RAM/tmpfs *writable* mount; mount types are `ext2|dir|devs|proc` (+ undocumented `devpts`/`sys`); DataDevice is read-only and non-executable; writes to the ext2 root land in the IndexedDB overlay; IDBDevice is a block-level cache+persistence layer. All backed by direct quotes above.\n- **Medium/low confidence (genuine doc gaps):** (a) exact IDBDevice write-back vs write-through/flush-batching behavior — undocumented, needs measurement; (b) whether any *undocumented* in-memory mount type exists — none found in docs or two production mount configs, but the type union is known-incomplete; (c) no public CheerpX 1.3.x changelog with per-version I/O notes was locatable.\n\nKey source URLs: https://cheerpx.io/docs/guides/File-System-support · https://cheerpx.io/docs/guides/input-output · https://cheerpx.io/docs/reference/CheerpX.Linux/create · https://cheerpx.io/docs/getting-started · https://cheerpx.io/docs/faq · https://cheerpx.io/docs/reference/CheerpX.OverlayDevice/create · https://cheerpx.io/docs/reference/CheerpX.IDBDevice · https://labs.leaningtech.com/blog/webvm-20 · leaningtech/webvm `src/lib/WebVM.svelte` (lines ~283–308).\n\nLocal evidence in this repo: `/tmp/gh-issue-solver-1781373396637/web/glue/cheerpx-bridge.js` (mount topology, lines 316–334) and `/tmp/gh-issue-solver-1781373396637/web/glue/workspace-fs.js` (the existing JS-side IndexedDB workspace store) — both already match the upstream WebVM pattern, and neither uses a RAM/tmpfs mount."

This means that the system is not a black-box, but CheerpX has a complete view of all the processes and threads currently executing.\"\n\n  (Source: `https://labs.leaningtech.com/blog/cx-10`.) It won't speed up compilation, but it keeps the terminal/page responsive while a long `cargo build` runs, and it aligns with the engine's `Atomics.wait`-based blocking model (which can't run on the page's main thread). Validate empirically against 1.3.3 — worker placement isn't a documented `create()` option.\n2. **Don't expect `-j N` to parallelize compilation.** With one emulated CPU, parallel jobs just context-switch. `cargo build -j 1` (or letting Cargo default) avoids scheduling/memory overhead from spawning many concurrent rustc processes that can't actually run in parallel. Test both, but the theoretical ceiling is single-core.\n3. **Optimize the single core instead of chasing cores.** Levers that actually move the needle: `CARGO_PROFILE_*_CODEGEN_UNITS`, `opt-level`/debug settings, `CARGO_INCREMENTAL`, thinner dependency trees, and reducing disk I/O latency (relevant to your Part 1 RAM-cache/write-back work — the CheerpX 1.0 post cites ~20–40 ms per-block disk latency, so I/O is a real bottleneck that compounds on a single core).\n4. **Keep the service-worker header injection** — it's the sole reason CheerpX runs on GitHub Pages. Don't remove `serviceWorker.js`.\n5. **If true parallel compilation is a hard requirement,** it isn't achievable inside one CheerpX guest today. The only parallel-across-cores path would be *outside* the guest — e.g., multiple independent CheerpX instances each in its own worker compiling different crates — which is unsupported, memory-heavy (each instance maps an ~11200-page / ~700 MB+ shared memory), and would need a custom build-sharding layer.
