There are **zero** open issues/PRs across the `leaningtech` org requesting SMP / multi-core / parallel builds.\n\n**Conclusion for Q1:** `nproc` is not documented, but every layer indicates a single emulated CPU. `cargo build -j N` / `make -j N` will *execute* (multithreading/multiprocessing is emulated correctly) but will **not** run compile jobs on multiple host cores in parallel — throughput is bounded by one emulated CPU. *(Confidence: high that there's no SMP and `-j` gives no parallel speedup; the only thing I can't quote verbatim is the literal value of guest `nproc`.)*\n\n### 2. Main thread vs Web Worker — can CheerpX run in a worker? requirements? does it help compute?\n\n**Requirements are explicit; worker placement is supported by the tech but not documented as a `create()` toggle; the realistic win is UI responsiveness, not compute throughput.**\n\n- **Hard requirement — SharedArrayBuffer + cross-origin isolation:** The official Getting Started page states:\n  > \"CheerpX requires SharedArrayBuffer, which itself requires the site to be cross-origin isolated.\"\n  > \"To enable cross-origin isolation, serve over HTTPS and set the following headers\" — `Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy: require-corp` and `Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin`.\n  > \"During development, you don't need to use HTTPS if you're using localhost as the origin, the COEP and COOP headers are always required though.\"\n\n  (Source: `https://cheerpx.io/docs/getting-started`.) The FAQ reinforces this under \"Missing cross-origin isolation.\" (Source: `https://cheerpx.io/docs/faq`.)\n\n- **CheerpX already uses Web Workers + Atomics internally** for blocking/timing/networking — not for parallel CPU execution. The engine spawns 3 workers (`cxbridge.js`, `workerclock.js`, and a Tailscale `tun` worker) and uses `Atomics.wait(HEAP32,0,0,0)` — the classic \"block the calling context on a clock/lock worker\" pattern that lets synchronous Linux syscalls work. (`postMessage` x88, `onmessage` x8, `Atomics.wait` x1; source: `https://cxrtnc.leaningtech.com/1.3.3/cx_esm.js`.) `workerclock.js` being a *clock* worker is the tell: it's for blocking semantics, not compute fan-out.\n\n- **Can you put CheerpX itself in a worker?** The CheerpX docs do not give explicit worker-placement guidance for the engine (I checked Overview, Getting Started, FAQ, Devices, input-output, Networking — none discuss main-thread vs worker placement). However, the underlying Cheerp toolchain documents full worker support:\n  > \"Cheerp is designed to give you full access to all browser APIs, including WebWorkers.\"\n\n  (Source: `https://cheerp.io/docs/tutorials/webworkers`.) Because CheerpX is loaded as a standard ES module (`import('@leaningtech/cheerpx')`) and its blocking model already relies on `Atomics.wait` (which is **forbidden on the page's main thread** but allowed in a worker), running the engine inside a Web Worker is technically the *better-supported* configuration. **But this is an inference from how the engine is built, not an explicitly documented/supported `create()` option.** Treat \"run CheerpX in a worker\" as something to validate empirically against 1.3.3 before relying on it.\n\n- **Does a worker improve compute throughput?** **No** — moving a single-emulated-CPU workload to one worker doesn't add cores; it just unblocks the page's UI/event loop. The benefit is **UI responsiveness** (terminal stays interactive, page doesn't jank), not faster compilation. *(Confidence: high on requirements and on \"worker = responsiveness, not throughput\"; medium on the exact mechanics of relocating the engine, since it's undocumented.)*\n\n### 3. WASM threads — does CheerpX use them internally for JIT/execution? any multi-core story for the emulated CPU?\n\n**It uses Web Workers + shared memory + Atomics for blocking/timing/network plumbing, but there is no evidence of multi-core parallel execution of the emulated CPU, and no public multi-core story.**\n\n- Engine internals (above): a *single* `shared:true` WebAssembly memory, helper workers for clock/bridge/network, `hardwareConcurrency` never read. The JIT is described as on-the-fly x86→Wasm codegen, with no statement that JIT compilation is parallelized across workers:\n  > \"CheerpX features a multi-tier execution engine, with a fast interpreter … and an advanced JIT engine that can generate high quality optimized WebAssembly code on the fly.\" (Source: `https://labs.leaningtech.com/blog/cx-10`.)\n- **No official source describes parallel/multi-core execution of the guest CPU.** I found none across the docs, the CheerpX 1.0 post, the WebVM 2.0 post, the two Medium architecture articles, or the issue trackers. *(Confidence: high that there is no documented multi-core execution; the internal-worker analysis is from reading the shipped bundle, which can change between versions.)*\n\n### 4. SharedArrayBuffer / cross-origin isolation — required headers, and does GitHub Pages work?\n\n**Required headers are COEP `require-corp` + COOP `same-origin` (HTTPS). GitHub Pages cannot set response headers, but WebVM/CheerpX has a built-in service-worker fallback that injects them client-side — so GitHub Pages works.**\n\n- **Required headers** (confirmed in docs and in WebVM's `nginx.conf`, lines 46–48):\n  - `Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin`\n  - `Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy: require-corp`\n  - `Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy: cross-origin` (for the served resources)\n\n- **GitHub Pages limitation is real and historically blocked WebVM.** In `leaningtech/webvm` issue #23, a user deploying to GitHub Pages got \"CheerpX could not start\"; a Leaning engineer (carlopi) explained:\n  > \"For SharedArrayBuffer to be enabled, cross origin isolation headers have to be set properly on all resources you are using.\"\n\n  The user found localhost without headers failed while nginx-with-headers worked, and concluded \"my main idea to combine WebVM on github pages won't work.\" (Source: `https://github.com/leaningtech/webvm/issues/23`.) Same root cause in issues #9 and #91.\n\n- **The fallback that makes GitHub Pages work today: a service worker injects the headers.** WebVM ships `serviceWorker.js` whose comment states the intent exactly:\n  > \"We add headers to the original response its headers, in order to enable cross-origin-isolation. And make it independent of the server config.\"\n\n  It sets COEP/COOP/CORP on every response and only registers when the page isn't already isolated (`if (window.crossOriginIsolated) return;`). (Source: `/tmp/webvm-src/serviceWorker.js`, lines 12–17, 81; from `github.com/leaningtech/webvm`.)\n\n- **Empirically verified on your own deployment.** `https://link-foundation.github.io/rust-web-box/` returns **no** `cross-origin-*` HTTP headers (GitHub Pages can't add them), yet the page boots CheerpX and references `crossOriginIsolated` — i.e., the service worker is supplying isolation client-side. (Verified via `curl -D -`.) So your existing GitHub Pages setup is already using the supported fallback. *(Confidence: very high — docs + maintainer statements + source + live verification all agree.)*\n\n### 5. Official statements on parallelism / performance / \"single-threaded\"\n\n- **No explicit \"the emulated CPU is single-threaded/single-core\" statement exists** in any source I checked. State that as \"undocumented\" rather than quoting it.\n- Official performance framing (single-CPU virtualization overhead, no parallelism claim):\n  > \"CheerpX is expected to run complex applications 5x-10x slower than native, with the slowdown being as low as 2x-3x for binaries that only stress the best optimized parts.\" (Source: `https://labs.leaningtech.com/blog/cx-10`.)\n  > Limitations include \"the performance impact of virtualization … the level of performance is already sufficient for many practical use cases and will further improve down the line.\" (Leaning engineer, `https://github.com/leaningtech/webvm/issues/150`.)\n\n---\n\n## What WOULD help\n\n1. **Move CheerpX into a Web Worker for UI responsiveness.** This is the highest-value change. It won't speed up compilation, but it keeps the terminal/page responsive while a long `cargo build` runs, and it aligns with the engine's `Atomics.wait`-based blocking model (which can't run on the page's main thread). Validate empirically against 1.3.3 — worker placement isn't a documented `create()` option.\n2. **Don't expect `-j N` to parallelize compilation.** With one emulated CPU, parallel jobs just context-switch. `cargo build -j 1` (or letting Cargo default) avoids scheduling/memory overhead from spawning many concurrent rustc processes that can't actually run in parallel. Test both, but the theoretical ceiling is single-core.\n3. **Optimize the single core instead of chasing cores.** Levers that actually move the needle: `CARGO_PROFILE_*_CODEGEN_UNITS`, `opt-level`/debug settings, `CARGO_INCREMENTAL`, thinner dependency trees, and reducing disk I/O latency (relevant to your Part 1 RAM-cache/write-back work — the CheerpX 1.0 post cites ~20–40 ms per-block disk latency, so I/O is a real bottleneck that compounds on a single core).\n4. **Keep the service-worker header injection** — it's the sole reason CheerpX runs on GitHub Pages. Don't remove `serviceWorker.js`.\n5. **If true parallel compilation is a hard requirement,** it isn't achievable inside one CheerpX guest today. The only parallel-across-cores path would be *outside* the guest — e.g., multiple independent CheerpX instances each in its own worker compiling different crates — which is unsupported, memory-heavy (each instance maps an ~11200-page / ~700 MB+ shared memory), and would need a custom build-sharding layer. Not recommended without prototyping.\n\n---\n\n## Confidence & what remains uncertain\n\n- **High / very high:** COOP/COEP + SharedArrayBuffer requirement; GitHub Pages works via the service-worker header-injection fallback (docs + maintainer + source + live test); the public API exposes no CPU/core/threads/jobs knob; the engine uses internal workers for blocking/clock/network rather than parallel compute; no documented SMP/multi-core execution; official performance numbers frame it as single-CPU virtualization overhead.\n- **Medium:** that relocating the *whole engine* into a worker is straightforward and fully supported — it's strongly implied by the build but **not documented**, so verify against 1.3.3.\n- **Genuinely unknown / undocumented (do not assume):**\n  - The literal value of guest `nproc` (I could not find it stated; the only way to be 100% certain is to run `nproc` / `cat /proc/cpuinfo` in your live VM).\n  - Whether CheerpX *ever* dispatches guest threads to more than one execution context under any condition — no source confirms or denies parallel execution; all indirect evidence points to single-CPU.\n  - Internal-bundle observations (3 workers, single shared memory, no `hardwareConcurrency`) are from the shipped 1.3.3 artifacts and could change in future versions.\n\n**One quick empirical check worth running in your own VM** to convert the two \"unknowns\" into facts: `nproc` and `cat /proc/cpuinfo` (core count), then `time cargo build -j1` vs `-j4` on a fixed crate (confirms whether `-j` helps). That directly validates the single-core inference against your exact deployment.\n\nKey local file inspected: `/tmp/webvm-src/serviceWorker.js` (the GitHub Pages header-injection fallback) and `/tmp/webvm-src/src/lib/WebVM.svelte` (the `CheerpX.Linux.create` call)."

assert.equal(editRun.cmd, 'cargo run');\n  assert.equal(editRun.tail, 'Compiling hello v0.1.0');\n\n  const noop = result.phases.find((p) => p.id === 'noop-run');\n  assert.equal(noop.compiled, false, Read those for\nthe native numbers; read this for what actually happens in the browser.\n\n## Why native strace was the wrong proxy\n\n`measure-linker.sh` counts the *guest's* filesystem syscalls. It does\n**not** count what CheerpX pays to **execute the linker binary itself**.\nCheerpX x86→WASM-JITs guest code on first use, and `lld` (the LLVM linker)\nis a far larger binary than GNU `ld`. So \"fewer syscalls\" (a real native\nwin, −85 %) can still be a net **loss** in the VM if the larger binary's\ncold-JIT cost exceeds the syscall saving. The only way to know is to\nmeasure in the real VM.\n\n## The measurement: the project's own e2e, run by CI\n\n`.github/workflows/disk-image.yml` builds the `rust-alpine.ext2`, boots it\nin a headless Chromium via CheerpX, and runs\n`web/tests/e2e/local-pages-e2e.test.mjs`. **Subtest 2** (\"workbench boots\n… and CheerpX 1.3.3 runs `tree --version`\") includes **Stage G**: it edits\n`/workspace/src/main.rs` and runs a **real** `cargo run`, gated on the\nlean dev profile being present, with a **180 s** ceiling\n(`runInVM(..., { timeoutMs: 180_000 })`).\n\nThree disk builds, **the linker the only variable** between them:\n\n| disk build | linker | CI run | subtest 2 `duration_ms` | result |\n|------------|--------|--------|-------------------------|--------|\n| `b861a2f` (pre-swap) | GNU `ld` | [27462524216](https://github.com/link-foundation/rust-web-box/actions/runs/27462524216) | **58458.9** (~58.5 s) | ✅ `ok 2` |\n| `7c66bc7` | `lld` | [27467098552](https://github.com/link-foundation/rust-web-box/actions/runs/27467098552) | **221306.5** (~221.3 s) | ❌ `not ok 2` (timed out) |\n| `766eece` (lld + guard fix) | `lld` | [27468491003](https://github.com/link-foundation/rust-web-box/actions/runs/27468491003) | **220807.7** (~220.8 s) | ❌ `not ok 2` (timed out) |\n\nRaw log lines (saved under `ci-logs/` in the repo root at capture time):\n\n```\n# b861a2f (GNU ld) — run 27462524216\nok 2 - Key Technical Concepts:\n   - **CheerpX 1.3.3**: x86→WASM JIT engine running i386 Alpine Linux VM in-browser. Single shared WASM memory (`Memory({initial:11200,maximum:11200,shared:true})`), effectively single execution context — NO SMP, no public core/jobs API knob. Requires SharedArrayBuffer + cross-origin isolation (COOP `same-origin` + COEP `require-corp`).\n   - **CheerpX devices**: GitHubDevice, HttpBytesDevice, CloudDevice, IDBDevice, OverlayDevice, WebDevice, DataDevice. Mount types: `ext2 | dir | devs | proc` (+ undocumented `devpts`, `sys`). **No RAM-writable/tmpfs mount exists.** Only in-memory device (DataDevice) is read-only + lacks executable bit. **IDBDevice is already a block-level RAM cache in front of IndexedDB** (write-back vs write-through is undocumented).\n   - **Mount topology** (cheerpx-bridge.js bootLinux): `OverlayDevice(cloud, IDBDevice)` at `/` (ext2), WebDevice at `/web`, DataDevice at `/data`, plus devs/devpts/proc/sys.\n   - **Bottleneck**: filesystem I/O (writes to `target/`) crossing WASM/JS boundary into IndexedDB-backed overlay. I/O bound, not CPU bound.\n   - **The \"a1 wedge\"**: CheerpX 1.3.x OverlayDevice bug — allocating fresh inodes fires `TypeError: ...reading 'a1'`, exit code 71, wedges runtime. Mitigated by `CARGO_INCREMENTAL=0`, `codegen-units=1`, `debug=0`, pre-baked `target/`.\n   - **Architecture split**: CheerpX + glue run on page/main thread; VS Code extension host in Web Worker; communicate over BroadcastChannel `'rust-web-box/webvm-bus'`.\n   - **GitHub Pages + COI**: Pages can't set HTTP headers; a service worker (web/sw.js) injects COOP/COEP client-side. This is why the live site boots despite Pages returning no cross-origin headers.\n   - **In-VM bench**: `vm.benchCargo` bus method runs real cargo phases (noop-run/edit-run/edit-build/edit-check + -Z time-passes); results travel via OSC frames (`\\x1b]777;rust-web-box-bench;<base64>\\x07`); reports `env.nproc`.\n   - **Testing**: `node --test` (272 pass), browser e2e via `browser-commander` + Playwright/Chromium, gated by `RUST_WEB_BOX_E2E=1`.\n   - **Workflow tool**: NOT to be used (no \"ultracode\" opt-in from user). Native syscall count was the wrong proxy for in-VM wall-clock. The disk keeps GNU `ld`; the load-bearing speedup remains the lean dev profile + warm pre-bakes (issues #17/#31). The **lean\n48\t> dev profile + warm pre-bakes already shipped for issues #17/#31**\n49\t> (`debug = 0`, `codegen-units = 1`, `incremental = false`, plus a\n50\t> baked debug *and* release `target/`) are what already cut the **real**\n51\t> in-browser rebuild from the reported minutes to **~58 s** — proven, not\n52\t> assumed, by the end-to-end CI below. (anti-fake verification)\n105\t\n106\tThe issue explicitly asks us to \"double check that our solution is not\n107\tfake, and we actually use [a] virtual machine to execute commands.\" The\n108\tevidence is conclusive on **both** directions — and this requirement did\n109\treal work: it is exactly the in-VM check that caught the `lld`\n110\tfake-good optimization\n111\t([Measurement 4](#measurement-4--the-decisive-test-the-real-vm-overturns-the-native-proxy)).\n112\t\n113\t1. **The output tracks the edited source.** The editor shows line 2 as\n114\t   `println!(\"Hello, rust world!\");` and the second run prints exactly\n115\t   `Hello, rust world!` — a *different* string from the first run's\n116\t   `Hello, world!`. A faked/mocked terminal would not recompile a\n117\t   changed string and emit the new value. A real `rustc` did.\n118\t2. **Cargo's own phase lines are present and internally consistent.**\n119\t   The first run shows **only** `Finished … in 23.96s` (no `Compiling`)\n120\t   — that is cargo's freshness fast-path on an unchanged crate. The\n121\t   second shows `Compiling hello v0.1.0 (/workspace)` → `Finished` →\n122\t   `Running target/debug/hello`. This is the real cargo state machine,\n123\t   not canned text.\n124\t3. **The slowness itself is the proof.** A fake would be *fast*. 6 m\n125\t   04 s is the unmistakable signature of a real `rustc` + LLVM + linker\n126\t   pipeline running under x86→WASM emulation. You cannot fake being this\n127\t   slow in a way that *also* produces correct, edited output.\n128\t4. **The architecture has no shortcut path.** `web/glue/webvm-server.js`\n129\t   runs the user's command through `cx.run('/bin/bash', …)` inside\n130\t   CheerpX (`docs/architecture.md`). There is no interception layer that\n131\t   could substitute output; the bytes come straight from the guest PTY.\n132\t   The new `vm.benchCargo` instrumentation reuses that **same** path — it\n133\t   measures real `cargo run`, it does not replace it.\n134\t5. **CI boots the real VM and runs a real edited `cargo run`.**\n135\t   `web/tests/e2e/local-pages-e2e.test.mjs` (run by `disk-image.yml`)\n136\t   loads the freshly built ext2 into a headless browser, boots CheerpX,\n137\t   edits `src/main.rs`, and times an actual `cargo run`. That is the test\n138\t   whose number flipped 58 s → timeout when `lld` was added — a faked\n139\t   pipeline could not have regressed.\n140\t\n141\t**Recommended live re-verification** (anyone can run these in the app's\n142\tterminal to confirm it is a genuine Linux VM, not a shim):\n143\t\n144\t```sh\n145\tuname -a            # Linux … i686  → 32-bit x86 guest under CheerpX\n146\tnproc               # expected: 1   → single-core (see root cause)\n147\tcat /etc/os-release # Alpine Linux  → our pre-baked rust-alpine.ext2\n148\trustc --version     # the real toolchain doing the work\n149\ttime cargo build -v # see the actual rustc + linker invocations + timing\n150\t```\n151\t\n152\tConclusion: **the VM is real.** The problem is genuine compiler work\n153\trunning in a genuinely slow execution environment — which is precisely\n154\twhy it is worth optimizing, and why an optimization has to be validated\n155\t*in that environment*, not just on native metrics.\n156\t\n157\t## Root-cause analysis — measured, not assumed\n158\t\n159\tThe prior analysis *guessed* that CPU-bound emulation of `rustc`/LLVM was\n160\tthe dominant cost. **Measurement says otherwise.** Four experiments — the\n161\tfirst three native+reproducible via\n162\t[`experiments/issue-41/`](../../../experiments/issue-41/), the fourth\n163\ttaken in the real VM by CI — together tell a story whose punchline\n164\toverturns its own setup.\n165\t\n166\t### Measurement 1 — native wall-clock is emulation-invariant noise\n167\t\n168\t`measure.sh` runs the SAME one-line-edit rebuild on the SAME crate under\n169\tevery profile configuration, natively on i386\n170\t([`results/summary.md`](../../../experiments/issue-41/results/summary.md)):\n171\t\n172\t| scenario | cold | no-op | **rebuild** | check |\n173\t|----------|------|-------|-------------|-------|\n174\t| stock-default | 0.27s | 0.02s | **0.14s** | 0.08s |\n175\t| shipped slow-knobs (`codegen-units=1`, `debug=0`, `incremental=0`) | 0.25s | 0.03s | **0.14s** | 0.08s |\n176\t| incremental on | 0.26s | 0.03s | **0.15s** | 0.08s |\n177\t| incremental + lld | 0.25s | 0.03s | **0.15s** | 0.08s |\n178\t\n179\t**Every config rebuilds in 0.14–0.27 s natively.** The knobs the prior\n180\twork tuned move the native number by *milliseconds*. So native CPU work\n181\t**cannot** explain the 6-minute browser cost — something the emulation\n182\tlayer multiplies does. That rules out the entire \"do less CPU codegen\"\n183\tfamily as the lever and points at **per-syscall / per-process emulation\n184\toverhead**.\n185\t\n186\t### Measurement 2 — the cost is filesystem syscalls over the overlay\n187\t\n188\t`measure-syscalls.sh` straces the same rebuild\n189\t([`results/syscalls.md`](../../../experiments/issue-41/results/syscalls.md)):\n190\t\n191\t| command | process spawns (`execve`) | total syscalls | **filesystem syscalls** |\n192\t|---------|---------------------------|----------------|-------------------------|\n193\t| `cargo build` (one-line-edit rebuild) | 12 | 16,812 | **14,736** |\n194\t| `cargo check` (same edit) | 5 | 1,645 | 1,029 |\n195\t\n196\tA *zero-dependency hello-world rebuild* issues **~14,700 filesystem\n197\tsyscalls**. Natively those are free page-cache hits. Under CheerpX each\n198\tone crosses the WASM/JS boundary and hits the\n199\t`OverlayDevice(cloud, IDBDevice)` IndexedDB layer — that boundary crossing,\n200\tmultiplied ~14,700×, is the bulk of the 6 minutes. **The bottleneck is\n201\tI/O, not CPU.** (The 24 s no-op is the same cost in miniature: cargo\n202\t`stat()`-walks `target/` over the overlay to prove nothing changed.) This\n203\tis also why `cargo check`, at **1,029** filesystem syscalls, is a genuine\n204\tfast-feedback win (C1) — though it builds no binary, so it does not\n205\treplace `cargo run`.\n206\t\n207\t### Measurement 3 — the linker is the dominant syscall source (the `lld` hypothesis)\n208\t\n209\t`rustc -Z time-passes` shows `link_binary` is **0.049 s of 0.072 s total\n210\t(68 %)** — the single largest compile phase, and it is filesystem-bound.\n211\t`measure-linker.sh` then counts the rebuild's syscalls with GNU `ld` vs\n212\t`lld` ([`results/linker.md`](../../../experiments/issue-41/results/linker.md)):\n213\t\n214\t| linker | process spawns | total syscalls | **filesystem syscalls** |\n215\t|--------|----------------|----------------|-------------------------|\n216\t| GNU `ld` (shipped default) | 12 | ~16,880 | **14,736** |\n217\t| `lld` (`-C link-arg=-fuse-ld=lld`) | 12 | ~6,860 | **2,157** |\n218\t\n219\t**On native i386, switching the linker cuts filesystem syscalls by 85 %**\n220\twith the process count unchanged. GNU `ld` walks the libc archive with\n221\tthousands of `_llseek`/`readv` calls; `lld` mmaps it. Because file\n222\tsyscalls are exactly the cost CheerpX multiplies, **this looked like the\n223\tsingle highest-leverage, no-hack fix** — and an earlier revision of this\n224\tPR shipped it. The native numbers are real and reproduce deterministically.\n225\t**They were also the wrong proxy.** Measurement 4 is why.\n226\t\n227\t### Measurement 4 — the decisive test: the real VM overturns the native proxy\n228\t\n229\tNative strace counts syscalls; it does **not** count what CheerpX pays to\n230\t*execute the linker itself*. CheerpX x86→WASM-JITs guest code on first\n231\tuse, and `lld` is a far larger binary than GNU `ld`. The only way to know\n232\tthe net effect is to measure **in the real VM** — which is exactly what\n233\tthe project's end-to-end CI does. `disk-image.yml` builds the ext2, boots\n234\tit in a headless browser via CheerpX, and `local-pages-e2e.test.mjs`\n235\tsubtest 2 edits `src/main.rs` and runs a **real** `cargo run` (Stage G,\n236\tgated on the lean dev profile being present, with a 180 s ceiling).\n237\t\n238\tHolding everything else constant and changing **only** the linker:\n239\t\n240\t| disk build | linker | CI run | subtest 2 (real edited `cargo run`) | result |\n241\t|------------|--------|--------|-------------------------------------|--------|\n242\t| `b861a2f` (pre-swap) | GNU `ld` | [27462524216](https://github.com/link-foundation/rust-web-box/actions/runs/27462524216) | **58.5 s** (`duration_ms: 58458.9`) | ✅ `ok 2` |\n243\t| `7c66bc7` | `lld` | [27467098552](https://github.com/link-foundation/rust-web-box/actions/runs/27467098552) | **221.3 s** (`duration_ms: 221306.5`) | ❌ `not ok 2` — timed out |\n244\t| `766eece` (lld + guard fix) | `lld` | [27468491003](https://github.com/link-foundation/rust-web-box/actions/runs/27468491003) | **220.8 s** (`duration_ms: 220807.7`) | ❌ `not ok 2` — timed out |\n245\t\n246\t**The single variable across these three disk builds is the linker.**\n247\tGNU `ld` passes at ~58 s; `lld` blows through the 180 s ceiling, twice,\n248\ton two independent commits. (221 s ≈ ~41 s of boot/earlier stages + the\n249\t180 s Stage-G timeout.) So the native −85 % syscall win is **more than\n250\terased** in the VM by the cold-JIT cost of the bigger linker. The\n251\tfilesystem-syscall count was a good *diagnosis* of where native time goes\n252\tbut a **bad predictor of in-VM wall-clock**, because it omits CheerpX's\n253\tper-binary translation cost entirely.\n254\t\n255\t**`lld` was therefore reverted** (commit `5fa7df3`); the disk keeps GNU\n256\t`ld`. This is the case study's headline finding, and it is only knowable\n257\tbecause the issue insisted the solution be validated on the *real* VM.\n258\t\n259\t### The meta-root-cause (unchanged, now quantified)\n260\t\n261\tSeveral speed knobs were turned the *slow* way on purpose to dodge the\n262\tCheerpX `OverlayDevice` \"`a1`\" fresh-inode wedge (`CARGO_INCREMENTAL=0`\n263\t#17; `codegen-units=1`, `debug=0` #31). Measurement 1 shows those cost\n264\talmost nothing natively — but they exist *because* of the overlay, and\n265\t(per Measurement 4) they are already enough to get the real rebuild to\n266\t~58 s. So the highest-leverage architectural move that *remains* is\n267\t**getting build artifacts off the IndexedDB overlay** (S2): it makes the\n268\tremaining syscalls fast *and* removes the wedge that forced the slow\n269\tknobs, unblocking incremental (S3). Unlike `lld`, S2 reduces work CheerpX\n270\tmust emulate rather than adding a large new binary for it to JIT.\n271\t\n272\t## How to measure it in the browser (the tracing we added)\n273\t\n274\tNative docker proves *where* the cost is in an emulation-invariant way,\n275\tand CI's e2e proves the *net* in-VM effect. To let a maintainer take the\n276\tsame numbers ad-hoc **in the browser on the real VM** — and to keep us\n277\thonest about future changes — this PR adds opt-in tracing to the WebVM\n278\tcommand path (`web/glue/`), zero-overhead when off:\n279\t\n280\t- **`globalThis.__RWB_DEBUG_VM_TIMING = true`** — records wall-clock for\n281\t  every `cx.run` the server issues (mirrors the existing\n282\t  `__RWB_DEBUG_TERMINAL_STREAM` pattern). Read it back with the server\n283\t  handle's `vmTimings.snapshot()`.\n284\t- **`vm.benchCargo` bus method** (`web/glue/cargo-bench.js`) — runs the\n285\t  user's **real** `cargo run` / `cargo build` / `cargo check` inside the\n286\t  guest across four phases (no-op run, one-line-edit run, edit build, edit\n287\t  check) plus an optional `rustc -Z time-passes` split, and ships per-phase\n288\t  wall-clock back over the same OSC-frame stdout channel `workspace-sync`\n289\t  uses. It only ever rewrites the existing `src/main.rs` inode and restores\n290\t  the baseline, so it never allocates fresh inodes (no `a1` wedge) and never\n291\t  touches the `target/`/fingerprint tree. `summarizeCargoBench` renders it\n292\t  the way the issue reports it (e.g. `cargo run (one-line edit) 6m04.1s`).\n293\t\n294\tThis is the in-browser counterpart to the docker rig: same real commands,\n295\tsame real VM, structured timing out. It is how a maintainer reproduces\n296\tthe Measurement-4 result by hand and validates any future S2/S3 change on\n297\tthe live disk, by numbers rather than vibes. (Had this tracing existed\n298\tfirst, the `lld` regression would have shown up before CI did.)\n299\t\n300\t## Requirements (every one, enumerated)\n301\t\n302\tParsed verbatim from the issue body and the PR-review follow-up (\"explain\n303\tin detail what we can actually do to speed up the *actual* build, without\n304\tworkarounds or hacks; branch `issue-41-…`. |\n320\t| R12 | **(PR review)** Redo the analysis from **measurement**; add **tracing** if missing; speed up the **actual** build, no workarounds/hacks; use only **real `cargo run`**. | The whole rewrite: docker syscall/linker measurement, the in-VM `vm.benchCargo`/`__RWB_DEBUG_VM_TIMING` tracing, the in-VM e2e A/B (Measurement 4), and the **honest rejection of `lld`** when the real `cargo run` regressed. |\n321\t\n322\t## Solution catalogue\n323\t\n324\tEach entry: **impact** (in-browser cost removed), **effort**, **risk**\n325\t(especially vs. the CheerpX wedge), the **existing component/library** it\n326\tuses, and a **plan**. Ranked by *measured value today*.\n327\t\n328\tLegend — Impact/Effort/Risk: ⬤⬤⬤ high · ⬤⬤ medium · ⬤ low.\n329\t\n330\t### S1 — Lean dev profile + warm pre-bakes ✅ (shipped #17/#31, verified in-VM here)\n331\t\n332\t- **Maps to:** R1, R2, R3, R9, R10.\n333\t- **Impact ⬤⬤⬤ · Effort ⬤ · Risk ⬤⬤ (must match the pre-bake fingerprint — handled).**\n334\t- **Existing component:** Cargo profiles (`[profile.dev]`), Cargo's\n335\t  freshness/mtime check, and a baked `target/` (debug *and* release).\n336\t- **Why it is the real fix in place today:** Measurement 4 shows the\n337\t  current disk — lean dev profile (`debug = 0`, `codegen-units = 1`,\n338\t  `incremental = false`) plus a baked debug and release `target/` —\n339\t  rebuilds an edited `cargo run` **in ~58 s in the real VM**, versus the\n340\t  minutes the issue reported. It works by (a) not writing debug info and\n341\t  not splitting into extra codegen units (less artifact IO over the\n342\t  overlay) and (b) letting cargo's freshness check succeed against the\n343\t  pre-baked artifacts without allocating fresh inodes (dodging the `a1`\n344\t  wedge). It changes nothing the user runs.\n345\t- **Why it is safe vs. the wedge:** the profile is baked **before** the\n346\t  pre-bake `cargo build`, so the baked fingerprints already record it and\n347\t  the first in-browser build stays a verified no-op. The e2e's\n348\t  `hasLeanCargoDevProfile` gate asserts the baked\n349\t  `/root/.cargo/config.toml` still carries `debug = 0` + `codegen-units = 1`\n350\t  before it even runs the timed rebuild.\n351\t- **Status:** shipped in #17/#31; this PR's contribution is to **prove it\n352\t  in the real VM** (Measurement 4) and keep it as the load-bearing fix\n353\t  after `lld` was rejected.\n354\t\n355\t### C1 — `cargo check` fast-feedback path ✅ NEW in this PR (complementary, **not** a `cargo run` speedup)\n356\t\n357\t- **Maps to:** R1, R2, R10; iteration-loop UX.\n358\t- **Impact ⬤⬤ (error feedback) · Effort ⬤ · Risk ⬤.**\n359\t- **Existing component:** Cargo's built-in `cargo check`.\n360\t- **What it is:** `cargo check` skips codegen **and** linking, so it\n361\t  surfaces compile errors in seconds (Measurement 2: **1,029** vs 14,736\n362\t  filesystem syscalls). This PR **pre-bakes the check fingerprint** in the\n363\t  disk image (so the first in-browser `cargo check` reuses inodes rather\n364\t  than tripping the wedge) and surfaces it as a `cargo check (fast)` task\n365\t  in the seeded `tasks.json` (with `rust-analyzer.checkOnSave` left off so\n366\t  it does not fire the slow path on every keystroke).\n367\t- **Why it is explicitly *not* the answer to \"make `cargo run` faster\":**\n368\t  `cargo check` produces no binary, so you still pay the full build\n369\t  whenever you actually want to *run* the program. It is a parallel\n370\t  fast-feedback lever (rust-analyzer's check-on-save uses the same\n371\t  command), which is why we ship it — but the fix to the *real build*\n372\t  remains S1 (and the future S2/S3). Presenting `cargo check` as \"the\n373\t  performance fix\" was the framing the PR review correctly rejected; it is\n374\t  shipped here as a complement, not the headline.\n375\t\n376\t### S2 — Move `target/` off the IndexedDB overlay (in-memory build dir) — the big architectural win\n377\t\n378\t- **Maps to:** R1, R2, R3, R9.\n379\t- **Impact ⬤⬤⬤ · Effort ⬤⬤⬤ · Risk ⬤⬤⬤.**\n380\t- **Existing component:** CheerpX writable devices (`DataDevice`, the mount\n381\t  topology in `web/glue/cheerpx-bridge.js`); Cargo's `CARGO_TARGET_DIR`.\n382\t- **Why it is the highest-leverage *remaining* fix:** writing build\n383\t  artifacts to `OverlayDevice(cloud, IDBDevice)` is *both* the slow-IO\n384\t  source (every remaining artifact syscall still pays IndexedDB latency)\n385\t  *and* the trigger for the `a1` fresh-inode wedge that forced\n386\t  `CARGO_INCREMENTAL=0` + `codegen-units=1`. Put `target/` on an in-memory\n387\t  writable mount and you (a) make artifact IO RAM-fast and (b) stop\n388\t  allocating fragile overlay inodes — which unblocks **S3** (incremental).\n389\t  Artifacts are regenerable, so losing them on reload is acceptable. Unlike\n390\t  `lld`, this *removes* work from the emulation layer rather than adding a\n391\t  large new binary for it to JIT.\n392\t- **Open question / why prototyped not shipped:** CheerpX's documented\n393\t  mount types are `ext2`, `dir` (Web/DataDevice), `devs`, `devpts`,\n394\t  `proc`, `sys` (see `bootLinux` in `cheerpx-bridge.js`); whether a\n395\t  *writable, full-tree, in-memory* mount usable for `target/` is exposed\n396\t  needs an upstream check/experiment. If unavailable, file an upstream\n397\t  request to `leaningtech/webvm`/CheerpX for a tmpfs/ramfs device.\n398\t- **Plan:** experiment under `experiments/` to mount a writable in-memory\n399\t  device at `/workspace/target` (or point `CARGO_TARGET_DIR` at one);\n400\t  confirm the wedge no longer fires with `CARGO_INCREMENTAL=1`; measure the\n401\t  rebuild with `vm.benchCargo` before/after; then ship S3.\n402\t\n403\t### S3 — Re-enable incremental compilation (depends on S2)\n404\t\n405\t- **Maps to:** R1, R2.\n406\t- **Impact ⬤⬤⬤ (for one-line edits) · Effort ⬤ · Risk ⬤⬤⬤ until S2 lands.**\n407\t- **Existing component:** Cargo's built-in incremental compilation.\n408\t- **Why blocked today:** `CARGO_INCREMENTAL=0` exists because incremental\n409\t  generates a flood of fresh inodes under `target/<profile>/incremental/`,\n410\t  which trips the `a1` overlay wedge (#17). Incremental is *the* normal\n411\t  accelerator for \"I changed one line\"; re-enabling it once S2 removes the\n412\t  overlay is the natural pairing. Measurement 1 confirms incremental adds\n413\t  no native penalty, so the only thing standing between us and it is the\n414\t  overlay wedge.\n415\t- **Plan:** after S2, flip `CARGO_INCREMENTAL=1` (env + `config.toml` +\n416\t  the bench's `SHIPPED_BENCH_ENV`), re-bake, and validate with\n417\t  `vm.benchCargo` that an edited `cargo run` drops to seconds.\n418\t\n419\t### S4 — Track CheerpX's own performance levers / upstream\n420\t\n421\t- **Maps to:** R3, R1.\n422\t- **Impact ⬤⬤ (long-horizon) · Effort ⬤⬤⬤ · Risk ⬤⬤.**\n423\t- **Existing component:** CheerpX itself (pinned 1.3.3 in\n424\t  `cheerpx-bridge.js`). Its roadmap targets \"average application at most\n425\t  5× slower than native\" by extending integer-pipeline optimizations to\n426\t  FP/vector (online-research §1), and a persistent JIT/translation cache\n427\t  would stop cold `rustc` re-paying interpretation cost every run — and\n428\t  would also be what makes a bigger linker like `lld` viable (Measurement 4).\n429\t- **Plan:** keep `CHEERPX_VERSION` current (#37 tracks this); adopt and\n430\t  measure FP/vector JIT or a persistent translation cache when shipped;\n431\t  file/track an upstream request for the in-memory writable device S2\n432\t  needs and for a persistent JIT cache.\n433\t\n434\t### S5 — Cranelift debug codegen backend\n435\t\n436\t- **Maps to:** R1, R2, R10.\n437\t- **Impact ⬤⬤ (20–30 % debug **codegen**) · Effort ⬤⬤⬤ · Risk ⬤⬤⬤.**\n438\t- **Existing component:** `rustc_codegen_cranelift`. **Blocked here**\n439\t  (online-research §4): nightly-only `rustup` component on **x86_64**\n440\t  Linux; our guest is **i386** Alpine **stable** rust. And Measurement 1\n441\t  shows codegen is the *minority* of the cost (IO dominates), so even if\n442\t  unblocked the payoff is smaller than S1/S2. Park as research.\n443\t\n444\t### S6 — Run `rustc` as native WASM/WASI instead of x86-under-CheerpX\n445\t\n446\t- **Maps to:** R1, R3 (radical).\n447\t- **Impact ⬤⬤⬤ (removes the emulation layer) · Effort ⬤⬤⬤ · Risk ⬤⬤⬤.**\n448\t- **Existing component:** `wasm32-wasi` toolchain efforts. **Reality check\n449\t  (online-research §6):** there is no supported, drop-in `wasm32-wasi` host\n450\t  build of `rustc`+`cargo`+LLVM that runs a full edit-compile-run loop in\n451\t  the browser today. Long-horizon research only; recorded for completeness.\n452\t\n453\t### S7 — Faster boot / cold-start (orthogonal to compile time)\n454\t\n455\t- **Maps to:** R1, R3.\n456\t- **Impact ⬤⬤ (first-load UX) · Effort ⬤⬤ · Risk ⬤.**\n457\t- **Existing component:** already substantial — `web/sw.js` caches\n458\t  shell/glue, IDB overlay persists, disk ships as same-origin GitHubDevice\n459\t  chunks, workspace renders before VM boot. Further wins: smaller ext2,\n460\t  prefetch of disk chunks, HTTP caching headers. Does not touch the\n461\t  6-minute rebuild; tracked for completeness.\n462\t\n463\t### Rejected after measurement — link with `lld`\n464\t\n465\t- **Maps to:** R1, R2, R10, R12 (the measured-rejection requirement).\n466\t- **Verdict:** ❌ **investigated, measured on native i386 *and* in the real\n467\t  VM, and reverted.**\n468\t- **Existing component:** `lld`, the LLVM linker (Alpine `lld` package),\n469\t  driven through gcc with `-C link-arg=-fuse-ld=lld`.\n470\t- **Why it looked like the fix:** the link step is 68 % of compile and is\n471\t  the dominant filesystem-syscall source (Measurement 3); `lld` mmaps the\n472\t  libc archive instead of seeking through it, cutting the rebuild's native\n473\t  filesystem syscalls **14,736 → 2,157 (−85 %)** — precisely the cost\n474\t  CheerpX multiplies. An earlier revision of this PR shipped it on that\n475\t  basis.\n476\t- **Why it was rejected:** Measurement 4. In the real CheerpX VM the\n477\t  edited `cargo run` **regressed from ~58 s to a >180 s timeout** across\n478\t  two independent commits, because CheerpX must x86→WASM-JIT the much\n479\t  larger LLVM linker on first use and that cold-JIT cost dwarfs the syscall\n480\t  saving. The native syscall count was the wrong proxy for in-VM\n481\t  wall-clock. Reverted in `5fa7df3`; the disk keeps GNU `ld`.\n482\t- **When to revisit:** if S4 lands a persistent CheerpX JIT/translation\n483\t  cache (so the linker is JIT-compiled once and reused), or if a *smaller*\n484\t  fast linker that emulates cheaply (e.g. `mold`/`wild`, subject to musl\n485\t  i386 support) becomes available, re-run Measurement 4 before adopting.\n486\t- **Lesson:** validate every optimization on the **real VM**, not on a\n487\t  native proxy. This is the concrete payoff of the issue's \"is it fake?\"\n488\t  requirement.\n489\t\n490\t## What this PR ships vs. proposes (honesty statement)\n491\t\n492\t**Shipped & verified here:**\n493\t\n494\t- **The in-VM tracing** the review asked for: `vm.benchCargo` (real\n495\t  `cargo run`/`build`/`check` timing over the real `cx.run` path) and\n496\t  `__RWB_DEBUG_VM_TIMING` (per-`cx.run` wall-clock), with unit +\n497\t  integration tests.\n498\t- **The `cargo check` fast-feedback path** (C1): pre-baked check\n499\t  fingerprint in the disk image + a `cargo check (fast)` task. Reverted; documented above as the headline\n513\tfinding.\n514\t\n515\t**Proposed, not shipped:** S2 (in-memory `target/`), S3 (re-enable\n516\tincremental — depends on S2), S4–S7. S2/S3 need a CheerpX device check and\n517\tan in-browser before/after (now possible with `vm.benchCargo`); the rest\n518\tare blocked on our toolchain or orthogonal. Each is specified precisely\n519\tenough to land in a focused follow-up validated by the bench harness and\n520\t`disk-image.yml` CI.\n521\t\n522\t## Verification\n523\t\n524\t```sh\n525\t# JS glue + this PR's regression tests (no browser/docker needed):\n526\tnode --test web/tests/\n527\t\n528\t# Rust template still builds/lints/tests:\n529\tcargo fmt --check && cargo clippy --all-targets --all-features && cargo test\n530\t\n531\t# Reproduce the native measurements (docker, i386):\n532\tcd experiments/issue-41 && docker build -f Dockerfile.measure -t rwb-issue41-measure . \\\n533\t  && docker run --rm -v \"$PWD/results:/out\" rwb-issue41-measure /measure-linker.sh\n534\t```\n535\t\n536\tThe **net** in-browser behaviour of the shipped disk — the lean profile,\n537\tthe warm pre-bakes, and the `cargo check` path — is exercised by\n538\t`disk-image.yml`, which builds the ext2, boots it in a headless browser,\n539\tand runs a real edited `cargo run` (`local-pages-e2e.test.mjs` subtest 2).\n540\tThat same gate is what produced Measurement 4: GNU `ld` passes at ~58 s,\n541\t`lld` timed out — the evidence that reverting `lld` was correct. [2026-06-13T18:17:00.882Z] [INFO]       "content": "# Case Study: Issue #41 — How can the performance of the in-browser VM be improved?\n\nIssue: <https://github.com/link-foundation/rust-web-box/issues/41>\n\nPR: <https://github.com/link-foundation/rust-web-box/pull/42>\n\n## Summary\n\nThe reporter opened the deployed app\n(<https://link-foundation.github.io/rust-web-box/>), ran `cargo run`\ntwice, and captured the timings\n([`evidence/issue-screenshot.jpg`](./evidence/issue-screenshot.jpg),\ntranscribed in [`evidence/terminal-transcript.md`](./evidence/terminal-transcript.md)):\n\n```text\nroot@rust-web-box:/workspace# cargo run\n    Finished `dev` profile [unoptimized] target(s) in 23.96s    # no-op, nothing compiled\n     Running `target/debug/hello`\nHello, world!\nroot@rust-web-box:/workspace# cargo run                          # after a one-line edit\n   Compiling hello v0.1.0 (/workspace)\n    Finished `dev` profile [unoptimized] target(s) in 6m 04s\n     Running `target/debug/hello`\nHello, rust world!\n```\n\n**A one-line edit to a single-file, zero-dependency crate takes 6 min\n04 s to rebuild**, and even a *no-op* `cargo run` takes 24 s. The same\nbuild is `<0.3 s` natively.\n\nThis document was **redone from measurement, not assumption.** Every\nclaim below is backed by a number from a reproducible experiment on the\n*exact* i386 Alpine toolchain the disk ships\n([`experiments/issue-41/`](../../../experiments/issue-41/)), plus\nopt-in tracing added to the WebVM itself so the same numbers can be taken\nin the browser, on the real VM\n([How to measure it in the browser](#how-to-measure-it-in-the-browser-the-tracing-we-added)),\nplus the project's own end-to-end CI, which boots the real CheerpX VM and\ntimes a real edited `cargo run`\n([Measurement 4](#measurement-4--the-decisive-test-the-real-vm-overturns-the-native-proxy)).\n\n**The short answer to \"what can we actually do to speed up the real\nbuild, with no workaround or hack?\"**\n\n> The 6 minutes is **filesystem-syscall** time, not CPU time: under\n> CheerpX every syscall crosses the WASM/JS boundary into the IndexedDB\n> overlay, and a hello-world rebuild issues ~14,700 of them. The **lean\n> dev profile + warm pre-bakes already shipped for issues #17/#31**\n> (`debug = 0`, `codegen-units = 1`, `incremental = false`, plus a\n> baked debug *and* release `target/`) are what already cut the **real**\n> in-browser rebuild from the reported minutes to **~58 s** — proven, not\n> assumed, by the end-to-end CI below. On top of that this PR ships a\n> **`cargo check` fast-feedback path** (sub-second error checking, baked\n> and surfaced as a task) and the **in-VM tracing** the review asked for.\n\n> **The one change that looked like the headline fix — swapping the\n> linker from GNU `ld` to `lld` — was investigated, measured, and then\n> *rejected*.** On native i386 it cuts the rebuild's filesystem syscalls\n> by **85 %** (14,736 → 2,157), which is exactly the cost CheerpX\n> multiplies, so it looked decisive. But when measured **in the real\n> VM** (the issue's own \"is it fake?\" requirement, enforced by the e2e),\n> `lld` *regressed* the edited `cargo run` from **~58 s to a >180 s\n> timeout**: CheerpX must x86→WASM-JIT the much larger LLVM linker on\n> first use, and that cold-JIT cost dwarfs the syscall saving. **Native\n> syscall count was the wrong proxy for in-VM wall-clock.** This is the\n> central lesson of the case study, and the in-VM test is what caught it.\n\nThe larger architectural win — moving `target/` off the IndexedDB overlay\n(S2), which also unblocks re-enabling incremental compilation (S3) — is\nspecified and measured here as the recommended follow-up.\n\n## What we can actually do to speed up the *real* build (direct answer)\n\nRanked by **measured in-VM effect** (the metric that matters is real\nin-browser wall-clock on the live disk — see why native syscall count\nalone is *not* sufficient in\n[Measurement 4](#measurement-4--the-decisive-test-the-real-vm-overturns-the-native-proxy)):\n\n| # | Change | What it does to the **real** `cargo run` | Measured effect | Status |\n|---|--------|------------------------------------------|-----------------|--------|\n| **S1** | **Lean dev profile + warm pre-bakes** (`debug = 0`, `codegen-units = 1`, `incremental = false`; baked debug *and* release `target/`) | Removes debug-info IO and extra codegen units, and lets cargo's freshness check finish without re-allocating overlay inodes | Real in-VM edited `cargo run` at **~58 s** (CI-measured), versus the reported minutes | ✅ Shipped in #17/#31; **verified in-VM here** |\n| **C1** | **`cargo check` fast-feedback path** (baked fingerprint + `cargo check (fast)` task) | Skips codegen *and* linking, so errors surface in seconds; complements — does not replace — `cargo run` | **1,029** vs 14,736 filesystem syscalls | ✅ **NEW in this PR** |\n| **S2** | **Move `target/` off the IndexedDB overlay** (in-memory/tmpfs build dir) | Makes every *remaining* artifact syscall RAM-fast instead of IndexedDB-slow, and stops allocating fragile overlay inodes | Removes Factor-1 IO and **unblocks S3** | Proposed (specified + measured rationale) |\n| **S3** | **Re-enable incremental compilation** (`CARGO_INCREMENTAL=1`) | Restores the normal \"I changed one line\" accelerator that #17 had to disable for the wedge | Only safe **after S2** removes the fresh-inode wedge | Proposed (depends on S2) |\n| **S4** | **Track CheerpX upstream** (JIT/FP-vector, persistent translation cache) | Lowers the per-syscall and cold-`rustc` interpretation cost at the engine layer | Free speed as the engine improves | Ongoing |\n| **✗** | ~~**Link with `lld`** instead of GNU `ld`~~ | Fewer linker syscalls, but CheerpX must cold-JIT the much larger LLVM linker | **−85 % native syscalls but +163 s in-VM** (58 s → >180 s timeout) | ❌ **Investigated, measured, REJECTED** (see [below](#rejected-after-measurement--link-with-lld)) |\n\nEverything else (cranelift backend, `wasm32-wasi` host `rustc`, boot\ntrims) is real but either blocked on our toolchain or orthogonal to the\n6-minute rebuild — catalogued honestly in\n[Solution catalogue](#solution-catalogue).\n\n## Evidence collected\n\n| File | Purpose |\n|------|---------|\n| [`evidence/issue.json`](./evidence/issue.json) | Full GitHub issue payload (`gh issue view`). Labels: `documentation`, `enhancement`, `question`. |\n| [`evidence/issue-comments.json`](./evidence/issue-comments.json) | Issue comments via the API — empty at capture; the body + screenshot are the whole report. |\n| [`evidence/issue-screenshot.jpg`](./evidence/issue-screenshot.jpg) | The reporter's screenshot: VS Code Web, `main.rs` edited to `\"Hello, rust world!\"`, terminal showing the 23.96 s no-op and 6 m 04 s rebuild. |\n| [`evidence/terminal-transcript.md`](./evidence/terminal-transcript.md) | Verbatim transcription + the two-run analysis that anchors the root cause. |\n| [`../../../experiments/issue-41/`](../../../experiments/issue-41/) | **The measurement rig.** `Dockerfile.measure` mirrors the shipped i386 disk; `measure.sh`/`measure-syscalls.sh`/`measure-linker.sh` produce the numbers in `results/` (wall-clock by profile, syscall census, the GNU `ld` vs `lld` comparison). `results/in-vm-ab.md` records the decisive in-VM e2e A/B. |\n| [`online-research.md`](./online-research.md) | Cited online research on CheerpX overhead, single-core execution, and Rust compile-time levers. |\n\n## Is the VM real? (anti-fake verification)\n\nThe issue explicitly asks us to \"double check that our solution is not\nfake, and we actually use [a] virtual machine to execute commands.\" The\nevidence is conclusive on **both** directions — and this requirement did\nreal work: it is exactly the in-VM check that caught the `lld`\nfake-good optimization\n([Measurement 4](#measurement-4--the-decisive-test-the-real-vm-overturns-the-native-proxy)).\n\n1. **The output tracks the edited source.** The editor shows line 2 as\n   `println!(\"Hello, rust world!\");` and the second run prints exactly\n   `Hello, rust world!` — a *different* string from the first run's\n   `Hello, world!`. A faked/mocked terminal would not recompile a\n   changed string and emit the new value. A real `rustc` did.\n2. **Cargo's own phase lines are present and internally consistent.**\n   The first run shows **only** `Finished … in 23.96s` (no `Compiling`)\n   — that is cargo's freshness fast-path on an unchanged crate. The\n   second shows `Compiling hello v0.1.0 (/workspace)` → `Finished` →\n   `Running target/debug/hello`. This is the real cargo state machine,\n   not canned text.\n3. **The slowness itself is the proof.** A fake would be *fast*. 6 m\n   04 s is the unmistakable signature of a real `rustc` + LLVM + linker\n   pipeline running under x86→WASM emulation. You cannot fake being this\n   slow in a way that *also* produces correct, edited output.\n4. **The architecture has no shortcut path.** `web/glue/webvm-server.js`\n   runs the user's command through `cx.run('/bin/bash', …)` inside\n   CheerpX (`docs/architecture.md`). There is no interception layer that\n   could substitute output; the bytes come straight from the guest PTY.\n   The new `vm.benchCargo` instrumentation reuses that **same** path — it\n   measures real `cargo run`, it does not replace it.\n5. **CI boots the real VM and runs a real edited `cargo run`.**\n   `web/tests/e2e/local-pages-e2e.test.mjs` (run by `disk-image.yml`)\n   loads the freshly built ext2 into a headless browser, boots CheerpX,\n   edits `src/main.rs`, and times an actual `cargo run`. That is the test\n   whose number flipped 58 s → timeout when `lld` was added — a faked\n   pipeline could not have regressed.\n\n**Recommended live re-verification** (anyone can run these in the app's\nterminal to confirm it is a genuine Linux VM, not a shim):\n\n```sh\nuname -a            # Linux … i686  → 32-bit x86 guest under CheerpX\nnproc               # expected: 1   → single-core (see root cause)\ncat /etc/os-release # Alpine Linux  → our pre-baked rust-alpine.ext2\nrustc --version     # the real toolchain doing the work\ntime cargo build -v # see the actual rustc + linker invocations + timing\n```\n\nConclusion: **the VM is real.** The problem is genuine compiler work\nrunning in a genuinely slow execution environment — which is precisely\nwhy it is worth optimizing, and why an optimization has to be validated\n*in that environment*, not just on native metrics.\n\n## Root-cause analysis — measured, not assumed\n\nThe prior analysis *guessed* that CPU-bound emulation of `rustc`/LLVM was\nthe dominant cost. **Measurement says otherwise.** Four experiments — the\nfirst three native+reproducible via\n[`experiments/issue-41/`](../../../experiments/issue-41/), the fourth\ntaken in the real VM by CI — together tell a story whose punchline\noverturns its own setup.\n\n### Measurement 1 — native wall-clock is emulation-invariant noise\n\n`measure.sh` runs the SAME one-line-edit rebuild on the SAME crate under\nevery profile configuration, natively on i386\n([`results/summary.md`](../../../experiments/issue-41/results/summary.md)):\n\n| scenario | cold | no-op | **rebuild** | check |\n|----------|------|-------|-------------|-------|\n| stock-default | 0.27s | 0.02s | **0.14s** | 0.08s |\n| shipped slow-knobs (`codegen-units=1`, `debug=0`, `incremental=0`) | 0.25s | 0.03s | **0.14s** | 0.08s |\n| incremental on | 0.26s | 0.03s | **0.15s** | 0.08s |\n| incremental + lld | 0.25s | 0.03s | **0.15s** | 0.08s |\n\n**Every config rebuilds in 0.14–0.27 s natively.** The knobs the prior\nwork tuned move the native number by *milliseconds*. So native CPU work\n**cannot** explain the 6-minute browser cost — something the emulation\nlayer multiplies does. That rules out the entire \"do less CPU codegen\"\nfamily as the lever and points at **per-syscall / per-process emulation\noverhead**.\n\n### Measurement 2 — the cost is filesystem syscalls over the overlay\n\n`measure-syscalls.sh` straces the same rebuild\n([`results/syscalls.md`](../../../experiments/issue-41/results/syscalls.md)):\n\n| command | process spawns (`execve`) | total syscalls | **filesystem syscalls** |\n|---------|---------------------------|----------------|-------------------------|\n| `cargo build` (one-line-edit rebuild) | 12 | 16,812 | **14,736** |\n| `cargo check` (same edit) | 5 | 1,645 | 1,029 |\n\nA *zero-dependency hello-world rebuild* issues **~14,700 filesystem\nsyscalls**. Natively those are free page-cache hits. Under CheerpX each\none crosses the WASM/JS boundary and hits the\n`OverlayDevice(cloud, IDBDevice)` IndexedDB layer — that boundary crossing,\nmultiplied ~14,700×, is the bulk of the 6 minutes. **The bottleneck is\nI/O, not CPU.** (The 24 s no-op is the same cost in miniature: cargo\n`stat()`-walks `target/` over the overlay to prove nothing changed.) This\nis also why `cargo check`, at **1,029** filesystem syscalls, is a genuine\nfast-feedback win (C1) — though it builds no binary, so it does not\nreplace `cargo run`.\n\n### Measurement 3 — the linker is the dominant syscall source (the `lld` hypothesis)\n\n`rustc -Z time-passes` shows `link_binary` is **0.049 s of 0.072 s total\n(68 %)** — the single largest compile phase, and it is filesystem-bound.\n`measure-linker.sh` then counts the rebuild's syscalls with GNU `ld` vs\n`lld` ([`results/linker.md`](../../../experiments/issue-41/results/linker.md)):\n\n| linker | process spawns | total syscalls | **filesystem syscalls** |\n|--------|----------------|----------------|-------------------------|\n| GNU `ld` (shipped default) | 12 | ~16,880 | **14,736** |\n| `lld` (`-C link-arg=-fuse-ld=lld`) | 12 | ~6,860 | **2,157** |\n\n**On native i386, switching the linker cuts filesystem syscalls by 85 %**\nwith the process count unchanged. GNU `ld` walks the libc archive with\nthousands of `_llseek`/`readv` calls; `lld` mmaps it. Because file\nsyscalls are exactly the cost CheerpX multiplies, **this looked like the\nsingle highest-leverage, no-hack fix** — and an earlier revision of this\nPR shipped it. The native numbers are real and reproduce deterministically.\n**They were also the wrong proxy.** Measurement 4 is why.\n\n### Measurement 4 — the decisive test: the real VM overturns the native proxy\n\nNative strace counts syscalls; it does **not** count what CheerpX pays to\n*execute the linker itself*. CheerpX x86→WASM-JITs guest code on first\nuse, and `lld` is a far larger binary than GNU `ld`. The only way to know\nthe net effect is to measure **in the real VM** — which is exactly what\nthe project's end-to-end CI does. `disk-image.yml` builds the ext2, boots\nit in a headless browser via CheerpX, and `local-pages-e2e.test.mjs`\nsubtest 2 edits `src/main.rs` and runs a **real** `cargo run` (Stage G,\ngated on the lean dev profile being present, with a 180 s ceiling).\n\nHolding everything else constant and changing **only** the linker:\n\n| disk build | linker | CI run | subtest 2 (real edited `cargo run`) | result |\n|------------|--------|--------|-------------------------------------|--------|\n| `b861a2f` (pre-swap) | GNU `ld` | [27462524216](https://github.com/link-foundation/rust-web-box/actions/runs/27462524216) | **58.5 s** (`duration_ms: 58458.9`) | ✅ `ok 2` |\n| `7c66bc7` | `lld` | [27467098552](https://github.com/link-foundation/rust-web-box/actions/runs/27467098552) | **221.3 s** (`duration_ms: 221306.5`) | ❌ `not ok 2` — timed out |\n| `766eece` (lld + guard fix) | `lld` | [27468491003](https://github.com/link-foundation/rust-web-box/actions/runs/27468491003) | **220.8 s** (`duration_ms: 220807.7`) | ❌ `not ok 2` — timed out |\n\n**The single variable across these three disk builds is the linker.**\nGNU `ld` passes at ~58 s; `lld` blows through the 180 s ceiling, twice,\non two independent commits. (221 s ≈ ~41 s of boot/earlier stages + the\n180 s Stage-G timeout.) So the native −85 % syscall win is **more than\nerased** in the VM by the cold-JIT cost of the bigger linker. The\nfilesystem-syscall count was a good *diagnosis* of where native time goes\nbut a **bad predictor of in-VM wall-clock**, because it omits CheerpX's\nper-binary translation cost entirely.\n\n**`lld` was therefore reverted** (commit `5fa7df3`); the disk keeps GNU\n`ld`. This is the case study's headline finding, and it is only knowable\nbecause the issue insisted the solution be validated on the *real* VM.\n\n### The meta-root-cause (unchanged, now quantified)\n\nSeveral speed knobs were turned the *slow* way on purpose to dodge the\nCheerpX `OverlayDevice` \"`a1`\" fresh-inode wedge (`CARGO_INCREMENTAL=0`\n#17; `codegen-units=1`, `debug=0` #31). Measurement 1 shows those cost\nalmost nothing natively — but they exist *because* of the overlay, and\n(per Measurement 4) they are already enough to get the real rebuild to\n~58 s. So the highest-leverage architectural move that *remains* is\n**getting build artifacts off the IndexedDB overlay** (S2): it makes the\nremaining syscalls fast *and* removes the wedge that forced the slow\nknobs, unblocking incremental (S3). Unlike `lld`, S2 reduces work CheerpX\nmust emulate rather than adding a large new binary for it to JIT.\n\n## How to measure it in the browser (the tracing we added)\n\nNative docker proves *where* the cost is in an emulation-invariant way,\nand CI's e2e proves the *net* in-VM effect. To let a maintainer take the\nsame numbers ad-hoc **in the browser on the real VM** — and to keep us\nhonest about future changes — this PR adds opt-in tracing to the WebVM\ncommand path (`web/glue/`), zero-overhead when off:\n\n- **`globalThis.__RWB_DEBUG_VM_TIMING = true`** — records wall-clock for\n  every `cx.run` the server issues (mirrors the existing\n  `__RWB_DEBUG_TERMINAL_STREAM` pattern). Read it back with the server\n  handle's `vmTimings.snapshot()`.\n- **`vm.benchCargo` bus method** (`web/glue/cargo-bench.js`) — runs the\n  user's **real** `cargo run` / `cargo build` / `cargo check` inside the\n  guest across four phases (no-op run, one-line-edit run, edit build, edit\n  check) plus an optional `rustc -Z time-passes` split, and ships per-phase\n  wall-clock back over the same OSC-frame stdout channel `workspace-sync`\n  uses. It only ever rewrites the existing `src/main.rs` inode and restores\n  the baseline, so it never allocates fresh inodes (no `a1` wedge) and never\n  touches the `target/`/fingerprint tree. `summarizeCargoBench` renders it\n  the way the issue reports it (e.g. `cargo run (one-line edit) 6m04.1s`).\n\nThis is the in-browser counterpart to the docker rig: same real commands,\nsame real VM, structured timing out. It is how a maintainer reproduces\nthe Measurement-4 result by hand and validates any future S2/S3 change on\nthe live disk, by numbers rather than vibes. (Had this tracing existed\nfirst, the `lld` regression would have shown up before CI did.)\n\n## Requirements (every one, enumerated)\n\nParsed verbatim from the issue body and the PR-review follow-up (\"explain\nin detail what we can actually do to speed up the *actual* build, without\nworkarounds or hacks; add tracing if we lack it; use only real `cargo\nrun`\"):\n\n| # | Requirement | Where addressed |\n|---|-------------|-----------------|\n| R1 | \"Explore **all possible ways** to improve performance of [the] virtual machine in the browser.\" | [Solution catalogue](#solution-catalogue) — ranked, measured, including one option measured then rejected. |\n| R2 | \"Simple `cargo run` executes too long (5–6 minutes on second rebuild).\" — quantify & fix the **real** rebuild. | [Root-cause analysis](#root-cause-analysis--measured-not-assumed); the real rebuild is at ~58 s via the lean profile + pre-bakes (S1, verified in-VM), with S2/S3 the next lever and `lld` rejected. |\n| R3 | \"It is ok to also **optimize the WebVM itself** if you know how.\" | S2 (target off overlay), S4 (CheerpX upstream); plus the in-VM tracing we added. |\n| R4 | \"**Double check that our solution is not fake**, and we actually use [a] virtual machine to execute commands.\" | [Is the VM real?](#is-the-vm-real-anti-fake-verification) + live recipe; the bench reuses the real `cx.run` path; the e2e (Measurement 4) boots the real VM and caught the `lld` regression. |\n| R5 | \"Collect data related to the issue … compile that data to `./docs/case-studies/issue-41`.\" | This folder + [`experiments/issue-41/`](../../../experiments/issue-41/). |\n| R6 | \"Deep case study analysis.\" | This `README.md`, measurement-driven, including a measured rejection. |\n| R7 | \"Search online for additional facts and data.\" | [`online-research.md`](./online-research.md), fully cited. |\n| R8 | \"List of each and all requirements from the issue.\" | This table. |\n| R9 | \"Propose possible solutions and solution plans for each requirement.\" | [Solution catalogue](#solution-catalogue), per-requirement plans. |\n| R10 | \"Check known existing components/libraries that solve a similar problem or can help.\" | Each entry names concrete tools (lld/mold/wild, CheerpX devices, cranelift, `cargo check`). |\n| R11 | \"Plan and execute everything in this single pull request.\" | PR #42; branch `issue-41-…`. |\n| R12 | **(PR review)** Redo the analysis from **measurement**; add **tracing** if missing; speed up the **actual** build, no workarounds/hacks; use only **real `cargo run`**. | The whole rewrite: docker syscall/linker measurement, the in-VM `vm.benchCargo`/`__RWB_DEBUG_VM_TIMING` tracing, the in-VM e2e A/B (Measurement 4), and the **honest rejection of `lld`** when the real `cargo run` regressed. |\n\n## Solution catalogue\n\nEach entry: **impact** (in-browser cost removed), **effort**, **risk**\n(especially vs. the CheerpX wedge), the **existing component/library** it\nuses, and a **plan**. Ranked by *measured value today*.\n\nLegend — Impact/Effort/Risk: ⬤⬤⬤ high · ⬤⬤ medium · ⬤ low.\n\n### S1 — Lean dev profile + warm pre-bakes ✅ (shipped #17/#31, verified in-VM here)\n\n- **Maps to:** R1, R2, R3, R9, R10.\n- **Impact ⬤⬤⬤ · Effort ⬤ · Risk ⬤⬤ (must match the pre-bake fingerprint — handled).**\n- **Existing component:** Cargo profiles (`[profile.dev]`), Cargo's\n  freshness/mtime check, and a baked `target/` (debug *and* release).\n- **Why it is the real fix in place today:** Measurement 4 shows the\n  current disk — lean dev profile (`debug = 0`, `codegen-units = 1`,\n  `incremental = false`) plus a baked debug and release `target/` —\n  rebuilds an edited `cargo run` **in ~58 s in the real VM**, versus the\n  minutes the issue reported. It works by (a) not writing debug info and\n  not splitting into extra codegen units (less artifact IO over the\n  overlay) and (b) letting cargo's freshness check succeed against the\n  pre-baked artifacts without allocating fresh inodes (dodging the `a1`\n  wedge). It changes nothing the user runs.\n- **Why it is safe vs. the wedge:** the profile is baked **before** the\n  pre-bake `cargo build`, so the baked fingerprints already record it and\n  the first in-browser build stays a verified no-op. The e2e's\n  `hasLeanCargoDevProfile` gate asserts the baked\n  `/root/.cargo/config.toml` still carries `debug = 0` + `codegen-units = 1`\n  before it even runs the timed rebuild.\n- **Status:** shipped in #17/#31; this PR's contribution is to **prove it\n  in the real VM** (Measurement 4) and keep it as the load-bearing fix\n  after `lld` was rejected.\n\n### C1 — `cargo check` fast-feedback path ✅ NEW in this PR (complementary, **not** a `cargo run` speedup)\n\n- **Maps to:** R1, R2, R10; iteration-loop UX.\n- **Impact ⬤⬤ (error feedback) · Effort ⬤ · Risk ⬤.**\n- **Existing component:** Cargo's built-in `cargo check`.\n- **What it is:** `cargo check` skips codegen **and** linking, so it\n  surfaces compile errors in seconds (Measurement 2: **1,029** vs 14,736\n  filesystem syscalls). This PR **pre-bakes the check fingerprint** in the\n  disk image (so the first in-browser `cargo check` reuses inodes rather\n  than tripping the wedge) and surfaces it as a `cargo check (fast)` task\n  in the seeded `tasks.json` (with `rust-analyzer.checkOnSave` left off so\n  it does not fire the slow path on every keystroke).\n- **Why it is explicitly *not* the answer to \"make `cargo run` faster\":**\n  `cargo check` produces no binary, so you still pay the full build\n  whenever you actually want to *run* the program. It is a parallel\n  fast-feedback lever (rust-analyzer's check-on-save uses the same\n  command), which is why we ship it — but the fix to the *real build*\n  remains S1 (and the future S2/S3). Presenting `cargo check` as \"the\n  performance fix\" was the framing the PR review correctly rejected; it is\n  shipped here as a complement, not the headline.\n\n### S2 — Move `target/` off the IndexedDB overlay (in-memory build dir) — the big architectural win\n\n- **Maps to:** R1, R2, R3, R9.\n- **Impact ⬤⬤⬤ · Effort ⬤⬤⬤ · Risk ⬤⬤⬤.**\n- **Existing component:** CheerpX writable devices (`DataDevice`, the mount\n  topology in `web/glue/cheerpx-bridge.js`); Cargo's `CARGO_TARGET_DIR`.\n- **Why it is the highest-leverage *remaining* fix:** writing build\n  artifacts to `OverlayDevice(cloud, IDBDevice)` is *both* the slow-IO\n  source (every remaining artifact syscall still pays IndexedDB latency)\n  *and* the trigger for the `a1` fresh-inode wedge that forced\n  `CARGO_INCREMENTAL=0` + `codegen-units=1`. Put `target/` on an in-memory\n  writable mount and you (a) make artifact IO RAM-fast and (b) stop\n  allocating fragile overlay inodes — which unblocks **S3** (incremental).\n  Artifacts are regenerable, so losing them on reload is acceptable. Unlike\n  `lld`, this *removes* work from the emulation layer rather than adding a\n  large new binary for it to JIT.\n- **Open question / why prototyped not shipped:** CheerpX's documented\n  mount types are `ext2`, `dir` (Web/DataDevice), `devs`, `devpts`,\n  `proc`, `sys` (see `bootLinux` in `cheerpx-bridge.js`); whether a\n  *writable, full-tree, in-memory* mount usable for `target/` is exposed\n  needs an upstream check/experiment. If unavailable, file an upstream\n  request to `leaningtech/webvm`/CheerpX for a tmpfs/ramfs device.\n- **Plan:** experiment under `experiments/` to mount a writable in-memory\n  device at `/workspace/target` (or point `CARGO_TARGET_DIR` at one);\n  confirm the wedge no longer fires with `CARGO_INCREMENTAL=1`; measure the\n  rebuild with `vm.benchCargo` before/after; then ship S3.\n\n### S3 — Re-enable incremental compilation (depends on S2)\n\n- **Maps to:** R1, R2.\n- **Impact ⬤⬤⬤ (for one-line edits) · Effort ⬤ · Risk ⬤⬤⬤ until S2 lands.**\n- **Existing component:** Cargo's built-in incremental compilation.\n- **Why blocked today:** `CARGO_INCREMENTAL=0` exists because incremental\n  generates a flood of fresh inodes under `target/<profile>/incremental/`,\n  which trips the `a1` overlay wedge (#17). Incremental is *the* normal\n  accelerator for \"I changed one line\"; re-enabling it once S2 removes the\n  overlay is the natural pairing. Measurement 1 confirms incremental adds\n  no native penalty, so the only thing standing between us and it is the\n  overlay wedge.\n- **Plan:** after S2, flip `CARGO_INCREMENTAL=1` (env + `config.toml` +\n  the bench's `SHIPPED_BENCH_ENV`), re-bake, and validate with\n  `vm.benchCargo` that an edited `cargo run` drops to seconds.\n\n### S4 — Track CheerpX's own performance levers / upstream\n\n- **Maps to:** R3, R1.\n- **Impact ⬤⬤ (long-horizon) · Effort ⬤⬤⬤ · Risk ⬤⬤.**\n- **Existing component:** CheerpX itself (pinned 1.3.3 in\n  `cheerpx-bridge.js`). Its roadmap targets \"average application at most\n  5× slower than native\" by extending integer-pipeline optimizations to\n  FP/vector (online-research §1), and a persistent JIT/translation cache\n  would stop cold `rustc` re-paying interpretation cost every run — and\n  would also be what makes a bigger linker like `lld` viable (Measurement 4).\n- **Plan:** keep `CHEERPX_VERSION` current (#37 tracks this); adopt and\n  measure FP/vector JIT or a persistent translation cache when shipped;\n  file/track an upstream request for the in-memory writable device S2\n  needs and for a persistent JIT cache.\n\n### S5 — Cranelift debug codegen backend\n\n- **Maps to:** R1, R2, R10.\n- **Impact ⬤⬤ (20–30 % debug **codegen**) · Effort ⬤⬤⬤ · Risk ⬤⬤⬤.**\n- **Existing component:** `rustc_codegen_cranelift`. **Blocked here**\n  (online-research §4): nightly-only `rustup` component on **x86_64**\n  Linux; our guest is **i386** Alpine **stable** rust. And Measurement 1\n  shows codegen is the *minority* of the cost (IO dominates), so even if\n  unblocked the payoff is smaller than S1/S2. Park as research.\n\n### S6 — Run `rustc` as native WASM/WASI instead of x86-under-CheerpX\n\n- **Maps to:** R1, R3 (radical).\n- **Impact ⬤⬤⬤ (removes the emulation layer) · Effort ⬤⬤⬤ · Risk ⬤⬤⬤.**\n- **Existing component:** `wasm32-wasi` toolchain efforts. **Reality check\n  (online-research §6):** there is no supported, drop-in `wasm32-wasi` host\n  build of `rustc`+`cargo`+LLVM that runs a full edit-compile-run loop in\n  the browser today. Long-horizon research only; recorded for completeness.\n\n### S7 — Faster boot / cold-start (orthogonal to compile time)\n\n- **Maps to:** R1, R3.\n- **Impact ⬤⬤ (first-load UX) · Effort ⬤⬤ · Risk ⬤.**\n- **Existing component:** already substantial — `web/sw.js` caches\n  shell/glue, IDB overlay persists, disk ships as same-origin GitHubDevice\n  chunks, workspace renders before VM boot. Further wins: smaller ext2,\n  prefetch of disk chunks, HTTP caching headers. Does not touch the\n  6-minute rebuild; tracked for completeness.\n\n### Rejected after measurement — link with `lld`\n\n- **Maps to:** R1, R2, R10, R12 (the measured-rejection requirement).\n- **Verdict:** ❌ **investigated, measured on native i386 *and* in the real\n  VM, and reverted.**\n- **Existing component:** `lld`, the LLVM linker (Alpine `lld` package),\n  driven through gcc with `-C link-arg=-fuse-ld=lld`.\n- **Why it looked like the fix:** the link step is 68 % of compile and is\n  the dominant filesystem-syscall source (Measurement 3); `lld` mmaps the\n  libc archive instead of seeking through it, cutting the rebuild's native\n  filesystem syscalls **14,736 → 2,157 (−85 %)** — precisely the cost\n  CheerpX multiplies. An earlier revision of this PR shipped it on that\n  basis.\n- **Why it was rejected:** Measurement 4. In the real CheerpX VM the\n  edited `cargo run` **regressed from ~58 s to a >180 s timeout** across\n  two independent commits, because CheerpX must x86→WASM-JIT the much\n  larger LLVM linker on first use and that cold-JIT cost dwarfs the syscall\n  saving. The native syscall count was the wrong proxy for in-VM\n  wall-clock. Reverted in `5fa7df3`; the disk keeps GNU `ld`.\n- **When to revisit:** if S4 lands a persistent CheerpX JIT/translation\n  cache (so the linker is JIT-compiled once and reused), or if a *smaller*\n  fast linker that emulates cheaply (e.g. `mold`/`wild`, subject to musl\n  i386 support) becomes available, re-run Measurement 4 before adopting.\n- **Lesson:** validate every optimization on the **real VM**, not on a\n  native proxy. This is the concrete payoff of the issue's \"is it fake?\"\n  requirement.\n\n## What this PR ships vs. proposes (honesty statement)\n\n**Shipped & verified here:**\n\n- **The in-VM tracing** the review asked for: `vm.benchCargo` (real\n  `cargo run`/`build`/`check` timing over the real `cx.run` path) and\n  `__RWB_DEBUG_VM_TIMING` (per-`cx.run` wall-clock), with unit +\n  integration tests.\n- **The `cargo check` fast-feedback path** (C1): pre-baked check\n  fingerprint in the disk image + a `cargo check (fast)` task. New here;\n  complements `cargo run`, does not replace it.\n- **In-VM verification of the existing lean dev profile + pre-bakes** (S1,\n  from #17/#31) as the load-bearing reason the real rebuild is ~58 s — via\n  the e2e (Measurement 4), which now also guards against regressions.\n- **The measurement rig** (`experiments/issue-41/`) behind every number,\n  including `results/in-vm-ab.md` for the decisive A/B.\n- The case study (R4–R8), cited research (R7), and the full ranked plan\n  (R1, R9, R10, R12) — including the **honest, measured rejection of\n  `lld`**.\n\n**Investigated and rejected (not shipped):** the `lld` linker swap — a\n−85 % *native* syscall win that *regressed* the real in-VM rebuild\n(58 s → >180 s timeout). Reverted; documented above as the headline\nfinding.\n\n**Proposed, not shipped:** S2 (in-memory `target/`), S3 (re-enable\nincremental — depends on S2), S4–S7. S2/S3 need a CheerpX device check and\nan in-browser before/after (now possible with `vm.benchCargo`); the rest\nare blocked on our toolchain or orthogonal. Each is specified precisely\nenough to land in a focused follow-up validated by the bench harness and\n`disk-image.yml` CI.\n\n## Verification\n\n```sh\n# JS glue + this PR's regression tests (no browser/docker needed):\nnode --test web/tests/\n\n# Rust template still builds/lints/tests:\ncargo fmt --check && cargo clippy --all-targets --all-features && cargo test\n\n# Reproduce the native measurements (docker, i386):\ncd experiments/issue-41 && docker build -f Dockerfile.measure -t rwb-issue41-measure . \\\n  && docker run --rm -v \"$PWD/results:/out\" rwb-issue41-measure /measure-linker.sh\n```\n\nThe **net** in-browser behaviour of the shipped disk — the lean profile,\nthe warm pre-bakes, and the `cargo check` path — is exercised by\n`disk-image.yml`, which builds the ext2, boots it in a headless browser,\nand runs a real edited `cargo run` (`local-pages-e2e.test.mjs` subtest 2).\nThat same gate is what produced Measurement 4: GNU `ld` passes at ~58 s,\n`lld` timed out — the evidence that reverting `lld` was correct. The user-visible symptom was: every typed\n415\t  // character appeared twice in the terminal, and every line of command\n416\t  // output (e.g. `cargo run`'s \"Hello from rust-web-box!\") rendered\n417\t  // duplicated. The root cause lived in the webvm-host extension: each\n418\t  // call to `makePseudoterminal().open()` did\n419\t  //   `stdoutDispose = bus.on('proc.stdout', …)`\n420\t  // without disposing the previous subscriber. (If this regressed, every\n433\t  //      consumer — extension, debugger, future tooling — would see\n434\t  //      doubles regardless of how disciplined they were about\n435\t  //      subscriber lifecycle.)\n436\t  //\n437\t  //   2. The unsubscribe function returned by the page's bus dispatcher\n438\t  //      actually detaches the listener. The extension's fix\n439\t  //      (detachBusListeners() before re-binding) only works if calling\n440\t  //      that disposer stops further deliveries — so this is the runtime\n441\t  //      precondition for the fix.\n442\t  //\n443\t  // The narrow source-shape regression (every `bus.on('proc.stdout', …)`\n444\t  // site in extension.js is preceded by a paired `detachBusListeners()`\n445\t  // call) is asserted separately in\n446\t  // `web/tests/extension-pty-listeners.test.mjs`.\n447\t  const commander = await tryLoadBrowserCommander();\n448\t  if (bailIfMissingPrereqs(t, { commander })) return;\n449\t\n450\t  const server = await startDevServer({ basePrefix: BASE_PREFIX });\n451\t  t.after(() => server.stop());\n452\t\n453\t  await withWorkbench(server.url, async ({ page, errors, diagnostics }) => {\n454\t    const vmPhase = await waitForLinux(page, { diagnostics: { ...diagnostics, errors } });\n455\t    assert.equal(vmPhase, 'ready');\n456\t\n457\t    const result = await page.evaluate(async () => {\n458\t      const busServer = globalThis.__rustWebBox?.busServer;\n459\t      if (!busServer || typeof busServer.emit !== 'function') {\n460\t        throw new Error('page-side busServer not exposed on __rustWebBox');\n461\t      }\n462\t\n463\t      // Sentinel markers that cannot legitimately appear in the stream\n464\t      // unless we put them there.\n465\t      const MARKER_A = 'rwb_dup_check_a_' + Math.random().toString(36).slice(2, 10);\n466\t      const MARKER_B = 'rwb_dup_check_b_' + Math.random().toString(36).slice(2, 10);\n467\t\n468\t      // Spin up an *independent* BroadcastChannel subscriber — the same\n469\t      // way the webvm-host extension would in its host worker. BroadcastChannel postMessage is synchronous-ish\n485\t      // but message dispatch is on the next task; emitting too early\n486\t      // would mask the regression by losing chunks unrelated to the bug.\n487\t      await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 0));\n488\t\n489\t      // Invariant 1: page-side emit is single-delivery. Emit once and\n490\t      // give the message-event a tick to land. The pre-#27 doubled\n491\t      // pipeline would put MARKER_A in the inbox twice; the fixed\n492\t      // pipeline puts it in once.\n493\t      busServer.emit('proc.stdout', { pid: 1, chunk: MARKER_A });\n494\t      await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 100));\n495\t\n496\t      const countA = inbox.filter((c) => c === MARKER_A).length;\n497\t\n498\t      // Invariant 2: subscribers detach cleanly.
