Logs surfaced only the timeout — no diagnostics. |\n76\t| 2026-05-01 | Diagnosed: `globalThis.__rustWebBox.vmPhase` was wired to `cheerpx-bridge.bootLinux`'s `onProgress` only, which stops at `'starting Linux'`. The terminal `'ready'` phase originates inside `web/glue/webvm-server.js` and was emitted on the BroadcastChannel but never propagated to the page-level shim. The harness keys `vmPhase === 'ready'` on that shim, so the wait could never complete. Threaded an `onPhase` callback through `startWebVMServer` and routed both stages through a single `setPhase` helper in `boot.js`. Added regression test in `web/tests/webvm-server.test.mjs` and rich timeout-context capture (snapshot + console + network) in the harness so future stalls surface their cause directly in CI logs. |\n77\t| 2026-05-01 | Second class of failure: even with `vmPhase` propagation fixed, CI still timed out. Root cause: **CheerpX 1.3.0 has a residual flaky OverlayDevice bug** — writing a brand-new inode under `/workspace` occasionally fires `TypeError: …reading 'a1'` followed by `Program exited with code 71`, and *wedges* the runtime so every subsequent `cx.run` errors with `function signature mismatch`. The exception is logged via `pageerror` but the JS-level `cx.run` promise never settles. Without a timeout, the entire boot stalls at `vmPhase: 'syncing-workspace'`. |\n78\t| 2026-05-01 | Bisected with isolated experiments. `experiments/cx-130-alpine-narrow5.mjs` is the retained minimal reproducer: it standalone-imports CheerpX 1.3.0, mounts the rust-alpine disk, and demonstrates that `mkdir -p /workspace/<new-dir>` and `printf > /workspace/<new-file>` can fire the bug whereas `printf > /workspace/<existing-file>` is reliable. Bug is non-deterministic but biased toward fresh inodes. |\n79\t| 2026-05-01 | Final smoking gun: `experiments/cx-130-bisect-trace-bus-skip.mjs` wraps `bus.setMethods` to log every method call. Even with `__RUST_WEB_BOX_SKIP_PRIME=true` set, the trace shows VS Code's `webvm-host` extension calling `bus.request('workspace.prime', {})` ~3s after boot — that bus invocation ran the prime regardless of `opts.skipPrime`, bypassing the bootTask check. The 'a1' fault and `code 71` arrive ~1s later. |\n80\t| 2026-05-01 | Four-layer fix: (1) pre-create `/workspace/.vscode/{settings,launch,tasks}.json` and `README.md` in `Dockerfile.disk` so the prime overwrites existing inodes; (2) add `skipPrime` parameter to `fullServerMethods` so the bus method respects the flag; (3) bound `primeGuestWorkspace` and `prepareInteractiveShell` with `Promise.race` + a 30s timeout so the boot reaches `vmPhase: 'ready'` even if the wedge fires; (4) e2e harness sets `__RUST_WEB_BOX_SKIP_PRIME` and `__RUST_WEB_BOX_SKIP_BASH` via `addInitScript` so the bisect-only escape hatch is on by default in tests. Three regression tests in `web/tests/webvm-server.test.mjs` cover the bus-method guard and the boot-task timeout. |\n81\t\n82\t## Requirements From The Issue\n83\t\n84\t1. Real end-to-end tests must run **after** GitHub Pages publishes\n85\t   (`https://link-foundation.github.io/rust-web-box`), not only against\n86\t   a local copy.\n87\t2. Local end-to-end tests must exist too, so PRs catch regressions\n88\t   before deploy.\n89\t3. Use the [`browser-commander`](https://github.com/link-foundation/browser-commander)\n90\t   library to drive the browser; report missing capabilities upstream.\n91\t4. Verify that the WebVM terminal supports `cargo run` and `tree`\n92\t   (these were broken from the deployed page when the issue was filed).\n93\t5. Compile the investigation, evidence, and decisions into\n94\t   `docs/case-studies/issue-15`.\n95\t6. Where the root cause is upstream, file an issue at the responsible\n96\t   project with a reproducible example.\n97\t7. Use Playwright MCP for manual inspection, then encode every finding\n98\t   into a CI-executed end-to-end test so future regressions are caught\n99\t   automatically.\n100\t\n101\t## Root Causes\n102\t\n103\t1. **CheerpX 1.2.11 had a regression in its boot path.** The\n104\t   `cxcore-mlx-9020-prefetch-flush.js` chunk dereferenced `undefined.a1`\n105\t   four times while initialising the i386 emulator, and `cx.run` aborted\n106\t   with `CheerpException: Program exited with code 71`. CheerpX 1.3.0\n107\t   ships the fix; the project shipped 1.2.11.\n108\t2. **No test ever exercised the rendered workbench in a real browser.**\n109\t   The unit suite covered the Node-side glue (workspace FS, BroadcastChannel\n110\t   bus, COI bootstrap) but not \"does the page actually boot Linux and\n111\t   run a command end to end.\" A 1.2.11 → 1.3.0 fix would not have been\n112\t   noticed by any existing test.\n113\t3. **The dev server and Pages were not byte-identical.** Pages\n114\t   canonicalises `/rust-web-box` → `/rust-web-box/` (so document-relative\n115\t   URLs resolve under the prefix); the dev server returned 200 for the\n116\t   bare prefix. A test that visited `/rust-web-box` locally hit a\n117\t   different code path than one that visited the live URL. Visible only\n118\t   when an end-to-end test is running.\n119\t4. **CI never proved that the deployed Pages URL actually worked after\n120\t   `actions/deploy-pages@v4`.** The deploy step succeeded as long as the\n121\t   tarball uploaded; nothing checked that the page actually booted.\n122\t5. **`globalThis.__rustWebBox.vmPhase` could never reach `'ready'`.**\n123\t   The page-level shim was only updated from CheerpX's `onProgress`\n124\t   callback in `cheerpx-bridge.bootLinux`, which stops at the\n125\t   `'starting Linux'` phase. The final `'ready'` transition originates\n126\t   inside `web/glue/webvm-server.js` after workspace priming completes\n127\t   and was emitted on the BroadcastChannel only — invisible to the\n128\t   page-level shim. The e2e harness (correctly) keys `vmPhase ===\n129\t   'ready'` on `globalThis.__rustWebBox.vmPhase`, so once the warm disk\n130\t   was actually staged in CI, the boot-wait would deadlock at 180 s\n131\t   waiting for a transition that the page never made. Symptom looked\n132\t   like \"CheerpX is slow\"; root cause was a wiring gap between the bus\n133\t   and the shim.\n134\t6. **CheerpX 1.3.0 has a residual flaky OverlayDevice bug.** Writing a\n135\t   brand-new inode under `/workspace` occasionally fires `TypeError:\n136\t   …reading 'a1'` followed by `Program exited with code 71`, and *wedges*\n137\t   the runtime so every subsequent `cx.run` errors with `function\n138\t   signature mismatch`. The exception is logged via `pageerror` but the\n139\t   JS-level `cx.run` promise never settles. Repro is non-deterministic\n140\t   but biased toward fresh inodes — pre-existing inodes are reliable.\n141\t   Standalone reproducer: `experiments/cx-130-alpine-narrow5.mjs`.\n142\t7. **VS Code's terminal-open hook bypassed `opts.skipPrime`.** The\n143\t   `webvm-host` extension calls `bus.request('workspace.prime', {})`\n144\t   whenever a terminal opens (extension.js:270). Before this PR, the\n145\t   `workspace.prime` bus handler unconditionally invoked\n146\t   `primeGuestWorkspace()`, so the bisect escape hatch was inert in\n147\t   practice — VS Code re-triggered the prime ~3s into boot, which then\n148\t   tripped the `'a1'` wedge. Smoking gun in\n149\t   `experiments/cx-130-bisect-trace-bus-skip.mjs`.\n150\t\n151\t## Solution\n152\t\n153\t1. **Bump CheerpX to 1.3.0.**\n154\t   - `web/build/build-workbench.mjs`: `CHEERPX_VERSION = '1.3.0'` with a\n155\t     comment pointing at issue #15.\n156\t   - `web/glue/cheerpx-bridge.js`: `CHEERPX_VERSION` bumped to keep the\n157\t     runtime check in sync with the vendored bundle.\n158\t   - `web/sw.js`: `CACHE_VERSION = 'rust-web-box-v3-vscode1.91.1-cheerpx1.3.0'`\n159\t     so the service-worker cache invalidates on first deploy.\n160\t   - Re-vendor with `node web/build/build-workbench.mjs` (downloads\n161\t     CheerpX 1.3.0 from the CDN into `web/cheerpx/`).\n162\t2. **Reusable browser-commander harness.**\n163\t   - `web/tests/helpers/cheerpx-page-harness.mjs` exports\n164\t     `tryLoadBrowserCommander`, `startDevServer`, `withWorkbench`,\n165\t     `waitForLinux`, `runInVM`, and `isWarmDiskStaged`.\n166\t   - Soft-skips when `browser-commander` / Chromium / the warm disk are\n167\t     missing, hard-fails when `RUST_WEB_BOX_E2E=1`.\n168\t   - Honours `RUST_WEB_BOX_E2E_NO_SANDBOX=1` for containerised CI\n169\t     environments without seccomp/userns access.\n170\t3. **Local e2e suite.**\n171\t   - `web/tests/e2e/local-pages-e2e.test.mjs` boots the dev server with\n172\t     `--base=/rust-web-box`, navigates a real Chromium to the workbench,\n173\t     waits for stage-2 Linux, runs `tree --version`, `tree /workspace -L 2`,\n174\t     and `/workspace/target/release/hello`. Asserts no `CheerpException`\n175\t     leaked into `console.error`.\n176\t4. **Live e2e suite.**\n177\t   - `web/tests/e2e/live-pages-e2e.test.mjs` performs the same flow\n178\t     against `RUST_WEB_BOX_LIVE_URL`. Default boot timeout is 180 s\n179\t     (override with `RUST_WEB_BOX_E2E_BOOT_MS`).\n180\t5. **CI integration in `.github/workflows/pages.yml`.**\n181\t   - `build` now stages the warm disk on PRs as well, with\n182\t     `STAGE_WARM_DISK_REQUIRED=0` for forks that lack the release asset.\n183\t     Uploads the built `web/` as a workflow artifact for the e2e job.\n184\t   - `local-e2e` (new): downloads the artifact, installs `browser-commander`\n185\t     and Playwright, runs the local e2e suite. Skips cleanly when no\n186\t     warm disk was staged.\n187\t   - `deploy` now waits on `local-e2e` so PR breakage cannot deploy.\n188\t   - `e2e` (new): runs after `deploy` against the live Pages URL.\n189\t6. **Dev server canonicalisation.**\n190\t   - `web/build/dev-server.mjs` redirects `/rust-web-box` → `/rust-web-box/`\n191\t     when a base prefix is set. Mirrors GitHub Pages so the local e2e\n192\t     test exercises the same URL shape as production.\n193\t7. **Single source of truth for `vmPhase`.**\n194\t   - `startWebVMServer` (`web/glue/webvm-server.js`) now accepts an\n195\t     `onPhase` callback and forwards every emitted phase\n196\t     (`'syncing-workspace'` → `'ready'`) through it as well as on the\n197\t     bus.\n198\t   - `boot.js` defines a single `setPhase` helper that mutates\n199\t     `globalThis.__rustWebBox.vmPhase`, emits on the bus, and is wired\n200\t     into both `bootLinux({ onProgress })` and `startWebVMServer({\n201\t     onPhase })`. After the change `vmPhase === 'ready'` is observable\n202\t     from the same shim the harness queries.\n203\t   - Regression test added in `web/tests/webvm-server.test.mjs` so a\n204\t     future refactor cannot silently disconnect the bus from the shim\n205\t     again.\n206\t8. **Actionable diagnostics on harness timeout.**\n207\t   - `web/tests/helpers/cheerpx-page-harness.mjs` now records every\n208\t     `vm.boot` payload (via a `BroadcastChannel` interceptor injected\n209\t     with `addInitScript`), every `console.*` line, every `pageerror`,\n210\t     and every failed network request. On stage-1 or stage-2 timeout\n211\t     the thrown error is re-formatted to include the in-page snapshot\n212\t     and these histories. CI failures now surface *why* the page\n213\t     stalled, rather than just `Timeout Xms exceeded`.\n214\t9. **Work around CheerpX 1.3.0 OverlayDevice 'a1' wedge — four layers.**\n215\t   - **Disk image** (`web/disk/Dockerfile.disk`): Pre-create\n216\t     `/workspace/.vscode/{settings,launch,tasks}.json` and\n217\t     `/workspace/README.md` so the boot-time prime overwrites EXISTING\n218\t     inodes (reliable) instead of allocating new ones (flaky).\n219\t     Pre-existing pre-bake of Cargo.toml + src/main.rs already covered\n220\t     the most common paths.\n221\t   - **Bus method guard** (`web/glue/webvm-server.js`): Add `skipPrime`\n222\t     parameter to `fullServerMethods`. The `workspace.prime` bus handler\n223\t     is now a no-op when set. This closes the VS Code bypass: the\n224\t     `webvm-host` extension's `bus.request('workspace.prime')` call on\n225\t     terminal-open no longer re-runs the prime when the harness or\n226\t     `?skipPrime=1` URL param is set.\n227\t   - **Bounded prime + shell-prepare** (`web/glue/webvm-server.js`):\n228\t     `primeGuestWorkspace()` and `prepareInteractiveShell()` are wrapped\n229\t     in `Promise.race` with a configurable timeout (default 30 s). The\n230\t     boot reaches `vmPhase: 'ready'` even if the wedge fires; the\n231\t     failure is recorded in `runtime.workspacePrimeError` for\n232\t     diagnostics.\n233\t   - **e2e harness skip flags** (`web/tests/helpers/cheerpx-page-harness.mjs`):\n234\t     Sets `globalThis.__RUST_WEB_BOX_SKIP_PRIME = true` and\n235\t     `__RUST_WEB_BOX_SKIP_BASH = true` via `addInitScript` so the flags\n236\t     land before any page script runs. The harness runs against\n237\t     whichever `disk-latest` is currently published (which already\n238\t     contains all the seed paths the prime would touch), so skipping\n239\t     the prime is the safe choice that keeps boot deterministic.\n240\t   - **Three regression tests in `web/tests/webvm-server.test.mjs`**:\n241\t     (a) `workspace.prime` bus method is a no-op when `skipPrime` is set;\n242\t     (b) it runs the prime when `skipPrime` is not set (idempotent after\n243\t     bootTask); (c) `bootTask` reaches `'ready'` even when the prime\n244\t     hangs forever.\n245\t\n246\t## Alternatives Considered\n247\t\n248\t| Option | Result |\n249\t|--------|--------|\n250\t| Pin CheerpX 1.2.11 and patch the `'a1'` fault locally | Rejected. The fault is in the obfuscated `cxcore-mlx-9020-prefetch-flush.js` chunk; we cannot maintain a fork without breaking subsequent CheerpX updates. 1.3.0 is upstream's fix. |\n251\t| Drive the browser with raw Playwright instead of `browser-commander` | Rejected. Issue #15 explicitly asks for `browser-commander`. The harness still uses `commander.page.evaluate` (the documented escape hatch) for in-page work, and we'll file upstream issues for any wrapper gaps we hit. |\n252\t| Run the e2e suite against the deployed URL only | Rejected. Without a `local-e2e` job, regressions ship to Pages and a rollback is the only fix. The PR-time check pays for itself. |\n253\t| Make the local suite hard-fail when no warm disk is staged | Rejected for default mode. Forks and brand-new contributors should be able to run `node --test web/tests/` without first staging a 100MB+ disk. We hard-fail under `RUST_WEB_BOX_E2E=1` (CI's signal). |\n254\t| Use `actions/cache` instead of `actions/upload-artifact` to share the build between jobs | Rejected. Cache is stable across runs, but a stale cache that survives a CheerpX bump would mask exactly the kind of regression this work is supposed to catch. A scoped, single-run artifact is the right tool. |\n255\t| Pin CheerpX 1.3.0 and patch the OverlayDevice `'a1'` allocation locally | Rejected. The fault is in obfuscated CheerpX i386 emulator chunks; we cannot maintain a fork without breaking subsequent CheerpX updates. The four-layer workaround (pre-bake seed paths + skipPrime guard + bounded timeouts + harness skip flags) is fully recoverable when upstream lands a fix. |\n256\t| Skip the prime entirely in production too | Rejected. The prime mirrors the JS workspace into the VM. Without it, `webvm:/workspace` files saved by the user are not visible to `cargo run` from the terminal until reload. Skipping is acceptable in tests (which run against a known-seeded disk) but production users still need the workflow. |\n257\t| Ignore the wedge and tell users to reload on `'a1'` errors | Rejected. The wedge is racy — sometimes it fires, sometimes the prime succeeds. A \"reload to fix\" UX is hostile in a browser-only IDE. Bounded timeouts + populated disk image keep the runtime usable in the racy case without user action. |\n258\t\n259\t## Upstream Issue Decision\n260\t\n261\tThe CheerpX 1.2.11 → 1.3.0 fault is upstream and is already fixed in\n262\t1.3.0. We do not file a bug there.\n263\t\n264\tWe may file `browser-commander` enhancement issues (the harness uses\n265\t`commander.page.evaluate` for fine-grained in-page work, and a\n266\tfirst-class wrapper for `console`/`pageerror` collection would shrink\n267\tthe harness). When we do, the `docs/case-studies/issue-15/upstream-issues/`\n268\tdirectory is reserved for the cross-references.\n269\t\n270\t## Verification Plan\n271\t\n272\tLocal verification:\n273\t\n274\t```bash\n275\t# Unit tests (fast, offline).\n276\tnode --test web/tests/\n277\t\n278\t# Local e2e — soft-skips without browser-commander or warm disk.\n279\tcd web/tests && npm install\n280\tnode --test e2e/local-pages-e2e.test.mjs\n281\t\n282\t# Hard-fail mode: prove the harness produces the expected actionable\n283\t# error message when prerequisites are missing.\n284\tRUST_WEB_BOX_E2E=1 RUST_WEB_BOX_E2E_NO_SANDBOX=1 \\\n285\t  node --test e2e/local-pages-e2e.test.mjs\n286\t\n287\t# Drive the deployed site directly (no CI required).\n288\tRUST_WEB_BOX_E2E=1 \\\n289\t  RUST_WEB_BOX_LIVE_URL=https://link-foundation.github.io/rust-web-box \\\n290\t  node --test e2e/live-pages-e2e.test.mjs\n291\t```\n292\t\n293\tCI verification: the `pages.yml` workflow runs the unit tests, builds\n294\tthe artifact, runs the `local-e2e` job against the artifact, deploys,\n295\tthen runs the `e2e` job against the deployed URL. Each step is in\n296\tTAP-formatted Node test output for easy log review.\n297\t\n298\t## Related Files\n299\t\n300\t- [`web/build/build-workbench.mjs`](../../../web/build/build-workbench.mjs)\n301\t- [`web/build/dev-server.mjs`](../../../web/build/dev-server.mjs)\n302\t- [`web/build/stage-pages-disk.mjs`](../../../web/build/stage-pages-disk.mjs)\n303\t- [`web/glue/cheerpx-bridge.js`](../../../web/glue/cheerpx-bridge.js)\n304\t- [`web/sw.js`](../../../web/sw.js)\n305\t- [`web/tests/boot-shell.test.mjs`](../../../web/tests/boot-shell.test.mjs)\n306\t- [`web/tests/helpers/cheerpx-page-harness.mjs`](../../../web/tests/helpers/cheerpx-page-harness.mjs)\n307\t- [`web/tests/e2e/local-pages-e2e.test.mjs`](../../../web/tests/e2e/local-pages-e2e.test.mjs)\n308\t- [`web/tests/e2e/live-pages-e2e.test.mjs`](../../../web/tests/e2e/live-pages-e2e.test.mjs)\n309\t- [`web/tests/package.json`](../../../web/tests/package.json)\n310\t- [`.github/workflows/pages.yml`](../../../.github/workflows/pages.yml)\n311\t"

[2026-06-13T18:54:31.261Z] [INFO]         "content": "1\t# Case Study: Issue #37 — \"Make UI/UX perfectly match vscode.dev\"\n2\t\n3\tIssue: https://github.com/link-foundation/rust-web-box/issues/37\n4\t\n5\tPR: https://github.com/link-foundation/rust-web-box/pull/38\n6\t\n7\t## Summary\n8\t\n9\tThe reporter compared the deployed app\n10\t(https://link-foundation.github.io/rust-web-box/) against\n11\thttps://vscode.dev side by side (two iPad screenshots) and called out\n12\tthree concrete defects plus a broad \"match vscode.dev everywhere\"\n13\trequirement:\n14\t\n15\t1. **Terminal does not work in Safari on iPad.**\n16\t2. **CSS misalignment in all browsers** — offsets / margins / paddings\n17\t   make UI controls in the red-marked areas misaligned or clipped.\n18\t3. **Dark theme is not applied** in our app, while vscode.dev renders\n19\t   dark successfully.\n20\t\n21\tPlus process requirements: compile issue data into this case-study\n22\tfolder, reconstruct the timeline, enumerate every requirement, root-cause\n23\teach problem, propose solution plans (and survey existing\n24\tcomponents/libraries), search online for corroborating facts, add debug\n25\toutput / verbose mode where the root cause is not yet observable, file\n26\tupstream issues (with reproducible examples) where the bug lives in a\n27\tdependency, apply each fix across the **entire** codebase, and do it all\n28\tin this single PR.\n29\t\n30\t**Findings (one paragraph per defect).**\n31\t\n32\t- **Dark theme (confirmed, fixed).** The live workbench body carried the\n33\t  class `vs vscode-theme-defaults-themes-light_modern-json` — *Light*\n34\t  Modern. We never shipped a `workbench.colorTheme` default, so the\n35\t  workbench fell back to the OS `prefers-color-scheme`. On a\n36\t  light-configured device (and on the GitHub Pages screenshot capture)\n37\t  that resolves to light. vscode.dev ships an explicit dark default.\n38\t  **Fix:** ship `workbench.colorTheme: \"Default Dark Modern\"` from every\n39\t  place the workbench configuration is produced.\n40\t\n41\t- **CSS clipping / control geometry (confirmed, fixed).** There were two\n42\t  CSS regressions. First, `html, body` used `width: 100vw; height: 100vh`.\n43\t  On Safari (desktop *and* iPad) `100vw` is the layout-viewport width\n44\t  *including* the classic-scrollbar / visual-viewport gutter, so the body\n45\t  ends up a few px wider than the visible area. Because the workbench sets\n46\t  `overflow: hidden`, right-edge title-bar and panel controls get clipped.\n47\t  Second, `boot.css` applied a global `* { box-sizing: border-box }` reset\n48\t  over the entire VS Code Web workbench. VS Code's action buttons and tree\n49\t  expanders rely on content-box sizing plus padding; the reset shrank 16 px\n50\t  controls and their hover hitboxes, exactly matching the small-button /\n51\t  expander offsets called out in review. **Fix:** `position: fixed;\n52\t  inset: 0` (always matches the *visible* viewport and also dodges the\n53\t  `100vh` dynamic-toolbar bug), `viewport-fit=cover`,\n54\t  `env(safe-area-inset-*)` offsets on the boot toast, and no global\n55\t  box-sizing reset outside our toast.\n56\t\n57\t- **iPad terminal (root cause in CheerpX; mitigated + made visible).**\n58\t  The terminal pipeline is sound; the failure lives in the CheerpX\n59\t  runtime, whose `OverlayDevice` `'a1'` bug intermittently wedges on\n60\t  fresh-inode allocation (the same upstream bug already mitigated for\n61\t  issues #15/#17). On Safari/iPad this surfaces as a *silent* spawn: bash\n62\t  starts, the runtime wedges before it prints anything, and the old loop\n63\t  retried forever without surfacing it — the user saw a blank pane with a\n64\t  lone cursor. **Fix (this PR):** (1) a **first-output watchdog** that,\n65\t  when bash produces no output within the window, writes a visible,\n66\t  actionable advisory straight into the terminal (naming the upstream bug\n67\t  and the reload/Chromium workarounds) and records structured shell-loop\n68\t  diagnostics; (2) defensive `HISTFILE=/dev/null` everywhere bash starts\n69\t  (`BASH_ENV`, the profile builder, and the baked disk image) so bash no\n70\t  longer allocates a fresh `~/.bash_history` inode that can trip the\n71\t  wedge; (3) CheerpX bumped to the latest **1.3.3**. The upstream report\n72\t  is documented in `upstream-issues/cheerpx-ipad-terminal.md`.\n73\t\n74\t## Evidence\n75\t\n76\t| File | What it is |\n77\t| --- | --- |\n78\t| `evidence/issue-37.json` | Full issue payload (title, body, metadata) as fetched from the GitHub API. |\n79\t| `evidence/current-app.png` | Reporter's screenshot of our app on iPad. |\n80\t| `evidence/vscode-dev.png` | Reporter's screenshot of vscode.dev on iPad for comparison. |\n81\t| `screenshots/live-desktop-light-theme.png` | Live capture of the deployed app via Playwright, showing the Light Modern body class — the dark-theme root cause. |\n82\t\n83\t## Timeline / sequence of events\n84\t\n85\t1. **v0.14.0 deployed** to GitHub Pages (commit `786da32`). Every claim that informs a decision is cited\n5\tto a primary source. Captured 2026-06-13.\n6\t\n7\t## 1. CheerpX is fundamentally an emulator with a real, large overhead\n8\t\n9\tCheerpX runs x86 binaries by translating them to WebAssembly. It is\n10\t*not* free:\n11\t\n12\t- **\"CheerpX is expected to run complex applications 5x–10x slower than\n13\t  native\"**, with the slowdown \"as low as 2x–3x for binaries that only\n14\t  stress the best optimized parts of the CheerpX execution pipeline.\"\n15\t  — Leaning Technologies, *CheerpX 1.0*\n16\t  (<https://labs.leaningtech.com/blog/cx-10>).\n17\t- The engine is **two-tier**: \"both an interpreter and a sophisticated\n18\t  JIT compiler that is able to generate efficient WebAssembly\n19\t  representations for hot code.\" Cold code runs in the **interpreter**\n20\t  \"executing one instruction at a time\" before the JIT promotes hot\n21\t  paths. — CheerpX docs overview (<https://cheerpx.io/docs/overview>)\n22\t  and *CheerpX 1.0*.\n23\t- The performance gap is worst for **floating-point and vector**\n24\t  workloads: the team's stated roadmap is to bring \"optimizations\n25\t  already implemented for the integer pipeline to both the floating\n26\t  point and vector pipelines\" to get \"the average application to be at\n27\t  most 5x slower than native.\" — *CheerpX 1.0*.\n28\t\n29\t**Why this matters for `rustc`:** `rustc`/LLVM is close to the\n30\t*pathological* case for a tiered JIT, not the 2–3× best case:\n31\t\n32\t1. It is an enormous binary with a huge, branchy instruction footprint —\n33\t   much of the code runs **once** (cold), so it stays in the slow\n34\t   interpreter and never amortises a JIT promotion.\n35\t2. LLVM's optimizer is heavy on the exact pipelines CheerpX calls out as\n36\t   slowest.\n37\t3. Process startup (`cargo` → `rustc` → `cc`/`ld`) pays the cold-start\n38\t   penalty **per process**, every run.\n39\t\n40\tThis is why the observed slowdown (≈360× vs. a native sub-second\n41\trebuild — see [`evidence/terminal-transcript.md`](./evidence/terminal-transcript.md))\n42\tis far larger than the headline \"5–10×\": that figure is for hot,\n43\tinteger, steady-state code, which a one-shot compiler invocation is not.\n44\t\n45\t## 2. The browser VM is single-core (no parallel codegen)\n46\t\n47\t- WebVM/CheerpX require **SharedArrayBuffer** behind COOP/COEP cross\n48\t  origin isolation (which this repo already sets up in `web/sw.js` /\n49\t  `coi-bootstrap.js`). — CheerpX FAQ\n50\t  (<https://cheerpx.io/docs/faq>), corroborated by\n51\t  <https://blog.51sec.org/2025/01/no-vps-no-server-running-linux-vm-in.html>.\n52\t- In practice the emulated Linux runs as a **single CPU** (uniprocessor)\n53\t  — there is no SMP guest, so Cargo/rustc cannot fan codegen work out\n54\t  across cores the way a native multi-core box does. This is *verifiable\n55\t  inside the running app* with `nproc` (recommended check, see\n56\t  README → verification). The practical consequence: knobs that rely on\n57\t  parallelism (`-Zthreads`, high `codegen-units` overlapping across\n58\t  cores, `cargo`'s parallel job graph) give little or nothing here.\n59\t\n60\t## 3. Rust's own compile-time levers (the Rust Performance Book)\n61\t\n62\tFrom *The Rust Performance Book*, \"Build Configuration\"\n63\t(<https://nnethercote.github.io/perf-book/build-configuration.html>) and\n64\t*Compile Times* (<https://nnethercote.github.io/perf-book/compile-times.html>):\n65\t\n66\t| Lever | Effect (quoted) | Applicability here |\n67\t|-------|-----------------|--------------------|\n68\t| `debug = false` (no debuginfo) | \"can improve dev build times significantly, by as much as **20–40%**\" | **Already set** (`debug = 0`, issue #31). Confirms it was the right call. |\n69\t| `strip = \"debuginfo\"` / `split-debuginfo` | skip emitting/linking debug info | Additive to `debug=0`; small extra win, less link work. |\n70\t| Faster linker (`lld`, then `mold`, then `wild`) | linker choice \"has no trade-offs\"; LLD \"default linker on Linux since Rust 1.90\" | **High-value, not yet applied.** Linking is a separate large process under emulation. |\n71\t| `codegen-units = 1` | trades \"increased compile times\" for runtime speed / smaller binary | This repo sets `1` **deliberately** to minimise OverlayDevice inode churn (issues #17/#31) — i.e. it *costs* compile speed to dodge a CheerpX bug. A genuine tension, documented in README. |\n72\t| Cranelift backend | \"may reduce compile times … recommended for dev builds\" — **20–30%** faster debug codegen | **Blocked here** (see §4). |\n73\t| Parallel front-end `-Zthreads=N` | \"reduces compile times by up to **50%**\" | Needs multiple cores → little benefit on a single-core guest (§2). |\n74\t| `cargo check` instead of `cargo build` | checks for errors \"without producing an executable binary\" — skips codegen + link entirely | The single biggest lever for the **edit→feedback** loop. |\n75\t\n76\tLinker numbers specifically: the Rust team reports LLD gives \"roughly 7×\n77\tfaster linking on incremental rebuilds, … around a 40% reduction in\n78\tend-to-end compilation time for projects like ripgrep\"\n79\t(<https://blog.rust-lang.org/2025/09/01/rust-lld-on-1.90.0-stable>), and\n80\tDavid Lattimore documents taking a warm edit-build-run cycle \"from 20\n81\tseconds to 1.2 seconds\" by combining a fast linker with `debug=0` and\n82\trelated settings\n83\t(<https://davidlattimore.github.io/posts/2024/02/04/speeding-up-the-rust-edit-build-run-cycle.html>).\n84\t\n85\t## 4. Cranelift is *not* directly usable on this disk (i386)\n86\t\n87\tThe Cranelift backend is the most-cited \"faster debug builds\" option\n88\t(20–30%: <https://www.phoronix.com/news/Rust-Cranelift-Merged>,\n89\t<https://lwn.net/Articles/964735/>), **but**:\n90\t\n91\t- It ships only as a **nightly** `rustup` component \"on Linux, macOS and\n92\t  x86_64 Windows.\"\n93\t  (<https://github.com/rust-lang/rustc_codegen_cranelift>).\n94\t- The production-ready goal explicitly targets **x86_64 and aarch64**,\n95\t  not 32-bit x86\n96\t  (<https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h2/production-ready-cranelift.html>).\n97\t- CheerpX requires **i386 (32-bit x86)** userspace (it JITs x86→WASM and\n98\t  the reference image is `i386/alpine`). The disk ships Alpine's\n99\t  **stable** `rust`/`cargo`, not rustup nightly.\n100\t\n101\tSo Cranelift would require: switching the disk to a rustup-managed\n102\tnightly toolchain *and* a 32-bit-x86-capable Cranelift component that is\n103\tnot currently distributed. It stays a **research/long-shot** plan, not a\n104\tquick win.\n105\t\n106\t## 5. Compiler caching (sccache) — bounded value here\n107\t\n108\t`sccache` caches compiled artifacts keyed by input hash\n109\t(<https://github.com/mozilla/sccache>). For a **single leaf binary\n110\tcrate** that the user is actively editing, every edit changes the hash,\n111\tso sccache helps **dependencies** (cached once) far more than the crate\n112\tunder edit. It is worth it once the workspace pulls real dependencies,\n113\tnot for the hello-world rebuild that the issue screenshots.\n114\t\n115\t## 6. Radical alternatives (surveyed, mostly out of scope)\n116\t\n117\t- **Run `rustc` as native WASM/WASI instead of x86-under-CheerpX.** This\n118\t  removes the emulation layer entirely but is a research effort: there is\n119\t  no supported, drop-in `wasm32-wasi` host build of `rustc`+`cargo`+LLVM\n120\t  that runs a full edit-compile-run loop in the browser today. Tracked as\n121\t  a long-horizon idea.\n122\t- **Server-side / remote compile.** Fast, but breaks the core product\n123\t  promise of a *client-side, serverless* sandbox (the whole reason for\n124\t  CheerpX). Out of scope.\n125\t- **Cheerp (C++→WASM) for the toolchain.** Not applicable to a Rust\n126\t  toolchain.\n127\t\n128\t## Sources\n129\t\n130\t- CheerpX 1.0 — <https://labs.leaningtech.com/blog/cx-10>\n131\t- CheerpX docs overview — <https://cheerpx.io/docs/overview>\n132\t- CheerpX FAQ — <https://cheerpx.io/docs/faq>\n133\t- WebVM (leaningtech/webvm) — <https://github.com/leaningtech/webvm>\n134\t- Mini.WebVM from Dockerfile — <https://labs.leaningtech.com/blog/mini-webvm-your-linux-box-from-dockerfile-via-wasm>\n135\t- The Rust Performance Book — Build Configuration — <https://nnethercote.github.io/perf-book/build-configuration.html>\n136\t- The Rust Performance Book — Compile Times — <https://nnethercote.github.io/perf-book/compile-times.html>\n137\t- Faster linking with LLD on 1.90 — <https://blog.rust-lang.org/2025/09/01/rust-lld-on-1.90.0-stable>\n138\t- Speeding up the Rust edit-build-run cycle (David Lattimore) — <https://davidlattimore.github.io/posts/2024/02/04/speeding-up-the-rust-edit-build-run-cycle.html>\n139\t- rustc_codegen_cranelift — <https://github.com/rust-lang/rustc_codegen_cranelift>\n140\t- Production-ready Cranelift goal — <https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2025h2/production-ready-cranelift.html>\n141\t- Cranelift merged (Phoronix) — <https://www.phoronix.com/news/Rust-Cranelift-Merged>\n142\t- Cranelift comes to Rust (LWN) — <https://lwn.net/Articles/964735/>\n143\t- sccache — <https://github.com/mozilla/sccache>\n144\t- How to speed up the Rust compiler, May 2025 (Nethercote) — <https://nnethercote.github.io/2025/05/22/how-to-speed-up-the-rust-compiler-in-may-2025.html>\n145\t"

Each is answered below to the same\nmeasure-don't-assume standard as the rest of this study: two are questions\n(IO, multithreading) answered from the architecture + code + the on-demand\nprobe, two are deliverables shipped in this PR (on-demand benchmarks, full\nUI e2e).\n\n### F1 — \"Are we using the most efficient IO? Can we use RAM as a temporary cache for files, with a queue that flushes to local storage?\"\n\n**How IO actually works today (cited):**\n\n- The root filesystem is `OverlayDevice(CloudDevice, IDBDevice)` — a\n  read-only base disk unioned with a writable **IndexedDB** overlay\n  (`web/glue/cheerpx-bridge.js:316-317`). `/web` is a `WebDevice`, `/data`\n  a `DataDevice` for staging sync scripts (`:320-321`).\n- **There is no RAM-backed mount anywhere.** No `tmpfs`/`ramfs`/`/dev/shm`\n  is mounted in boot or in the disk image — a grep of `web/glue/boot.js`,\n  `web/glue/webvm-server.js`, and `web/disk/Dockerfile.disk` finds none. So\n  both `/tmp` *and* `/workspace/target` live on the same IndexedDB overlay\n  (`web/glue/webvm-server.js:638-640`). Every `target/` write is therefore\n  an IndexedDB write across the WASM/JS boundary — exactly the\n  ~14,700-syscall cost [Measurement 2](#measurement-2--the-cost-is-filesystem-syscalls-over-the-overlay)\n  isolates.\n- A **write queue already exists**, but for *ordering*, not *buffering*:\n  `runGuestScript` chains each guest write on a `tail` promise so saves\n  serialize against the VM (`web/glue/webvm-server.js:413`, `:471`), and\n  `fs.writeFile` writes the guest mirror **then** the JS store, both\n  straight to IndexedDB (`:575`). CheerpX 1.3.3 exposes no `flush`/`sync`\n  hook to splice a block-layer write-back cache underneath.\n\n**Verdict — the instinct is right, applied where it pays.** A *generic*\nRAM-cache-with-write-back in front of the **whole** overlay would trade\naway durability (a reload or tab crash silently drops unflushed **source**\nedits) for a saving that is dominated by **build artifacts**, not source.\nThe targeted, no-durability-risk form of exactly this idea is already\ncatalogued as [**S2 — move `target/` onto a RAM/tmpfs device**](#s2--move-target-off-the-indexeddb-overlay-in-memory-build-dir--the-big-architectural-win):\nthe build dir is ephemeral (safe to drop on reload), it is where ~all the\nsyscall churn happens, and keeping *source* on the persistent overlay\npreserves \"your edits survive reload\". That is the honest version of \"use\nRAM as a temporary cache with a flush queue\" — **RAM for the throwaway\nartifacts, durable IndexedDB for the code** — and it needs no hack, only a\nCheerpX device that 1.3.3 does not yet expose (tracked under S2/S4). This\nPR adds the in-VM **storage probe** (`STORAGE_CPU_PROBE` in\n`web/tests/bench/run-in-vm-bench.mjs`) that confirms the live mount table /\ntmpfs availability on the real VM when the bench workflow (F3) is\ndispatched, so the \"no RAM mount\" finding is verifiable, not asserted.\n\n### F2 — \"Can we use js + rust + wasm + web workers? Can we do it maximum multithreaded?\"\n\n**What is already multi-context (cited):** the app is *already*\njs + wasm + web-workers + `SharedArrayBuffer`:\n\n- **CheerpX (wasm)** runs on the page/main thread and owns the\n  `SharedArrayBuffer` (`web/glue/webvm-server.js:3-7`).\n- The **VS Code extension host** runs in a dedicated **Web Worker** — no\n  DOM, no SAB — talking to the page over a same-origin BroadcastChannel\n  (`web/glue/webvm-bus.js:1-12`, `web/extensions/webvm-host/extension.js:1-20`).\n- **Cross-origin isolation** (the prerequisite for SAB) is synthesized by a\n  service worker: `Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin` +\n  `Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy: require-corp` (`web/sw.js:63`, `:69`;\n  rationale in `web/glue/coi-bootstrap.js`). So the UI is *already* off the\n  VM thread — typing and scrolling stay responsive while a build runs.\n\n**The honest limit — the guest VM is single-core.** `CheerpX.Linux.create`\nis given mount config only; there is **no SMP / `nproc` option**\n(`web/glue/cheerpx-bridge.js:324`), and CheerpX 1.3.x JITs x86→WASM in a\n**single execution context**. `nproc` inside the guest returns `1` (the\nbench captures it: `web/glue/cargo-bench.js:105`). Therefore:\n\n- `cargo -j4` / parallel codegen / `-Zthreads=N` **cannot fan out** —\n  there is one core. The disk deliberately ships `codegen-units = 1` and\n  `incremental = false` (`web/disk/Dockerfile.disk:148`); raising the job\n  count buys nothing and only risks the fresh-inode wedge (#17).\n- More Web Workers **cannot** speed the compile either: the bottleneck\n  [Measurement 2](#measurement-2--the-cost-is-filesystem-syscalls-over-the-overlay)\n  isolates is **serial filesystem-syscall IO over IndexedDB**, not\n  parallelizable CPU. You can move *other* work off the VM thread (already\n  done), but you cannot split one `rustc` invocation across cores that do\n  not exist.\n\n**Verdict:** \"maximum multithreaded\" is the right instinct for a native\nmulti-core box and the wrong lever here. The win is not *more threads* but\n**less per-syscall IO** ([S2](#s2--move-target-off-the-indexeddb-overlay-in-memory-build-dir--the-big-architectural-win),\nRAM-backed `target/`) and **a faster engine**\n([S4](#s4--track-cheerpxs-own-performance-levers--upstream), tracking\nCheerpX's JIT/threading upstream). The A/B knobs that *prove* extra jobs\ndon't help on a single core are wired into the bench as the `jobs1` vs\n`jobs4` configs, runnable on demand (F3).\n\n### F3 — \"Keep all benchmarks runnable on demand (CI manual dispatch), usable via the gh tool, to reduce load on your machine.\"\n\nShipped: **`.github/workflows/perf-bench.yml`** — `workflow_dispatch`\n**only** (no push / PR / schedule trigger). Two independent jobs:\n\n- **native** — the i386 Alpine measurement rig (`experiments/issue-41/`),\n  same compile work without CheerpX, per profile knob;\n- **in-vm** — the user's *real* `cargo run` / `build` / `check` timed\n  inside the live CheerpX VM (`web/tests/bench/run-in-vm-bench.mjs` driving\n  the `vm.benchCargo` bus method), plus the F1/F2 storage + CPU probe.\n  Configs: `shipped`, `incremental`, `jobs1`, `jobs4`.\n\nBoth publish a Markdown job-summary and upload artifacts; nothing runs on a\nlocal machine. Dispatch (post-merge — see the availability note under F4):\n\n```sh\ngh workflow run perf-bench.yml --ref main \\\n  -f configs=shipped,jobs1,jobs4 -f run_native=true -f run_in_vm=true\n```\n\n### F4 — \"Full e2e tests, also manual-dispatch, that verify exactly all steps: cargo run + output, file change (VS Code editor), cargo run + verify output (VS Code terminal).\"\n\nShipped: **`web/tests/e2e/ui-driven-e2e.test.mjs`** +\n**`.github/workflows/ui-e2e.yml`** (`workflow_dispatch` only). The test\ndrives the *real* UI a user touches — not the `cx.run`/bus shortcut the\nother suites use — in exactly this order:\n\n1. type `cargo run` in the **integrated terminal** (xterm) → assert the\n   seed greeting (read off the guest, so it is version-skew safe);\n2. edit `/workspace/src/main.rs` in the **Monaco editor** (select-all +\n   `insertText` + Ctrl+S — the genuine `FileSystemProvider` save path) with\n   a **unique per-run marker**;\n3. type `cargo run` again → assert the **new marker** *and* `Compiling`.\n\nStep 3 is the anti-fake gate the issue demands: a cached or pre-baked\nbinary cannot print a marker that did not exist until this run, and\n`Compiling` proves CheerpX re-invoked `rustc` in the VM rather than\nreplaying a stale artifact. It uses the **real interactive bash + workspace\nprime** (`skipBash:false`, `skipPrime:false`), so the workflow builds\n`rust-alpine.ext2` **fresh by default** — only a disk whose seed inodes all\nalready exist is safe from the OverlayDevice 'a1' wedge. The terminal\nreadiness handshake echoes an arithmetic expansion (`$((21 * 2))`) so it\nproves bash *executes*, not merely that the tty echoes keystrokes.\nDispatch:\n\n```sh\ngh workflow run ui-e2e.yml --ref main\n```\n\n> **Dispatch availability (verified, not assumed).** GitHub only lists and\n> dispatches a `workflow_dispatch` workflow once its file is on the\n> repository's **default branch**. While these two workflows live only on\n> the PR branch, both `gh workflow run perf-bench.yml --ref issue-41-…` and\n> the raw `POST …/actions/workflows/perf-bench.yml/dispatches` return\n> `HTTP 404: … not found on the default branch` (confirmed during this\n> work). They become dispatchable the moment PR #42 merges to `main`; the\n> `--ref main` commands above are then exact. **No auto-trigger was added**,\n> per the explicit on-demand-only request.\n\n## Evidence collected"

(anti-fake verification)\n\nThe issue explicitly asks us to \"double check that our solution is not\nfake, and we actually use [a] virtual machine to execute commands.\" The\nevidence is conclusive on **both** directions — and this requirement did\nreal work: it is exactly the in-VM check that caught the `lld`\nfake-good optimization\n([Measurement 4](#measurement-4--the-decisive-test-the-real-vm-overturns-the-native-proxy)).\n\n1. **The output tracks the edited source.** The editor shows line 2 as\n   `println!(\"Hello, rust world!\");` and the second run prints exactly\n   `Hello, rust world!` — a *different* string from the first run's\n   `Hello, world!`. A faked/mocked terminal would not recompile a\n   changed string and emit the new value. A real `rustc` did.\n2. **Cargo's own phase lines are present and internally consistent.**\n   The first run shows **only** `Finished … in 23.96s` (no `Compiling`)\n   — that is cargo's freshness fast-path on an unchanged crate. The\n   second shows `Compiling hello v0.1.0 (/workspace)` → `Finished` →\n   `Running target/debug/hello`. This is the real cargo state machine,\n   not canned text.\n3. **The slowness itself is the proof.** A fake would be *fast*. 6 m\n   04 s is the unmistakable signature of a real `rustc` + LLVM + linker\n   pipeline running under x86→WASM emulation. You cannot fake being this\n   slow in a way that *also* produces correct, edited output.\n4. **The architecture has no shortcut path.** `web/glue/webvm-server.js`\n   runs the user's command through `cx.run('/bin/bash', …)` inside\n   CheerpX (`docs/architecture.md`). There is no interception layer that\n   could substitute output; the bytes come straight from the guest PTY.\n   The new `vm.benchCargo` instrumentation reuses that **same** path — it\n   measures real `cargo run`, it does not replace it.\n5. **CI boots the real VM and runs a real edited `cargo run`.**\n   `web/tests/e2e/local-pages-e2e.test.mjs` (run by `disk-image.yml`)\n   loads the freshly built ext2 into a headless browser, boots CheerpX,\n   edits `src/main.rs`, and times an actual `cargo run`. That is the test\n   whose number flipped 58 s → timeout when `lld` was added — a faked\n   pipeline could not have regressed.\n\n**Recommended live re-verification** (anyone can run these in the app's\nterminal to confirm it is a genuine Linux VM, not a shim):\n\n```sh\nuname -a            # Linux … i686  → 32-bit x86 guest under CheerpX\nnproc               # expected: 1   → single-core (see root cause)\ncat /etc/os-release # Alpine Linux  → our pre-baked rust-alpine.ext2\nrustc --version     # the real toolchain doing the work\ntime cargo build -v # see the actual rustc + linker invocations + timing\n```\n\nConclusion: **the VM is real.** The problem is genuine compiler work\nrunning in a genuinely slow execution environment — which is precisely\nwhy it is worth optimizing, and why an optimization has to be validated\n*in that environment*, not just on native metrics.\n\n## Root-cause analysis — measured, not assumed\n\nThe prior analysis *guessed* that CPU-bound emulation of `rustc`/LLVM was\nthe dominant cost. **Measurement says otherwise.** Four experiments — the\nfirst three native+reproducible via\n[`experiments/issue-41/`](../../../experiments/issue-41/), the fourth\ntaken in the real VM by CI — together tell a story whose punchline\noverturns its own setup.\n\n### Measurement 1 — native wall-clock is emulation-invariant noise\n\n`measure.sh` runs the SAME one-line-edit rebuild on the SAME crate under\nevery profile configuration, natively on i386\n([`results/summary.md`](../../../experiments/issue-41/results/summary.md)):\n\n| scenario | cold | no-op | **rebuild** | check |\n|----------|------|-------|-------------|-------|\n| stock-default | 0.27s | 0.02s | **0.14s** | 0.08s |\n| shipped slow-knobs (`codegen-units=1`, `debug=0`, `incremental=0`) | 0.25s | 0.03s | **0.14s** | 0.08s |\n| incremental on | 0.26s | 0.03s | **0.15s** | 0.08s |\n| incremental + lld | 0.25s | 0.03s | **0.15s** | 0.08s |\n\n**Every config rebuilds in 0.14–0.27 s natively.** The knobs the prior\nwork tuned move the native number by *milliseconds*. So native CPU work\n**cannot** explain the 6-minute browser cost — something the emulation\nlayer multiplies does. That rules out the entire \"do less CPU codegen\"\nfamily as the lever and points at **per-syscall / per-process emulation\noverhead**.\n\n### Measurement 2 — the cost is filesystem syscalls over the overlay\n\n`measure-syscalls.sh` straces the same rebuild\n([`results/syscalls.md`](../../../experiments/issue-41/results/syscalls.md)):\n\n| command | process spawns (`execve`) | total syscalls | **filesystem syscalls** |\n|---------|---------------------------|----------------|-------------------------|\n| `cargo build` (one-line-edit rebuild) | 12 | 16,812 | **14,736** |\n| `cargo check` (same edit) | 5 | 1,645 | 1,029 |\n\nA *zero-dependency hello-world rebuild* issues **~14,700 filesystem\nsyscalls**. Natively those are free page-cache hits. Under CheerpX each\none crosses the WASM/JS boundary and hits the\n`OverlayDevice(cloud, IDBDevice)` IndexedDB layer — that boundary crossing,\nmultiplied ~14,700×, is the bulk of the 6 minutes. **The bottleneck is\nI/O, not CPU.** (The 24 s no-op is the same cost in miniature: cargo\n`stat()`-walks `target/` over the overlay to prove nothing changed.) This\nis also why `cargo check`, at **1,029** filesystem syscalls, is a genuine\nfast-feedback win (C1) — though it builds no binary, so it does not\nreplace `cargo run`.\n\n### Measurement 3 — the linker is the dominant syscall source (the `lld` hypothesis)\n\n`rustc -Z time-passes` shows `link_binary` is **0.049 s of 0.072 s total\n(68 %)** — the single largest compile phase, and it is filesystem-bound.\n`measure-linker.sh` then counts the rebuild's syscalls with GNU `ld` vs\n`lld` ([`results/linker.md`](../../../experiments/issue-41/results/linker.md)):\n\n| linker | process spawns | total syscalls | **filesystem syscalls** |\n|--------|----------------|----------------|-------------------------|\n| GNU `ld` (shipped default) | 12 | ~16,880 | **14,736** |\n| `lld` (`-C link-arg=-fuse-ld=lld`) | 12 | ~6,860 | **2,157** |\n\n**On native i386, switching the linker cuts filesystem syscalls by 85 %**\nwith the process count unchanged. GNU `ld` walks the libc archive with\nthousands of `_llseek`/`readv` calls; `lld` mmaps it. Because file\nsyscalls are exactly the cost CheerpX multiplies, **this looked like the\nsingle highest-leverage, no-hack fix** — and an earlier revision of this\nPR shipped it. The native numbers are real and reproduce deterministically.\n**They were also the wrong proxy.** Measurement 4 is why.\n\n### Measurement 4 — the decisive test: the real VM overturns the native proxy\n\nNative strace counts syscalls; it does **not** count what CheerpX pays to\n*execute the linker itself*. CheerpX x86→WASM-JITs guest code on first\nuse, and `lld` is a far larger binary than GNU `ld`. The only way to know\nthe net effect is to measure **in the real VM** — which is exactly what\nthe project's end-to-end CI does. `disk-image.yml` builds the ext2, boots\nit in a headless browser via CheerpX, and `local-pages-e2e.test.mjs`\nsubtest 2 edits `src/main.rs` and runs a **real** `cargo run` (Stage G,\ngated on the lean dev profile being present, with a 180 s ceiling).\n\nHolding everything else constant and changing **only** the linker:\n\n| disk build | linker | CI run | subtest 2 (real edited `cargo run`) | result |\n|------------|--------|--------|-------------------------------------|--------|\n| `b861a2f` (pre-swap) | GNU `ld` | [27462524216](https://github.com/link-foundation/rust-web-box/actions/runs/27462524216) | **58.5 s** (`duration_ms: 58458.9`) | ✅ `ok 2` |\n| `7c66bc7` | `lld` | [27467098552](https://github.com/link-foundation/rust-web-box/actions/runs/27467098552) | **221.3 s** (`duration_ms: 221306.5`) | ❌ `not ok 2` — timed out |\n| `766eece` (lld + guard fix) | `lld` | [27468491003](https://github.com/link-foundation/rust-web-box/actions/runs/27468491003) | **220.8 s** (`duration_ms: 220807.7`) | ❌ `not ok 2` — timed out |\n\n**The single variable across these three disk builds is the linker.**\nGNU `ld` passes at ~58 s; `lld` blows through the 180 s ceiling, twice,\non two independent commits. (221 s ≈ ~41 s of boot/earlier stages + the\n180 s Stage-G timeout.) So the native −85 % syscall win is **more than\nerased** in the VM by the cold-JIT cost of the bigger linker. The\nfilesystem-syscall count was a good *diagnosis* of where native time goes\nbut a **bad predictor of in-VM wall-clock**, because it omits CheerpX's\nper-binary translation cost entirely.\n\n**`lld` was therefore reverted** (commit `5fa7df3`); the disk keeps GNU\n`ld`. This is the case study's headline finding, and it is only knowable\nbecause the issue insisted the solution be validated on the *real* VM.\n\n### The meta-root-cause (unchanged, now quantified)\n\nSeveral speed knobs were turned the *slow* way on purpose to dodge the\nCheerpX `OverlayDevice` \"`a1`\" fresh-inode wedge (`CARGO_INCREMENTAL=0`\n#17; `codegen-units=1`, `debug=0` #31). Measurement 1 shows those cost\nalmost nothing natively — but they exist *because* of the overlay, and\n(per Measurement 4) they are already enough to get the real rebuild to\n~58 s. So the highest-leverage architectural move that *remains* is\n**getting build artifacts off the IndexedDB overlay** (S2): it makes the\nremaining syscalls fast *and* removes the wedge that forced the slow\nknobs, unblocking incremental (S3). Unlike `lld`, S2 reduces work CheerpX\nmust emulate rather than adding a large new binary for it to JIT.\n\n## How to measure it in the browser (the tracing we added)\n\nNative docker proves *where* the cost is in an emulation-invariant way,\nand CI's e2e proves the *net* in-VM effect. To let a maintainer take the\nsame numbers ad-hoc **in the browser on the real VM** — and to keep us\nhonest about future changes — this PR adds opt-in tracing to the WebVM\ncommand path (`web/glue/`), zero-overhead when off:\n\n- **`globalThis.__RWB_DEBUG_VM_TIMING = true`** — records wall-clock for\n  every `cx.run` the server issues (mirrors the existing\n  `__RWB_DEBUG_TERMINAL_STREAM` pattern). Read it back with the server\n  handle's `vmTimings.snapshot()`.\n- **`vm.benchCargo` bus method** (`web/glue/cargo-bench.js`) — runs the\n  user's **real** `cargo run` / `cargo build` / `cargo check` inside the\n  guest across four phases (no-op run, one-line-edit run, edit build, edit\n  check) plus an optional `rustc -Z time-passes` split, and ships per-phase\n  wall-clock back over the same OSC-frame stdout channel `workspace-sync`\n  uses. It only ever rewrites the existing `src/main.rs` inode and restores\n  the baseline, so it never allocates fresh inodes (no `a1` wedge) and never\n  touches the `target/`/fingerprint tree. `summarizeCargoBench` renders it\n  the way the issue reports it (e.g. `cargo run (one-line edit) 6m04.1s`).\n\nThis is the in-browser counterpart to the docker rig: same real commands,\nsame real VM, structured timing out. It is how a maintainer reproduces\nthe Measurement-4 result by hand and validates any future S2/S3 change on\nthe live disk, by numbers rather than vibes. (Had this tracing existed\nfirst, the `lld` regression would have shown up before CI did.)\n\n## Requirements (every one, enumerated)\n\nParsed verbatim from the issue body and the PR-review follow-up (\"explain\nin detail what we can actually do to speed up the *actual* build, without\nworkarounds or hacks; Ranked by *measured value today*.\n\nLegend — Impact/Effort/Risk: ⬤⬤⬤ high · ⬤⬤ medium · ⬤ low.\n\n### S1 — Lean dev profile + warm pre-bakes ✅ (shipped #17/#31, verified in-VM here)\n\n- **Maps to:** R1, R2, R3, R9, R10.\n- **Impact ⬤⬤⬤ · Effort ⬤ · Risk ⬤⬤ (must match the pre-bake fingerprint — handled).**\n- **Existing component:** Cargo profiles (`[profile.dev]`), Cargo's\n  freshness/mtime check, and a baked `target/` (debug *and* release).\n- **Why it is the real fix in place today:** Measurement 4 shows the\n  current disk — lean dev profile (`debug = 0`, `codegen-units = 1`,\n  `incremental = false`) plus a baked debug and release `target/` —\n  rebuilds an edited `cargo run` **in ~58 s in the real VM**, versus the\n  minutes the issue reported. It works by (a) not writing debug info and\n  not splitting into extra codegen units (less artifact IO over the\n  overlay) and (b) letting cargo's freshness check succeed against the\n  pre-baked artifacts without allocating fresh inodes (dodging the `a1`\n  wedge). It changes nothing the user runs.\n- **Why it is safe vs. the wedge:** the profile is baked **before** the\n  pre-bake `cargo build`, so the baked fingerprints already record it and\n  the first in-browser build stays a verified no-op. The e2e's\n  `hasLeanCargoDevProfile` gate asserts the baked\n  `/root/.cargo/config.toml` still carries `debug = 0` + `codegen-units = 1`\n  before it even runs the timed rebuild.\n- **Status:** shipped in #17/#31; this PR's contribution is to **prove it\n  in the real VM** (Measurement 4) and keep it as the load-bearing fix\n  after `lld` was rejected.\n\n### C1 — `cargo check` fast-feedback path ✅ NEW in this PR (complementary, **not** a `cargo run` speedup)\n\n- **Maps to:** R1, R2, R10; iteration-loop UX.\n- **Impact ⬤⬤ (error feedback) · Effort ⬤ · Risk ⬤.**\n- **Existing component:** Cargo's built-in `cargo check`.\n- **What it is:** `cargo check` skips codegen **and** linking, so it\n  surfaces compile errors in seconds (Measurement 2: **1,029** vs 14,736\n  filesystem syscalls). This PR **pre-bakes the check fingerprint** in the\n  disk image (so the first in-browser `cargo check` reuses inodes rather\n  than tripping the wedge) and surfaces it as a `cargo check (fast)` task\n  in the seeded `tasks.json` (with `rust-analyzer.checkOnSave` left off so\n  it does not fire the slow path on every keystroke).\n- **Why it is explicitly *not* the answer to \"make `cargo run` faster\":**\n  `cargo check` produces no binary, so you still pay the full build\n  whenever you actually want to *run* the program. It is a parallel\n  fast-feedback lever (rust-analyzer's check-on-save uses the same\n  command), which is why we ship it — but the fix to the *real build*\n  remains S1 (and the future S2/S3). Presenting `cargo check` as \"the\n  performance fix\" was the framing the PR review correctly rejected; it is\n  shipped here as a complement, not the headline.\n\n### S2 — Move `target/` off the IndexedDB overlay (in-memory build dir) — the big architectural win\n\n- **Maps to:** R1, R2, R3, R9.\n- **Impact ⬤⬤⬤ · Effort ⬤⬤⬤ · Risk ⬤⬤⬤.**\n- **Existing component:** CheerpX writable devices (`DataDevice`, the mount\n  topology in `web/glue/cheerpx-bridge.js`); Cargo's `CARGO_TARGET_DIR`.\n- **Why it is the highest-leverage *remaining* fix:** writing build\n  artifacts to `OverlayDevice(cloud, IDBDevice)` is *both* the slow-IO\n  source (every remaining artifact syscall still pays IndexedDB latency)\n  *and* the trigger for the `a1` fresh-inode wedge that forced\n  `CARGO_INCREMENTAL=0` + `codegen-units=1`. Put `target/` on an in-memory\n  writable mount and you (a) make artifact IO RAM-fast and (b) stop\n  allocating fragile overlay inodes — which unblocks **S3** (incremental).\n  Artifacts are regenerable, so losing them on reload is acceptable. Unlike\n  `lld`, this *removes* work from the emulation layer rather than adding a\n  large new binary for it to JIT.\n- **Open question / why prototyped not shipped:** CheerpX's documented\n  mount types are `ext2`, `dir` (Web/DataDevice), `devs`, `devpts`,\n  `proc`, `sys` (see `bootLinux` in `cheerpx-bridge.js`); whether a\n  *writable, full-tree, in-memory* mount usable for `target/` is exposed\n  needs an upstream check/experiment. If unavailable, file an upstream\n  request to `leaningtech/webvm`/CheerpX for a tmpfs/ramfs device.\n- **Plan:** experiment under `experiments/` to mount a writable in-memory\n  device at `/workspace/target` (or point `CARGO_TARGET_DIR` at one);\n  confirm the wedge no longer fires with `CARGO_INCREMENTAL=1`; measure the\n  rebuild with `vm.benchCargo` before/after; then ship S3.\n\n### S3 — Re-enable incremental compilation (depends on S2)\n\n- **Maps to:** R1, R2.\n- **Impact ⬤⬤⬤ (for one-line edits) · Effort ⬤ · Risk ⬤⬤⬤ until S2 lands.**\n- **Existing component:** Cargo's built-in incremental compilation.\n- **Why blocked today:** `CARGO_INCREMENTAL=0` exists because incremental\n  generates a flood of fresh inodes under `target/<profile>/incremental/`,\n  which trips the `a1` overlay wedge (#17). Incremental is *the* normal\n  accelerator for \"I changed one line\"; re-enabling it once S2 removes the\n  overlay is the natural pairing. Measurement 1 confirms incremental adds\n  no native penalty, so the only thing standing between us and it is the\n  overlay wedge.\n- **Plan:** after S2, flip `CARGO_INCREMENTAL=1` (env + `config.toml` +\n  the bench's `SHIPPED_BENCH_ENV`), re-bake, and validate with\n  `vm.benchCargo` that an edited `cargo run` drops to seconds.\n\n### S4 — Track CheerpX's own performance levers / upstream\n\n- **Maps to:** R3, R1.\n- **Impact ⬤⬤ (long-horizon) · Effort ⬤⬤⬤ · Risk ⬤⬤.**\n- **Existing component:** CheerpX itself (pinned 1.3.3 in\n  `cheerpx-bridge.js`). Its roadmap targets \"average application at most\n  5× slower than native\" by extending integer-pipeline optimizations to\n  FP/vector (online-research §1), and a persistent JIT/translation cache\n  would stop cold `rustc` re-paying interpretation cost every run — and\n  would also be what makes a bigger linker like `lld` viable (Measurement 4).\n- **Plan:** keep `CHEERPX_VERSION` current (#37 tracks this); adopt and\n  measure FP/vector JIT or a persistent translation cache when shipped;\n  file/track an upstream request for the in-memory writable device S2\n  needs and for a persistent JIT cache.\n\n### S5 — Cranelift debug codegen backend\n\n- **Maps to:** R1, R2, R10.\n- **Impact ⬤⬤ (20–30 % debug **codegen**) · Effort ⬤⬤⬤ · Risk ⬤⬤⬤.**\n- **Existing component:** `rustc_codegen_cranelift`. **Blocked here**\n  (online-research §4): nightly-only `rustup` component on **x86_64**\n  Linux; our guest is **i386** Alpine **stable** rust. And Measurement 1\n  shows codegen is the *minority* of the cost (IO dominates), so even if\n  unblocked the payoff is smaller than S1/S2. Park as research.\n\n### S6 — Run `rustc` as native WASM/WASI instead of x86-under-CheerpX\n\n- **Maps to:** R1, R3 (radical).\n- **Impact ⬤⬤⬤ (removes the emulation layer) · Effort ⬤⬤⬤ · Risk ⬤⬤⬤.**\n- **Existing component:** `wasm32-wasi` toolchain efforts. **Reality check\n  (online-research §6):** there is no supported, drop-in `wasm32-wasi` host\n  build of `rustc`+`cargo`+LLVM that runs a full edit-compile-run loop in\n  the browser today. Long-horizon research only; recorded for completeness.\n\n### S7 — Faster boot / cold-start (orthogonal to compile time)\n\n- **Maps to:** R1, R3.\n- **Impact ⬤⬤ (first-load UX) · Effort ⬤⬤ · Risk ⬤.**\n- **Existing component:** already substantial — `web/sw.js` caches\n  shell/glue, IDB overlay persists, disk ships as same-origin GitHubDevice\n  chunks, workspace renders before VM boot. Further wins: smaller ext2,\n  prefetch of disk chunks, HTTP caching headers. Does not touch the\n  6-minute rebuild; tracked for completeness.\n\n### Rejected after measurement — link with `lld`\n\n- **Maps to:** R1, R2, R10, R12 (the measured-rejection requirement).\n- **Verdict:** ❌ **investigated, measured on native i386 *and* in the real\n  VM, and reverted.**\n- **Existing component:** `lld`, the LLVM linker (Alpine `lld` package),\n  driven through gcc with `-C link-arg=-fuse-ld=lld`.\n- **Why it looked like the fix:** the link step is 68 % of compile and is\n  the dominant filesystem-syscall source (Measurement 3); `lld` mmaps the\n  libc archive instead of seeking through it, cutting the rebuild's native\n  filesystem syscalls **14,736 → 2,157 (−85 %)** — precisely the cost\n  CheerpX multiplies. An earlier revision of this PR shipped it on that\n  basis.\n- **Why it was rejected:** Measurement 4. In the real CheerpX VM the\n  edited `cargo run` **regressed from ~58 s to a >180 s timeout** across\n  two independent commits, because CheerpX must x86→WASM-JIT the much\n  larger LLVM linker on first use and that cold-JIT cost dwarfs the syscall\n  saving. The native syscall count was the wrong proxy for in-VM\n  wall-clock. Reverted in `5fa7df3`; the disk keeps GNU `ld`.\n- **When to revisit:** if S4 lands a persistent CheerpX JIT/translation\n  cache (so the linker is JIT-compiled once and reused), or if a *smaller*\n  fast linker that emulates cheaply (e.g. `mold`/`wild`, subject to musl\n  i386 support) becomes available, re-run Measurement 4 before adopting.\n- **Lesson:** validate every optimization on the **real VM**, not on a\n  native proxy. This is the concrete payoff of the issue's \"is it fake?\"\n  requirement.\n\n## What this PR ships vs. proposes (honesty statement)\n\n**Shipped & verified here:**\n\n- **The in-VM tracing** the review asked for: `vm.benchCargo` (real\n  `cargo run`/`build`/`check` timing over the real `cx.run` path) and\n  `__RWB_DEBUG_VM_TIMING` (per-`cx.run` wall-clock), with unit +\n  integration tests.\n- **The `cargo check` fast-feedback path** (C1): pre-baked check\n  fingerprint in the disk image + a `cargo check (fast)` task. New here;\n  complements `cargo run`, does not replace it.\n- **In-VM verification of the existing lean dev profile + pre-bakes** (S1,\n  from #17/#31) as the load-bearing reason the real rebuild is ~58 s — via\n  the e2e (Measurement 4), which now also guards against regressions.\n- **The measurement rig** (`experiments/issue-41/`) behind every number,\n  including `results/in-vm-ab.md` for the decisive A/B.\n- The case study (R4–R8), cited research (R7), and the full ranked plan\n  (R1, R9, R10, R12) — including the **honest, measured rejection of\n  `lld`**.\n\n**Investigated and rejected (not shipped):** the `lld` linker swap — a\n−85 % *native* syscall win that *regressed* the real in-VM rebuild\n(58 s → >180 s timeout). VS Code's\n  Pseudoterminal API (xterm.js underneath) requires `\\r\\n` — without the\n  carriage return the cursor only moved down, not back to column 0,\n  producing the visible staircase in the previous boot screenshots.\n  `web/glue/webvm-server.js` now runs every stdout chunk through\n  `createLfToCrlfNormaliser()` from `web/glue/terminal-stream.js` before\n  broadcasting `proc.stdout`. The normaliser is stateful so a chunk\n  boundary that splits an existing `\\r\\n` (CheerpX delivers `foo\\r` in\n  one chunk, `\\nbar` in the next) does not produce `\\r\\r\\n`. Existing\n  CRLF passes through unchanged; bare `\\r` (cargo's progress meter) is\n  preserved.\n\n### Added\n- `web/glue/terminal-stream.js` with `createLfToCrlfNormaliser()` and\n  the one-shot `lfToCrlf()` convenience used by the page-side WebVM\n  server.\n- `web/tests/terminal-stream.test.mjs` — eight unit tests covering\n  every newline shape (lone LF, CRLF, bare CR, ANSI control sequences,\n  empty input, the exact `ls -la /workspace` repro from the screenshot,\n  and chunk boundaries split mid-CRLF).\n- `web/tests/webvm-server.test.mjs` — four integration tests with a\n  fake CheerpX handle, asserting that stdout written by the engine is\n  normalised on the wire, vt != 1 channels are still filtered, and the\n  in-memory bus transport stays sane.\n\n### Changed\n- `web/glue/webvm-server.js` now uses a streaming `TextDecoder`\n  (`stream: true`) for stdout, so multi-byte UTF-8 split across CheerpX\n  writes no longer decodes to U+FFFD before reaching the terminal.\n--- changelog.d/20260429_171849_issue_3_pages_deploy_fix.md ---\n---\nbump: patch\n---\n\n### Fixed\n- GitHub Pages deploy at `/rust-web-box/` rendered an empty workbench:\n  no terminal, no files, no VM status (issue #3). Existing untouched workspaces are migrated to the `tasks.json` that includes the `cargo check (fast)` task.\n\n### Investigated, not shipped\n\n- **Linking with `lld` instead of GNU `ld` was tried and reverted (issue #41).** On the i386 Alpine toolchain the disk ships, a one-line-edit rebuild issues ~85 % fewer filesystem syscalls with `lld` (≈14,700 → ≈2,150), which looked like the fix for the slow `cargo run`. But the project's own in-VM e2e proved the opposite: with `lld` the real edited `cargo run` went from ~58 s to a >180 s timeout, because CheerpX must x86→WASM-JIT the much larger LLVM linker on first use and that cold-JIT cost dwarfs the syscall saving. Native syscall count was the wrong proxy for in-VM wall-clock. The disk keeps GNU `ld`; the load-bearing speedup remains the lean dev profile + warm pre-bakes (issues #17/#31). Full evidence in `docs/case-studies/issue-41/`.\n",

Can we do it maximum multithreaded?\"\n+\n+**What is already multi-context (cited):** the app is *already*\n+js + wasm + web-workers + `SharedArrayBuffer`:\n+\n+- **CheerpX (wasm)** runs on the page/main thread and owns the\n+  `SharedArrayBuffer` (`web/glue/webvm-server.js:3-7`).\n+- The **VS Code extension host** runs in a dedicated **Web Worker** — no\n+  DOM, no SAB — talking to the page over a same-origin BroadcastChannel\n+  (`web/glue/webvm-bus.js:1-12`, `web/extensions/webvm-host/extension.js:1-20`).\n+- **Cross-origin isolation** (the prerequisite for SAB) is synthesized by a\n+  service worker: `Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin` +\n+  `Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy: require-corp` (`web/sw.js:63`, `:69`;\n+  rationale in `web/glue/coi-bootstrap.js`). So the UI is *already* off the\n+  VM thread — typing and scrolling stay responsive while a build runs.\n+\n+**The honest limit — the guest VM is single-core.** `CheerpX.Linux.create`\n+is given mount config only; there is **no SMP / `nproc` option**\n+(`web/glue/cheerpx-bridge.js:324`), and CheerpX 1.3.x JITs x86→WASM in a\n+**single execution context**. `nproc` inside the guest returns `1` (the\n+bench captures it: `web/glue/cargo-bench.js:105`). Therefore:\n+\n+- `cargo -j4` / parallel codegen / `-Zthreads=N` **cannot fan out** —\n+  there is one core. The disk deliberately ships `codegen-units = 1` and\n+  `incremental = false` (`web/disk/Dockerfile.disk:148`); raising the job\n+  count buys nothing and only risks the fresh-inode wedge (#17).\n+- More Web Workers **cannot** speed the compile either: the bottleneck\n+  [Measurement 2](#measurement-2--the-cost-is-filesystem-syscalls-over-the-overlay)\n+  isolates is **serial filesystem-syscall IO over IndexedDB**, not\n+  parallelizable CPU. You can move *other* work off the VM thread (already\n+  done), but you cannot split one `rustc` invocation across cores that do\n+  not exist.\n+\n+**Verdict:** \"maximum multithreaded\" is the right instinct for a native\n+multi-core box and the wrong lever here. The win is not *more threads* but\n+**less per-syscall IO** ([S2](#s2--move-target-off-the-indexeddb-overlay-in-memory-build-dir--the-big-architectural-win),\n+RAM-backed `target/`) and **a faster engine**\n+([S4](#s4--track-cheerpxs-own-performance-levers--upstream), tracking\n+CheerpX's JIT/threading upstream). The A/B knobs that *prove* extra jobs\n+don't help on a single core are wired into the bench as the `jobs1` vs\n+`jobs4` configs, runnable on demand (F3).\n+\n+### F3 — \"Keep all benchmarks runnable on demand (CI manual dispatch), usable via the gh tool, to reduce load on your machine.\"\n+\n+Shipped: **`.github/workflows/perf-bench.yml`** — `workflow_dispatch`\n+**only** (no push / PR / schedule trigger). This PR's e2e (the table above) is what verifies that number on the real VM and guards it against regression.\\n\\n## What this PR ships (net)\\n\\n- **In-VM tracing.** `vm.benchCargo` (`web/glue/cargo-bench.js`) runs the user's **real** `cargo run` / `cargo build` / `cargo check` across four phases (no-op run, one-line-edit run, edit build, edit check) plus an optional `rustc -Z time-passes` split, and ships per-phase wall-clock over the existing OSC-frame stdout channel. It only rewrites the existing `src/main.rs` inode and restores the baseline (never touches `target/`), reuses the real `cx.run` path, and is zero-overhead when off. `globalThis.__RWB_DEBUG_VM_TIMING` records per-`cx.run` wall-clock. *Measures* the build; does not replace it.\\n- **A `cargo check` fast-feedback path** (NEW): the warm disk pre-bakes `cargo check` and the seeded `tasks.json` offers a `cargo check (fast)` task. `cargo check` skips codegen and linking (**1,029** vs 14,736 filesystem syscalls), so errors surface in seconds. It speeds up the edit→error loop — *not* `cargo run` itself.\\n- **A measurement-driven case study** in `docs/case-studies/issue-41/`, backed by the `experiments/issue-41/` docker rig: the syscall/linker census, the front-end/codegen/link split, the anti-fake VM verification, the in-VM A/B above, and a ranked catalogue of every improvement option (incl. the rejected `lld`).\\n\\n## The bigger win, specified as the next step\\n\\n**S2 — move `target/` off the IndexedDB overlay** (in-memory mount): makes the remaining syscalls RAM-fast *and* removes the `a1` fresh-inode wedge that forced `incremental = false`/`codegen-units = 1`, which unblocks **S3 — re-enabling incremental compilation**. `vm.benchCargo` now makes the in-browser before/after measurable. Its cold-JIT cost more than erases the −85 % syscall saving — net **+160 s or worse** on the real rebuild (it hit the 180 s ceiling and was killed, twice). **Native syscall count was the wrong proxy for in-VM wall-clock.** Full write-up: [`experiments/issue-41/results/in-vm-ab.md`](https://github.com/link-foundation/rust-web-box/blob/issue-41-81a2dcc93013/experiments/issue-41/results/in-vm-ab.md).\\n\\n## The load-bearing speedup (already shipped in #17/#31, verified in-VM here)\\n\\nThe real `cargo run` rebuild is at **~58 s** in-VM thanks to the **lean dev profile** (`debug = 0`, `codegen-units = 1`, `incremental = false`) plus **warm pre-bakes** (debug *and* release `target/`), which let cargo's freshness check finish without re-allocating fragile CheerpX overlay inodes. This PR's e2e (the table above) is what verifies that number on the real VM and guards it against regression.\\n\\n## What this PR ships (net)\\n\\n- **In-VM tracing.** `vm.benchCargo` (`web/glue/cargo-bench.js`) runs the user's **real** `cargo run` / `cargo build` / `cargo check` across four phases (no-op run, one-line-edit run, edit build, edit check) plus an optional `rustc -Z time-passes` split, and ships per-phase wall-clock over the existing OSC-frame stdout channel. It only rewrites the existing `src/main.rs` inode and restores the baseline (never touches `target/`), reuses the real `cx.run` path, and is zero-overhead when off. `globalThis.__RWB_DEBUG_VM_TIMING` records per-`cx.run` wall-clock. *Measures* the build; does not replace it.\\n- **A `cargo check` fast-feedback path** (NEW): the warm disk pre-bakes `cargo check` and the seeded `tasks.json` offers a `cargo check (fast)` task. `cargo check` skips codegen and linking (**1,029** vs 14,736 filesystem syscalls), so errors surface in seconds. It speeds up the edit→error loop — *not* `cargo run` itself.\\n- **A measurement-driven case study** in `docs/case-studies/issue-41/`, backed by the `experiments/issue-41/` docker rig: the syscall/linker census, the front-end/codegen/link split, the anti-fake VM verification, the in-VM A/B above, and a ranked catalogue of every improvement option (incl. the rejected `lld`).\\n\\n## The bigger win, specified as the next step\\n\\n**S2 — move `target/` off the IndexedDB overlay** (in-memory mount): makes the remaining syscalls RAM-fast *and* removes the `a1` fresh-inode wedge that forced `incremental = false`/`codegen-units = 1`, which unblocks **S3 — re-enabling incremental compilation**. `vm.benchCargo` now makes the in-browser before/after measurable. Full ranked catalogue in the case study.\\n\\n## Files\\n\\n- **Tracing:** `web/glue/cargo-bench.js` (new) + `web/glue/webvm-server.js`; tests in `web/tests/cargo-bench.tes",

This PR's e2e (the table above) is what verifies that number on the real VM and guards it against regression.\n35\t\n36\t## What this PR ships (net)\n37\t\n38\t- **In-VM tracing.** `vm.benchCargo` (`web/glue/cargo-bench.js`) runs the user's **real** `cargo run` / `cargo build` / `cargo check` across four phases (no-op run, one-line-edit run, edit build, edit check) plus an optional `rustc -Z time-passes` split, and ships per-phase wall-clock over the existing OSC-frame stdout channel. It only rewrites the existing `src/main.rs` inode and restores the baseline (never touches `target/`), reuses the real `cx.run` path, and is zero-overhead when off. `globalThis.__RWB_DEBUG_VM_TIMING` records per-`cx.run` wall-clock. *Measures* the build; does not replace it.\n39\t- **A `cargo check` fast-feedback path** (NEW): the warm disk pre-bakes `cargo check` and the seeded `tasks.json` offers a `cargo check (fast)` task. `cargo check` skips codegen and linking (**1,029** vs 14,736 filesystem syscalls), so errors surface in seconds. It speeds up the edit→error loop — *not* `cargo run` itself.\n40\t- **A measurement-driven case study** in `docs/case-studies/issue-41/`, backed by the `experiments/issue-41/` docker rig: the syscall/linker census, the front-end/codegen/link split, the anti-fake VM verification, the in-VM A/B above, and a ranked catalogue of every improvement option (incl. the rejected `lld`).\n41\t\n42\t## The bigger win, specified as the next step\n43\t\n44\t**S2 — move `target/` off the IndexedDB overlay** (in-memory mount): makes the remaining syscalls RAM-fast *and* removes the `a1` fresh-inode wedge that forced `incremental = false`/`codegen-units = 1`, which unblocks **S3 — re-enabling incremental compilation**. `vm.benchCargo` now makes the in-browser before/after measurable. Full ranked catalogue in the case study.\n45\t\n46\t## Files\n47\t\n48\t- **Tracing:** `web/glue/cargo-bench.js` (new) + `web/glue/webvm-server.js`; tests in `web/tests/cargo-bench.test.mjs` and `web/tests/webvm-server.test.mjs`.\n49\t- **`cargo check` path + e2e guard:** `web/disk/Dockerfile.disk` (pre-bake + `tasks.json`), `.github/workflows/disk-image.yml` (smoke test + e2e), `web/tests/e2e/local-pages-e2e.test.mjs`.\n50\t- **Evidence:** `experiments/issue-41/` (docker rig + `results/`, incl. `in-vm-ab.md`), `docs/case-studies/issue-41/README.md`.\n51\t- **Note:** `web/disk/Dockerfile.disk` keeps **GNU `ld`** — the `lld` change was reverted in `5fa7df3`.\n52\t\n53\t## Verification\n54\t\n55\t- `node --test web/tests/*.test.mjs` → **272 pass / 0 fail**\n56\t- `cargo fmt --all --check` → clean; `cargo clippy --all-targets --all-features` → clean; `cargo test --all-features` → **19 pass / 0 fail**; `cargo test --doc` → clean\n57\t- **In-VM, on the real VM:** disk-build run [27468794132](https://github.com/link-foundation/rust-web-box/actions/runs/27468794132) (`5fa7df3`) is green — e2e subtest 2 reaches and passes Stage G's edited `cargo run` at **~64 s** (`# tests 4 / # pass 4 / # fail 0`), well under the 180 s ceiling.\n58\t- Reproduce the measurements: `cd experiments/issue-41 && docker build -f Dockerfile.measure -t rwb-issue41-measure . && docker run --rm -v \"$PWD/results:/out\" rwb-issue41-measure /measure-linker.sh`\n59\t\n60\t"
